gOttrg• PRESENTMENTS OF TFIE PAST. I, with eyelids closed, behold At times, imperfectly, as if a mist Had drawn itself across, at times most clear, These dear presentments of the past. The scene, The hour, I first confronted face to face The moitterable wonder of the sea; The birth of day, when snowy mountain peaks Were drench'd with glory by the climbing sun; A rose-clad cottage, sloping into shade Of apple-boughs ; a green path through a wood, With burning gold of broom on either hand; Night on an English river, meadows dark, Whose willows, drooping low with sorrowing leaves, At sound of sweet, sad music trembling near, Wept tears of moonlight in the sleepin,vtream. Solext and Danube.

RIVAL FLOWERS. Three winsome maidens, light-hearted and gay, Sat deep in the shade of the woodlands one ; Behind them the roses lit up the green gloom About them the heather Just flusbed into bloom. Said Mary to Jessie, "My rose is more sweet Than all the bright blossoms that grow at our feet; Your heather and bluebells more gaudy may be, But here's the wild rose of old England for me." "Nay," answered sweet Jessie, "I think, for my part, The heather and bluebells are nearer my heart, And here's the tall thistle—my own Scottish flower— Most honoured of all is its place in my bower." Then Norah looked up from her needle and said, "Come, pluck me a shamrock from yon grassy bed; There's nought with its beauty and grace to compare, And Erin's green badge is the onel will wear." The shamrock was found, and the maidens confessed! That, twined with each other, each flower looked its best. And Mary laughed out, in her light-hearted glee— , "Not rivals, but friends, are our emblems,' said she. "So give me the flowers, we are all of one mind— In badges for each they shall all be entwined. Rase, shamrock and thistle united, I ween, Will make a boquet that is fit for the queen." —Helen ..11-arion Burnside in the Girl's Own Paper.

Van Daub: 'You are criticising this picture a good deal. Did you ever draw one?" O'Sullivan: "Oh, yes!" Van Daub: "And pray where?" O'Sullivan: "In a raffle, my boy ?" Texas cow-boy, who has heard that a northern man has arrived in town with a bicycle, but thinks that it is ashooting weapon of some sort: "What may be the size of your bicycle, stranger ? " Bicyclist: "It is a fifty-six." Cow-boy: A fifty-six shooter! _Gewhillikins, you can be mayor of this town if you say so!" The butler of a certain Scotisli laird, who had been in the family for several years, at last resigned his situation, because his Lordship's wife was always scolding him. " Oh !" exclaimed his master, "if that be all, ye've very little to complain of." "Perhaps so," replied the butler; " but I have decided in my own mind to put up with it no longer." "G.:5 then," said his Lordsnip, ' and be thankful for the rest of your life that you are not married to her." THE IMPORTANCE OF PCNCTUALITY.—Method is the very hinge of bu.siness, and there is no method without punctuality. Punctuality is important because it sub- serves the peace and good temper of a family. Calmness of mind, which it produces, is another advantage of punctuality. A disorderly man is always in a hurry, he has no time to speak to you because he is going else- where, and when he gets there, be is too late for his busi- ness, or he must hurry away before he can finish it. Punctuality gives weight to character. SELF-DENIAL.—Few things can so speedily ruin an individual or corrupt a natioa as an unrestrained self- indulgence. When pleasure or ease comes to be the supreme motive, decay begins. This must ever be the case with imperfect and improvable beings. They can- not for ever sail with fair winds on placid seas; they must display energy, effort, striving, and occasionally make sacrifice. They must at times give up something to gain something better; they must lay down what is of less value before they can take up what is of more value. Would a man have sound health? He must sacrifice to a certain extent his desire for indulgence or

his craving for gain or fame. Would he attain eicellence in his work ? He must resign a life of easy leisure. Would he he virtuous? He must resist :temptation Would he live for others? He must leave off living only for himself. Curiae Wives.—lt has been said, and said truly, that the test of a man's regard for a woman is his willingness to give her his time, his society. Money he may bestow from lavishness or a sense of duty; seemly attentions he may bestow from courtly habits of attention; but when a man deliberately cultivates his wife's society, then all is right between them. It may be that there is much nonsense talked about women being educated to be the companions of their husbands. Men do not want argu- ment and clever discussion in their home lives; their combativeness is sufficiently exercised in the world's more public arena. What they want is goodness to which they can look up; sufficient culture to make the eye bright and the thought swift; a "mother wit" that is sometimes crushed and withered by overmuch book- learning, but which, allowed fair play, often developes in mature years to true wisdom; and warm affections, that out of their great storehouse can generally furnish ex- cuses for man's putulance and caprice—affections which show the beauty of constancy by bright example, and lead women to yield without murmuring on the frequent occasions when one or the other must bend.—From "Hubert Freeth's Prosperity." MR. RUSKIN'S IltONY.—That Mr. Ruskin was not desti- tute of irony may be seen in the following passage also from "Modern Painters," entitled The False Ideal of Landscape.—The Mill by Claude." The foreground is a piece of very lovely and perfect forest scenery, with a dance of peasants by a brook side; quite enough subject to form, in the hands of a master, an impressive and com- plete picture. On the other side of the brook, however, we have a piece of pastoral life; a man with some bulls and goats tumbling head foremost into the water, owing to some sudden paralytic affection of all their legs. Even this group is one too many; the shepherd had no business to drive his flock go near the dancers, and the dancers will certainly frighten the cattle. But when we look farther into the picture our feelings receive a sudden and violent sceack by the unexpected appearance, amidst things pas- toral and musical, of the military; a number of Roman soldiers riding in on hobby-horses, with a leader on foot, apparently encouraging them to make an immediate and decisive charge on the musicians. Beyond the soldiers is a !circular temple, in exceedingly bad repair; and close beside it, built against its very walls, a neat watermill in full work. By the mill flows alarge river with a weir all across it. The weir has not been made for the mill (for that receives its water from the hills by a trough carried over the temple), but it is particularly ugly and monotonous in its line of fall, and the water below forms a dead-looking pond, on which some people are fishing in punts. The banks of this river resemble in contour the later geological forma- tions around London, constituted chiefly of broken pots and oyster-shells. At an inconvenient distance from the waterside stands a city, composed of twenty-five round towers and a pyramid. Beyond the city is a handsome bridge; beyond the bridge, part of the Campagna, with fragments of aqueducts ; beyond the Campagna, the chain of the Alps; on the left, the cascades of Tivoli. A FINNISH PEASANT'S COURTSIIIP AND WEDDING.—A Finnish peasant when in love does not declare his affec- tion—save with his eyes, possibly, which are apt to speak volumes on such occasions. He entrusts his •sacret to some old dame, a mutual friend, who forthwith seeks out his inamorata and says to her all she can in favour of his suit, at the same titrfe tendering somepre- s-mt from him. Should the girl decline this the disap- pointed match-maker has the melancholy task of break- lag. the sad news to the woc-begone lover. If happier in her mission the loving pair are quickly betrothed, when a series of congratulations set in. The bride and bridegroom -elect are waited upon by their friends upon an early day after their engagement is made known, and they are to be congratulated again upon the occasion of the first as veAl as the last time of "asking" in church, for the banns must be published for rich and poor alike. The wedding invariably takes place in the same week in which they have been "asked" for the last time. The poorer class, whose house accommodation consists of one or, at most, two rooms, are married in the church, but the better-to-do have the ceremony performed at their own homes about -seven o'clock in the evening. A small square of carpet is laid upon the floor and cushions placed on this for the , happy couple to kneel upon. The " marskalkar " (best ' men) stand at each corner of the squaae holding lighted tapers during the ceremony, which is concluded by an ea.thertation from the priest, and congratulations and kisies all round. The party then eat, drink, smoke, and !I ince far into the night, and for several following even- ings. This for a peaiant would be a seriously expensiveaffair were it not that every guest leaves a,money con- tribution according to his or her means. Frequently as much as 600 marks, or £24, is subscribed on such occa- sions. Amongst the richer class the wedding arrange- ments are really costly affairs, the dais for the kneeling pairbeing of. the richest material, and the groomsme hearing massive silver ca.redelabra. The bride- is always dressed in pure white, with a long flowing veil and wreath of natural flowers. Four bridesmaids, also in white, wear armlets of natural flowers, as do the grooms- men favours Of the same on their coats. After the cere- mony itself, the supper is the great event of the evening, standing in place of our wedding breakfast. Served up at twelve o'clock, it is a really magnificent repast, the tables " groaning " under the weight. of a most varied collection of eatables and drinks.—Lezeure Hour. Public Analysts have submitted CADDUEr'S 4JOcOA to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imttatuins.— Advt.

The n-,ble silent men scattered here and there whom no morning newspaper makes mention of! They:are the salt of the earth. A country that has none or few of these is in a bad way; a forest that has no roots, all turned into leaves and boughs, which must wither and be no forest. "Now, sir, I hope we shall have no difficulty in getting you to speak up!" said a Boston attorney, in a very loud commanding voice. "I hope not, sir!" shouted the witness at the top of his lungs. "How dare you speak to me in that way?" "I can't speak no louder!" screamed the witness. " Have you been drinking?" "Yes, sir!" "I should infer so "—fiercely—" from your conduct. What have you been drinking?" " Corfee, sir!" hoarsely vociferated the witness. - "Something besides coffee, sir, you've been using! Don't look at me like that, sir !"—furiously—" look at the jury, sir! Did you have something in your coffee, sir?" "Yes, sir ! " "'What was it?" " Sugar !" "This man is no fool, your Honour—he is worse!" stormed: the counsel. "Now, sirrah"—turnine• to the witness—" look at me! What besides sugar did you take in your coffee this morning ? " The witness collected his forces, drew a deep breath, and, in a voice that could have been heard half a mile away, bellowed out, "A spune—a spune, and nothing else, sir" A FRENCHMAN'S .INGENUITY.—It is related of General Manteuffel, the late German Military Governor of Alsace, who hated all that was French, that he once at a public dinner engaged in a dispute with a French diplomat who maintained the superiority of the French workmen over the artisans of all other nations. "A thing so ugly does not exist that the skill and genius of a Frenchman can- not make of it a thing of beauty," he said. lAngered by the contradiction, the old solder pulled a hair from his ' bristly grey moustache, and, handing it to the French- man, said curtly, "Let him make a thing of beauty out of that then, and prove your claim." The Frenchman took the hair and sent in a letter to a well-known Parisian jeweller, with a statement of the case and an appeal to his patriotic pride, giving him no limit of ex- pense in executing the order. A week later the mail from Paris brought a neat little box for the general. In it was a handsome scarfpin made like a Prussian eagle, that held in its talons a stiff grey bristle, froth either end of which dangled a tiny golden ball. One was inscribed I Alsace, and the other Lorraine, and on the eagle's perch [were the words, "You hold them but by a hair." Tern WOODEN SENTINEL.—It is often a matter of won- der when we find what serious importance has been at- tached to mere forms and ceremonies, even when sepa- rated from everything that gives them meaning. Thus, in 1806, when the French were in Naples, and the Bour- bon court had fled into Sicily, a superannuated princess of that, royal house, of illegitimate birth, half-sister to the old King Ferdinand, was left behind uncared for. The new King, Joseph Bonaparte, provided her with a small income, but made her utterly wretched by refusing to continue the sentinel who had always mounted guard at her door. Over and over agaiia she petitioned and passionately pleaded for this nrivileoe, the want of which was breaking her heart and injuring her health to a really serious extent ; when someone proposed a wooden figure in a soldier's uniform, musket and all complete, to be mounted as guard at the inner door of her old house at Portici. The idea was adopted, and actually restored the old lady to health and cheerfulness, until the effect of passing it repeatedly without receiving the usual salute began to prey upon her mind, when she fell ill and soon after died. Ten years after travellers saw the wooden figure still standing sentinel by the outer door of the apartments she had occupied.—From "The World of Wanders." SECRET CHABERS IN SOME ANCIMENT HOUSES.—Plow- den Hall, county of Salop, with " gable ends, high chim- neys, its floors, staircases, and doors of solid oak, and walls covered with oak panelling," is described as being full of nooks and corners. There is a hiding hole in the closet of one of the bedrooms, where the boards of the flooring are so arranged as to be easily moved; and underneath is a trap-door, by which a small ladder leads down into a dark hole, where there is just room enough for a man to change his position with ease from a stand- ing to a sitting posture. There is a shelf, on which the concealed person could eat his food. Tradition states that a priest was actually concealed there fora fortnight whilst Cromwell's soldiers were posted outside the gates; and that these were obliged to leave without having dis- covered him. Besides this hiding place, there is an es- cape about the width and form of a chimney, reaching from one of the bedrooms down to the ground floor of the house, to which a man might be lowered by means of a. rope. There is also an outlet over the chapel through two trap-doors on to the roof, where a person might escape between the eaves of the house; and a portion of the flooring of the chapel is so formed as to lift up and cover a hiding place below for concealing the sacred vessels. Recusants and priests found refuge in Little Malvern Court in nee days of their persecution, the position of one or two hiding-places in the roof being still pointed out. A secret chamber in Lowstock Hall, in the parish of Bolton, Lancashire, which was pulled down in 1816, was associated with blood-stains on the hearth-stone of one of the rooms, and the supposed murder of a priest in the troubous times. In connection with Yorkshire, the old Red House is made mention of as having had a secret chamber and gallery underneath the roof. These were brought to light some years ago when workmen were employed in making repairs and alterations on the mansion. The noted royalist, Sir Henry Slingsbv, lay for a time concealed in the hiding-place thus skilfully contrived; but venturing forth one moonlight night to enjoy the freedom of a walk in his garden, he was seen by a man-servant, Iwho betrayed him to his enemies ; and soon after the gallant old colonel was seized, conveyed to London, and beheaded on Tower Hill. Kingerby Old Hall, situated in the same county, was also possessed of one or more secret chambers. Ashbourne Place, in Sussex, which was said to have been built by a brother of Bishop Juxon, was often made use of as a place of refuge by that persecuted prelate after the death of Charles I. At the time when his royal master was be- headed, Juxon was Bishop of London and Clerk of the Closet; and being implicitly trusted by his royal master, to whom he was devotedly attached, he received his last confidences on the scaffold, and his George, with the oft- referred-to word, "Remember !" The father of the pre- sent proprietor of Ashbourne, in opening a communica- tion between the back and front chambers, dis- covered a room, the existence of which was previously unknown, and to which access could only have been gained through the chimney-. In all probability, this curious retreat was Bishop Juxon's hiding-place. There is a gallery situated in the attic storey of the mansion at Stanford Court, in Worcestershire,-in which Arthur Salvin—an ancestor of the present proprietor of the estate, who lived in the reigns of Elizabeth and James I.—and his four sons and seven daughters, together with others of their kindred, are pourtrayed on the oak-pannelled walls ef the room as the costume of the day; the ladies in embroidered dresses, with jewelled ornaments. Underneath each fignre is a motto in Latin. Behind the panels are secret passages, which, previous to the alterations of modern times, extended over a great part of the mansion. Sanston Hall, the seat of the ancient family of Huddlestone, in Cambridgeshire was destroyed on account of the owner's adherence to the 'ancient faith, and rebuilt in the time of Queen Mary, when the precaution was taken to erect a chapel in the roof. It is approached by a winding staircase, which also gives access to a secret chamber. In the hiding place near the chapel in the roof at the top of,the old winding staircase, there were found some oyster-shells; and a fowl's bone were picked up in the one belonging to Lvdiate Hall—relics of some poor prisoner's solitary meat —Chambers's Journal.

An exchange says :—" No one is entitled to eat bread who is not capable of _producing it or its equivalent."

That is tough on the politician. - It is estimated that the value of the wheat crop in California this year will be nearly double that of last year, ; when it was worth £5,800,000. The yield of barley is _ _ .

placed at £3,200,000, against £1,800,000 last year. - • :NEW PHASE OF THE LAND QUESTION.—A gentleman\ who is agent for extensive estates in Sligo, Ireland, was surprised within the last few days by many of the tenants paying him not only the rent due last May, but the "gale" which fell due last month. He reminded them! that it was the custom of the estate to allow it to stand over,,but they replied that as they had the money they might as well clear off the debt, only asking that he would not visit them until this time 12 months. Of the others almost all paid a considerable portion of the rent I due, and asked him to wait for the rest till they had dis- posed of their crops. In no case was any abatement. asked for. How BurrERINE CAN BE DISGUISED.—AnI Australian paper has the following The perfectness to which! the manufacture of butterine has been brought was I made manifest in Romsey last week, when several good judges of dairy produce, having been asked to select the butter from two prints—one genuine and the other but- terine—all made the mistake of picking the imitation article and pronouncing it excellent butter.'" There is no doubt that prejudice would prevent butterine from becoming popular, but how are consumers tolkno-w when they are eating it if experts cannot distinguish it from butter? It is evident that legislation is required on the

subject. ALLEGED LANDLORD INTOLERANCE.—It is reported that a crofter in onelof the South Isles was recently engaged in getting signitures to a petition to the Crofiers''Com- mission, asking that a certain parish should be declared a crofting one within the meaning of the Act. The re- port goes on to say that the landlord somehow got a hint of this, and went to a large tenant, who had engaged the services of the crofter for the harvest, and told him he would not allow him to employ that man. It is also said that the crofter had had the privilege of grazing a few cattle on a hill in the vicinity, and that the landlord has prohibited him from doing this in future. CREAM BY PARCEL POST.—Allow me to suggest that farmers should send cream by parcel post. Tin bottles to hold a quart or a pint would only weigh from 4oz. to 60z., made of thin tin and could be made very cheap, so that a quart would not weigh when full quite 31b., and would go by post for 6d., and a pint by post for 4-d. Now, a quart of cream in London costs ss.—a ridiculous price,—but if supplied to families at 25., post paid, there are many thousands of families who would use large quantities of cream at that price. Allow 2d. for the bottle and 6d. for postage, that would leave the farmer is. 4d. net for a quart of cream, which is quite as much as he could get out of it if made into butter. A separator would enable the farmer to send off his cream "fresh" every day, and he would have " fresh " separated milk to feed his calves on. A bottle filled quite full of cream, then corked, and the cork fastened down 'with wire like soda water, would travel perfectly safely, and the cream would keep good for many days. If any went sour it would be used up for cooking or for making " real " cream cheese. Practical farmers should think over this suggestion.—G. A. H. THE CATTERICK SHORTHORN HERD. Mr. T. H. Hutchinson's herd of shorthorns, at Manor House, Cat- terick, which occupies quite a leading position, is every year gaining fresh fame in the market as well as in shows. Lately Mr. D. Mc.Lennan selected from it, for a client in South America, two fine young females, Lady Golightly and Victoria Fermosa, the price paid for the two being little short of £l,OOO. In addition to these, several less sensational but important sales have been made from the herd—seven young heifers, got by the Ardfert Abbey Riby bull, Riby King, having been sold by Mr. Hutchin- son for the handsome sum of £1,400—certainly a won- derful "record" for a comparatively young sire. Glad Tidings, the well-known prize cow, aroppeda fine heifer calf the other day, and Lady Pamela is safe on the way again. It will have been noticed that Mr. Hutchinson was one of the principal buyers at the Killerby sale last week. There he secured the grand old Hecuba cow, Princess Brigantine, and her four daughters, Princess Beatrice, Princess R'oyal, Princess Battenbera-, and calf at footl. The sum paid for the five was 7245., or rather more than 145grs. each. He likewise bought Queen of Scotia for 205g5., so that his fine herd is stronger at this ,1 moment even than it has ever been before. FATTENING PIGS.—The first stage of the fattening pig is that of the porker; that is, when the pig is killed, it weighs from 48 to 561 b., after being well fed from the time it was weaned. Pigs intended to be fed as porkers should be kept confined to the sty, their food varied occasionally, and given often, but not in such quantities as to cause any to be left over. Skim-milk or buttermilk I mixed with barl4 meal, oatmeal, or Indian meal, makes exquisite pork. The oatmeal and Indian meal should be well boiled, and then mixed with the milk; barley-meal may be mixed with the milk or with the porridge;without being cooked, and oatmeal is also sometimes given in a raw state; but pigs thrive better on those 'meals, or on rice, when they are boiled—at least until within ten days or so of:the time when the pig is to be killed,whenit may be given raw, mixed with some milk; a little pea-meal or bean-meal added will assist in rendering the pork firm. Some well- boiled potatoes may be given occasionally, mixed with milk, as a change of 'food, or a small quantity of pulped food with which meal has been mixed. Raw, unpre- pared roots of any kind should 'not be given to porkers, or to any pig which is fattening. The food of porkers should always be given slightly warm. Porkers should be fully fat at from four to five months old. NORTH LANCASHIRE NOTES.—" R." writes :—For nearly three weeks we have not had two successive fine days. On Saturday and Sunday I was over a good part of Low Furness, and was surprised to find so much barley still out. The grain is sprouting, the seeds growing up into the stooks, and the butts of the latter are rotting, the temperature being high for the time of year, and up to Sunday there was little wind. As the wind brought with it rain on Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday of this week, it has not improved matters. There is also a small pro- portion of wheat out yet, and here and there you can come on stooks of oats. The sparrows have been busy with the latter, and there will not be much beside the straw to house. The continued wet weather is also tell- ing on the root crops, and growth is checked. I notice that Lord Tollernache's sliding scale of rents is again under discussion, by which payments are to be adjusted according to prices current for produce. It is probable that it may work during a period of depression; but the result is to, in some respects, reduce individual inde- pendence, and should a cycle of batter tines set in, far- mers will be anxious to be once more relieved from its operation. Such is human nature in general. The plan partakes of grandmotherly legislation, and as such it will not be relished by farmers when the need is past. CATTLE DISEASES.—The Live Stock Journal says :—The opinion of Professor Brown, in reference to inoculation for pleuro-pneumonia, - will command wide attention. The conclusion of the professional head of the Agricul- tural Department is that it "inoculation is practised at all as an alternative to slaughter in the case of cattle which have been exposed to the contagion of pleuro- pneumonia, but are not discoverably affected, the in- oculated cattle should be kept in the infected place until they are in condition for the butcher. and the infected place should not be declared free while any of the in- oculated cattle remain alive. It will generally be agreed, after this declaration, that stamping out is the -easier way of getting rid of the disease. The Gazette' of last week contained the first returns of anthrax under the "Anthrax Order of 1886." From the official journal it appears that one outbreak occurred in the county of Lan- caster and another in Flintshire. In each case only one animal was attacked. This is so far satisfactory, as out- breaks of anthrax are usually not confined to solitary individual cases. And, as usual in England, the outbreaks reported are confined to cattle only. The contagion has not appeared amongst sheep and other farm stock, as on the Continent and elsewhere. Perhaps the returns are not yet as perfect as they should be. But a beginning has been made, and we may congratu- late ourselves that it is but a small beginning. May no larger ending follow! By the way, when are we to hear any more of the cultivation of the anthrax virus—the object of which was, in great part, the commission given by the Royal Agricultural Society of England to Profes- sors Robertson and Penberthy to pay a visit to M. Pasteur sore months ago? It is to be hoped they are not attempting to cultivate the bacillus near the stables, cowsheds, or dissecting room of the Royal Veterinary College, Camden Town, or their experiments are likely to be vitiated in no small degree thereby. But we are all anxious to know what is being done, and the doings of the learned professors should be made known as early as possible. Stock farmers in the present day are deeply concerned in all questions relating to the con- tagious diseases of animals.

"I remember," says Lord Eldor, "Mr. Justice Gould trying a case at York, and when he had proceeded for about two hours he observed: Here are only Celeven jurymen in the box; where is the twelfth?' Please you my lord,' said one of the eleven, he has gone away about some business, but he has left his verdict with me."

Two English tourists visited the field of Bannockburn, and a local cartwright pointed out with intelligence the positions of the contending armies, the stone in which the Bruce's standard was fixed, &c. &c. The tourists on leaving pressed their informant's acceptance of a gratuity, but "Na, na," replied the Scot, with noticeable pride, "It has cost you enough already." An absolute singleness of pursuit almost means a mind always in one attitude, an eye that regards every object, however many-sided, from one point of view, an intel- lectual dietary, beginning and ending with one article. Exclusiveness of this kind is apt to produce serious evils It disposes each man to exaggerate the force and value of his own particular attainment, and perhaps therewith Ins own importance. It deprives the mind of the refresh- ment which is healthily afforded by alteration of labour, and of the strength as well as the activity to be gained by alllwing varied subjects to evoke and put in exercise its wonderfully varied powers. div.head: THEFT BY A ST. FINLESS SALVA-
div.p: THEFT BY A ST. FINLESS SALVA-
TIONIST.

At Warrington Borough Court, on Wednesday, John Whalley (17), glassmaker, of 18, Lyon-street, St. Helens, was brought up in custody on.a charge of stealing an English lever watch and a chain, value 30s, from the house of James Green, forge- man, 26, Norman-street, off Chorley-street, Lyth- goe's-lane, on the Monday previous. Chief Con- stable Hunt, in telling the magistrates the particu- lars of the case, said that prisoner was a member of the Salvation Army at St. Helens, and the man whose property he had stolen was a member of the Army at Warrington. From what could be ascer- tained, it appeared that prisoner went to North- wich and other places in search of work, and on Saturday came to Warrington. In the evening he attended the Army meeting and made himself known to some of the members, saying that he was out of work and destitute. A collection was made for him, and prosecutor, with one or two more, went with him to seek for lodgings. They found a place, but Green, "out of the kindness of his heart," thought that it was scarcely comfortable enough, and said to prisoner "Come along with me, you shall not stop here; you shall share my bed until illonday." Prosecutor took prisoner to his house, where he had. food and lodg- ings until Monday morning. Green left him in bed at seven o'clock on that morning, and soon afterwards he came downstairs, and Mrs. , Green, the mother of the prosecutor, gave him breakfast. After he had gone she discovered that her son's watch and chain were missing. The matter was reported to the police, whose inquiries elicited that prisoner went from Warrington to Northwich, where he spent the night with the money collected for him by the Warrington "corps" of the army. On Tuesday he returned to St. Helens, and, on his mother telling him that the police had been looking, .for him, he made a clean breast of the affair, and admitted taking the watch. His mother saw the lieutenant of the army at St.. Helens, and a man named Chance was then selected to come to Warrington with prisoner and deliver up the property to the owner. Prisoner was taken to the Bridewell at Warrington, and when charged replied "I took them." As prisoner pleaded guilty no evidence was taken. One of the magistrates, Mr. Fairclough, told prisoner he had shown base ingratitude for the hospitality extended to him; he thought that the Salvation Army people had acted very well. Chief Constable Hunt concurred in the remark, and said that they had acted Well in every respect. Prisoner was sentenced to a month's im- prisonment with hard labour.

div.head: ENGLISH TOURISTS IN AMERICA-
div.p: ENGLISH TOURISTS IN AMERICA-
AT NIAGARA.

In the car for Niagara was an Englishman of the re- ceptive, guileless, thin type, inquisitive, and over- flowing with approval of everything American. He had light hair, sandy side-whiskers, a face that looked as if it had been scattered with soap and sand-paper, and he wore a sickly yellow travelling suit. He was ac- companied by his wife, a stout, resolute matron, in heavy boots, a serviceable stuff gown, with a lot of cotton lace fudged about her neck, and a broad- brimmed hat with a vegetable garden on top. The little man was always in pursuit of information, in his guide books or from his fellow-passengers, and when- ever he obtained any he invariably repeated it to his wife, who said "Fancy !" and "Now really !" in a rising inflection that expressed surprise and expectation.

Mr. King (an American fellow-passenger) was gradually drawn to these simple, unpretending people. He took for granted their ignorance of America—igno- rance of America being one of the branches taught in the English schools—and he soon discovered that they were citizens of the world. They not only knew the Continent very well, but they had ,f,pent a winter in Egypt, lived a year in India, and seen somethinc, of China and much of Japan. Although they had 'teen scarcely a fortnight in the United States, King doubted if there were ten women in the State of New York who knew as much of the flora of the country as this plain. featured, rich-voiced woman. They called King's attention to a great many features of the landscape he had never noticed before, and asked him a great many questions about farming and stock and wages that he could not answer. It appeared that Mr. Stanley-Stubbs, Stoke-Cruden—for that was the name and address of the present discoverers of America—had a herd of short- horns, and that Mrs. Stubbs was even more familiar with the herd-book than her husband.

It was dark when they came into the station at Niagara—dark and silent. Our American tourists, who were accustomed to the clamour of the hackmen here, and expected to be assaulted by a horde of wild Comanches in plain clothes, and torn limb from bag- gage, if not limb from limb, were unable to account for this silence, until they remembered that the State had bought the Falls, and the agents of the Government had suppressed many of the nuisances. It was possible now to hear the roar of the cataract. There were few people at the Cataract House, and either the bridal season had not set in, or in America a bride has been evolved who does nor show any consciousness of her new position. On the edge of the rapids, above the hotel, the old bath- house was in process of dern9lition, its shaking piazzas almost overhanging the flood. Some electric lamps shining through the trees made high lights on the crests of the rapids, while others near were in shadow and dark. The black mass of Goat Island appeared under the lightning flashes in the north-west sky, and whenever these quick gleams pierced the gloom, the frail bridge to the Island was outlined for a moment, and then vanished as if it had been swept away, and there could only be seen sparks of light in the houses on the Canada shore, which seemed very near. In this unknown, which was rather felt than seen, there was a sense of power and mystery which overcame the mind; and in the black night the roar, the cruel haste of the rapids, tossing white gleams and hurrying to the fatal plunge, begat a sort of terror in the spectators. It was a power implacable, vengeful, not to be measured. They strolled down to Prospect Park. The gate was closed. It had been the scene of an awful tragedy but a few minutes before. They did not know it, but they knew that the air shud- dered, and as they skirted the grounds along the way to the foot-bridge, the roar grew in their stunned ears. There, projected out into the night, were the cables of steel holding the frail platform over the abyss of night and terror. Beyond was Canada. What an impious thing it seemed—this trembling structure across the chasm! They advanced upon it. There were gleams upon the wild cascades below, and upon the mass of the American Fall. Below, down in the gloom, were patches of foam, slowly circling around in the eddy—no haste now, just sullen and black satisfaction in the awful tragedy of the fall. The whole was vague, fearful. Always the roar, the shuddering of the air. They walked On; they set foot on her Majesty's do- minions; they entered the Clifton House--quite Ameri- can, you know, with its new bar and offices. A subdued air about everybody here also, and the same quaking, shivering, and impending sense of irrepressible force. When they returned the moon was coming up, rising and struggling and making its way slowly through rugged masses of coloured clouds. The river could be plainly seen now, smooth, deep, and treacherous; the Falls on the American side showed fitfully in patches of light and foam ; the Horse Shoe, mostly -hidden by a cold silver mist, occasionally loomed up a white and ghastly mass. They stood for a long time looking down at the foot of the American Fail—the moon now showing clearly the plunge of the heavy columns—a column as stiff as if it were melted silver—hushed and frightened by the weird and appalling scene. They did not know at that mo- ment that where their eyes were riveted, there at the base of the fall, a man's body was churning about, plunged down and cast up, and beaten and whirled, imprisoned in the refluent eddy. But a body was there. In the morning a man's overcoat was found on the uara- pet, at the angle of the fall. Some one then remembered

I that in the evening, just before the Park gate closed, he had seen a man approach the angle of the wall where the overcoat was found. The man was never seen after that. Night first, and then the hungry water, swallowed him. One pictures the fearful leap into the dark, the midway repentance, perhaps, the despair of the plunge. A body cast in here is likely to tarry for days, eddying round and round, and tossed in that terrible maelstrom, before a chance current ejects it, and sends it down the fierce rapids below. The slight bridge to Goat Island appeared more pre- sumptuous by daylight, and the sharp slope of the rapids above it gave a new sense of the impetuosity of the torrent. As the visitors walked slowly on, past the now abandoned paper-mills and the other human im- pertinences, the elemental turmoil increased, and they seemed entering a world the foundations of which were broken up. Standing upon the platform at the top, they realised for the first time the immense might of the downpour of the American Fall, and noted the pale green colour, with here and there a violet tone, and the white cloud mass spurting out from the solid colour. On the foam-crested river lay a rainbow forming nearly a complete circle. The little steamer Maid of the Mist was coming up, riding the waves, dashed here and there by conflicting currents, but resolutely steaming on—such is the audacity of man—and poking her venturesome nose into the boiling foam under the Horse-shoe. On the deck are pigmy passengers in oil-skin suits, clumsy figures, like Arctic explorers. The boat tosses about like a chip, it heiitates and quivers, and then slowly swinging, darts away down the current, fleeing from the wrath of the waters, and pursued by the angry roar. Our party descended the winding staircase in the tower, and walked on the shelf under the mighty ledge to the entrance of the Cave of the Winds. The curtain of water covering this entrance was blown back and forth by the wind, now leaving the platform dry, and now deluging it. A woman in the pathway was beckoning frantically, and calling to a man who stood on the platform, entirely uncon- scious of danger, looking up to the green curtain and down into the boiling mist. It was Mrs. Stubbs; but she was shouting against Niagara, and her husband mistook her pantomime for gestures of wonder and ad- miration. Some moments passed, and then the curtain swung in, and tons of water drenched the Englishman, and for an instant hid him from sight. Then, as the curtain swung back he was seen clinging to the hand- rail, sputtering and astonished at such treatment. He came up the bank dripping, and declaring that it was extraordinary, most extraordinary, but he wouldn't have missed it for the world. From this platform one looks down the narrow slippery stairs that are lost in the boiling mist, and wonders at the daring that built these steps down into that hell, and carried the frail walk of planks over the boulders outside the fall. A party in oil-skins, making their way there, looked like lost men and women in a Dante Inferno. The turbulent waters dashed all round them; the mist occasionally wrapped them from sight; they clung to the rails they tried to speak te each other; their gestures seemed mo- tions of despair. There is nothing, after all, that the human race will not dare for a new sensation. - The walk around Goat Island is probably unsurpassed in the world for wonder and beauty. The Americans have every reason to be satisfied with their share of the fall; they get nowhere one single grand view like .that from the Canada side, but infinitely the deepest im- pression of majesty and power is obtained on Goat Island. There the spectator is in the midst of the war of nature. From the point of the Horse-shoe Fall our friends, speaking not much, but more and more deeply moved, strolled along in the lovely forest, in a rural solemnity, in a, local calm, almost a seclusion, except for the ever-present shuddering roar in the air. On the shore above the Horse-shoe they first comprehended the breadth, the great sweep, of the rapids. The white crests of waves in the west were coming out from under a black, lowering sky; all the foreground was in bright sunlight, dancing, sparkling, leaping, hurrying on, con- verging to the angle where the water becomes a deep emerald at the break and plunge. The rapids above are a series of shelves, bristling with jutting rocks and i lodged trunks of trees, and the wildness of the scene s intensified by the ragged fringe of evergreens on the opposite shore. The triple islands, the Three Sisters, in their picturesque wildness, appeared like playful freaks of nature in a momentary relaxation of the savage mood. Here is the finest view of the river; to one standing on the outermost island the great flood seems tumbling out of the sky. They continued along the bank of the river, which races by headlong, but close to the edge are numerous eddies, and places where one might step in and not be swept away. At length' they reached the point where the river divides, and the water stands for an instant almost still, hesitating whether to take the Canadian or the American plunge. Out a little way from the shore the waves leap and tumble, and the two currents are like racehorses parted on two ways to the goal. Just at this point the water swirls and lingers, having. lost all its fierceness and haste, and spreads itself out placidly dimpling in the sun. The relief from the dread of Niagara felt at this point of peace was onlytemporary. The dread returned when the party approached again the turmoil of the American Fall, and fell again under the influence of the merciless haste of the flood. And there every islet, every rock, every point, has its legend of terror; here a boat lodged with a man in it, and after a day and night of yap attempts to rescue him, thousands of people saw him take the frightful leap, throwing up his arms as he went over; here a young woman slipped, and was instantly whirled out of life; and from that point more than one dazed or frantic visitor had taken the suicidal leap. Death was near here and so easy.—From " Their Pilgrimage," by Chas. Dudley Warner, in " Harper's Monthly Magazine."

div.head: SHOCKING DEATH AT A CHEMICAL
div.p: SHOCKING DEATH AT A CHEMICAL
WORKS.

Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Royal Raven Hotel, St. Helens, on Wednesday, on the body of Patrick Ryan, thirty-four years of age, of 5, Crook-street, who received fatal injuries by fall- ing into a pan of boiling caustic at Messrs. Lockwood and Leith's Chemical Works.—The Coroner read the following letter from Mr. Richmond, Her Majesty's Inspector of Factories :—" It appears to me that the man must have got on the edge of the pan—a most dangerous and unnecessary proceeding; otherwise he could hardly have fallen feet first into the pan. There is no legal obliga- tion on the employers to fence such pans, and the Act only gives me authority to order a fence for pans near to or over which children or young persons are liable to pass or be employed. No doubt these pans would be safer if they could be railed, but I fear no rails could withstand the chemical action long."— Mr. John Leith, one of the proprietors, explained that the pan was about 10ft diameter and 7ft deep. Half of the depth was below the ground, so that it was about 3ft t3in out. Deceased and Thomas Gorry were putting up a shoot so that the liquid might be poured into it and go down to the settler.—Thomas Gerry stated that deceased got on the edge of the pan while witness took hold of the other end of the shoot to lift it up. He suddenly heard a splash and a shout, asd on looking up saw that deceased had fallen into the liquid. It was necessary for deceased to put his foot on the brickwork running round the pan, but the brickwork was three feet thick. It slant“.l upwards near the top. Witness could not see that there was any danger. Deceased shouted, "Are you ready ?" Witness stid, " Hold a bit ;" and then be heard the splash. Witness took hold of the de- ceased's arm, but could not pull him out until other men ar- rived. He was then taken to the hospital, where he died.— Mr. Leith said there was no necessity for deceased to go so near the edge. Men would go as near as possible, and wit- ness was constan,ly telling them not to go so near.—The Coroner said the jury had to decide whether death was ac- cidental, and whether they could suggest anything to pre- vent a similar accident occurring in the future.—A Juryman thought it was carelessness on the part of the men them- selves. They took no notice, as if there was no danger at all.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accid•ntal death," and made a presentment that the attention of her Majesty's Inspector of Workshops and Factories should be drawn to the construction of these pans, so that he might suggest such alterations as he might deem requisite.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS AT WARRINGTON.

Harry Toft, James Worrall, George Jolley, George Taylor, Thos. Henry Cleveland, Frederick Massey, John Titchard, and George Yoxall. SOITTII-EAST WARD.—Mr. Richard Walker Fran- comb (C), coal merchant, 49. Wilson Patten-street, proposed by Mr. S. M. Webster, seconded by Mr. John Musgrove Croley, and assented to by Messrs. Joseph Partington, Joseph Grounds, Thomas M. Hales, Charles Roddy, John Whitby, Wm. Fairhurst, Robt. FATALITY ON TFfE RAILWAY AT WARRINGTON.

On Saturday, Thomas Lane, 23 years of age, a carriage cleaner in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, was engaged at his occupation at Bank Quay station, when he, by some means or other, fell and was run over by some coal waggons that were being. shunted. His leg was broken, find he was at once conveyed to the Infirmary, where he died on the evening of the same day. Deceased, who had been in the employ of the company for about seven weeks, bad been living at 118, Mersey-street. On Monday Mr. S. Brighouse and a jury enquired into the circumstances of his death at the Wilson Patten Hotel. Mr. Ashurst, stationmaster at Bank Quay, was present. The following evidence was taken.—Edward Lane, brother of the deceased, said that the last time he saw his brother alive was about five weeks ago. Thomas Mellor, a carriage cleaner at Bank Quay, said that he and deceased were engaged on Saturday in washing a train that stood on the line, close to which a goods train was passing. Witness was at the van end of the train, and the deceased was at work only a short distance from him. He remembered seeing the deceased at work, but when he looked again the deceased was on the floor, and called out "My God, my God," The accident took place behind the platform on the high level, not far from • the stationmaster's office. The six-foot was between the train they were wash- ing and the passing train.—The jury, not thoroughly understanding how the accident happened, at thiS point went to view the place where it occurred. They found that brushes seven feet long , were used by the cleaners.—Witness Melilla., when the inquiry was resumed, said that the brush pro- duced Waii the one deceased had been using, as it had his name and mark on it. He had never seen any one knocked off the carriage steps whilst at work. He did not know how many trains passed this particular spot every hour. Witness was care- ful when at work, and had been warned to be so by the foreman. They were not supposed to work when there was any danger.—Mr. Ashurst asked to be allowed to put a question, when the Coroner said the company ought to have been in a position to send their solicitor to represent them, and plans also ought to have been produced. He could not allow them to be represented in any other way. He wrote to Mr. Preston on Sunday to tell him when the in- quest would be held.—James Lee, carriage cleaner, stated that there was only a space of three feet be- tween the footboard of one train and the axle box of the other. The washing was done in two places, but most of it where the present accident occurred. —The jury expressed the opinion that the place was a very dangerous one.—A verdict of "Accidental death was returned, the jury adding the following presentment :—" That the London and North- Western Railway Company are very much to blame for allowing carriages to be washed in such a dan- gerous place, and that a Government inspector iought to inspect the different places where carriages , are washed.' —The Coroner I not only forward the Iverdict to the London and North-Western Railway Company, but it also appears in the report I am bound to make on every death on the railway to the Secretary of State. I agree with the verdict, and I think the Company ought not to treat cases of this kind so lightly. This is a case where, if we had made no inspection, most probably we should have been misled. I think the least the Company could have done was to furnish us with a plan showing the locus in quo, and also have sent down their solici- tor, or some one from the solicitor's office to repre- sent them.

NEAR THE VILLAGE OF ZILLINGDORF, in Lower Austria, lives Maria Haas, an intelligent and industrious woman whose story of physical suffering and final relief, as related by herself, is of interest to English women. "1 was employed" she says," in the work of a large farmhouse. Overwork brought on sick headache, followed by a deathly fainting and sickness!. of the stomach, until I was unable to retain either food or drink. I was compelled to take to my bed for several weeks. Getting a little better from rest and quiet,.l sought to do some work, but was soon taken with a pain in my side, which in a little while seemed to spread over my whole body, and throbbed in my every limb. This was followed by a cough and shortness of breath, until finally I could not sew, and I took to my bed for the second, and, as I thought, for the last time. My friends told me that toy time had nearly come, and that I could not live longer than when the trees put on their green once more. Then I happened to get one of the Seigel pamphlets. I read it and my dear mother bought me a bottle of Seigel's Syrup, which I took vs - achy according to directions, and 1 had not taken the whole of it before I felt a change for the better. ?lb" last illness began June the 3rd, 1882, and continued to August 9th, when I began to take toe Syrup. Very soon I could do a little light work. . The cough left me, and I was no more troubled in breathing. Now I am perfectly cured. And oh, how happy I am! I can rot express enough gratitude for Seigel's Syrup. Noe/ I must tell you that the doctors in our district distiibue ted handbills cautioning people against the medicine, telling them it would do them no good, and many were thereby influenced to destroy the Seigel pamphlets ; but now wherever one is to be found it is kept like a relic. The few' preserved are borrowed to read, and I have lent mine for six miles around our district. People have come eighteen miles to get me to buy the medicine for them, knowing %het it cured me, and to be sure to get the right kind. I know a woman who was looking like death, and who told them there was no help for her, that she had consulted with several doctors, but none con!d help her.' I told her of Seigel's Syrup, and wrote the name down for her that she might make no mistake. She took my advice and the Syrup, and now she is in perfect health, and the people around us are amazed. The medicine has made such progress in out neighbourhood that people say they don't want the doctor any more, but they take the Syrup. Suf- ferers from gout who were confined to their bed and could hardly move a finger, have been cured by it. There is a girl in our district who caught a cold by going through some water, and was in bed five years with costiveness and rheumatic pains, and had to have an attendant to watch by her. There was not a doctor in the surrounding districts to whom her mother had not applied to relieve her child, but everyone crossed themselves and said they could not help her. Whenever the little bell rang which is rung in our place when somebody is dead, we thought surely it was for her, but Siegel'S Syrup and Pills saved her life, and now she is as- healthy as anybody, goes to church, and cm work even in the fields. Everybody was astonished when they saw her out, knowing how many years she had been in bed. To-day she adds her gratitude to mine for God's mercies and Seigel's Syrup." MARIA HAAS.

DANGERS OF TIIE SEASON. The time of year is rapidly approaching when we must consign our light garments to the dark closets, .41.nd begin to wear apparel better adapted to resist 'the attempts of Jack Frost. The poetical season of :autumn has closed, boats are housed, the tennis court is deserted, and even the great national pas- time, cricket, only flickers spasmodically in out-of- the way rural districts. Nature is robbed of all her pleasant aspects, and even her most ardent admirer can see nothing in the rain, and cold, and general dreariness, to gather • comfort from. We are decidedly at the mercy of the elements, and those who have a tendency to rheumatism, or weak chests, seek as much shelter as they can command. It is the beginning of the doctors' season, who reap their harvests from the seeds sown by our indiscretions and imprudent ex- posures. Exposing the body to lower temperatures than it is accustomed to, as now must daily occur with most of us, closes the pores of the skin instantly, and. thus drives the blood into the interior of the body, where it collects in some of the great organs, more often the kidneys, causing congestion or stag- nation, and stoppage of the natural functions of these delicate organs. This is the first result, and Nature seeking to remedy it by a violent effort, the nervous system is involved, and a shock occurs, known as the congestive chill, and then the mischief is done. Pneumonia, pleurisy, acute Bright's disease, or inflammation of the bowels sets it, and soon makes short work of the victim. Why cannot 'we learn caution? Why do we not make use of the lessons taught us, and keep the sewers of the body (the kidneys) in healthful condition. Kidney excretion is a vital function, on the proper per- formance of which depends the health and life. The kidneys excrete the poisonous acids, which retained in the system mean slow death. Caretully tabulated statistics show that 93 per cent. of all cas—es of sickness have their origin in obstructed kidneys, so one truth is clear, and that is. we should give them 93 per cent. of our attention to prevent disease. Until late years the medical profession has been unable to give us a remedy, harmless in itself, but which should have the power to act direct on the urine-secreting tubes; but lately a singularly fortunate discovery has supplied us with that which has been sought for so many years in vain, and Warner's SAFE Cure, the name of the ,yreparation (a high-grade medicine), is now placed within the reach of all. Its action is manifold; it relieves congestion, opens the pores of the skin, exercises its marvellous influence, particularly on the kid- neys, and enables the organs to shake off their evil, and, thus striking at the fountain-head, gives us blood pure and rich, as Nature intended we should possess. Thus, in order to prevent sickness at this time of year, when damp clothing, storms, &c., chill the •body, and congest the internal organs, clogging up the kidneys, and thus preventing their blood-purifying action, Warner's SAFE Cure should be taken to enable the kidneys to throw out the poisonous mat- ters, so that illness may be prevented, and life pro- longed. Says the Rev. There are hundreds of poor suf- ferers whom it would bless and restore." It is most desirable in regard to this remedy that we should take it in time. If you value your life, take no rest until you have it by you. You cannot avoid at all times the exposure incident to the climate, but you can, by the exercise of a little common sense, prevent illness which results from what would be described as criminal neglect under any other cir- cumstances. FOREIGN NEWS. THE BULGARIAN CRISIS: NOTE TO THE POWERS. TURKISH WAR PREPARATIONS. The Bulgarian Government addressed A Circular Note to the Powers on Saturday announcing that the Great Sobranje, after verifying the elections, will immediately proceed to the election of a new Pririce. CONSTANTINOPLE, SATURDAY.—The Turkish war prepara- tions continue on a large scale. All road-making has been stopped in Sri a. Two classes of reserves have been called out there. The Porte's information is that the Russian preparations at Sebastopol and Odessa still con- tinue. BRUSSELS, SUNDAY.—The " Nord " says :—" The crisia which had reached its culminating point last week is clear- ing up. The unanimity with which all the Powers, includ- ing England, reject the eventuality of the restoration of Prince Alexander of Battenberg to the Throne of Bulgaria affords reason for the hope that they understand the necessities of the situation. There is already a glimpse of the prospect of a rational and necessary solution of the Bul- garian question." ST. PETERSBURG. TUESDAY.—To-day's papers are occu- pied with speculations upon the resolutions that may be taken by the Bulgarian Sobranje. The " Novoe Vremva" says the re-election of Prince Alexander would justify a Russian occupation. SOFIA, SATURDAY.—GeneraI Kaulbars has called upon the members of the Minie•ry and Regency to abandon their journey to Tirnova and to prorogue the Sobranje for an indefinite period. The Government has declined to accede to General Kaulbar's request, and its members will start for Tirnova to-day. TIIINOTA, WEDNESDAY, 11 A.M. Intelligence received here states that General Kaulbars has sent a Note to the Bulgarian Government declaring that if the officers impli- cated in the csnspiracy against Prince Alexander are pun- ished Russia will have recourse to extreme measures. This is believed in Government circles to imply an intention on the part of Russia to occupy Bulgaria. THE RUSSIAN WAR VESSELS AT VARNA. ST. PETERSBURG, WEDNESDAY.—The "Official Messen- ger" to-day publishes the following :—" Owing to the anarchy existing throughout Bulgaria, our Consulates are no longer able to protect the lawful interests of Russian subjects residing in that country. After the departure of Baron Kaulbars from Varna, it happened that several Rus- sian subjects were arrested under illegal pretext. In view of this condition at affairs, the cruisers Zabraka and Pam jat Merkurija were despatched a few days ago to Varna." BULGARIA AND SERVIA. BELGRADE, WEDNESDAY.—The Servian Minister for Foreign Affairs and Dr. Stransky. the Bulgarian Diplomatic Agent, have signed the protocol of an agreement which contains the following stipulations :-1. The Bregovo question to be referred to a joint Servo• Bulgarian commission. 2. A treaty of commerce between the two countries to be con- cluded within six months. 3. The Servian emigrants to Bulgaria to be removed to a distance of 6(tkilometres from the Servian frontier. 4. The railway line between Makaret, Soils, and Tsaribrod to be constructed as soon as possible, and, if practicable, also the line between Nisch and Fleet.

ST. PETERSBURG, SUNDAY EVENING.—Thb Ceremony of unveiling the great war memorial was performed to-day with much pomp in the presence of the Czar and Czarina, the members of the Imperial family, the generals who com- manded in the war, and representatives of all branches of To all those immediately concerned the cere- monymyed.allions of geld, silver, and bronze, according to the rank of the recipient, were distributed. After the un- veiling of the manument. the Emperor and Empress attended a grand feast given to the troops at the expense of the city of St. Petersburg. This evening there is a banquet at the Imperial Palace, to which the generals and officers who took part in the day's ceremony have been invited. The city is illuminated. After the ceremony of unveiling the monument com- memorative of the Russo-Turkish war, the Czar and Czarina attended the luncheon given to the Russian on- cers. The Czar proposed their health, and thanked them, "in the name of him who was no longer among them," for the hardships they had undergone in the Russo-Turkish campaign. THE RUSSIAN CRUISERS AT VARNA. ST. PETERSBURG THURSDAY.--The German newspaper " Herold " mates that the two Russian cruisers which were sent to Varna have 400 troops on board, and that their com- mander has been ordered to occupy Varna should the Rus- sians who have been illegally arrested not be released. RUSSIAN INTRIGUES IN COREA. PERIN, THURSDLY.--The Chinese Government continues to feel anxiety regarding the attempts or the Russian Min- isters at Seoul to induce the Corean King to accept a Rus- sian protectorate. The views of Russia in this quarter be- came known to the Chinese authorities about three months ago. and since then large Chinese forces have been coliected in the provinces bordering on Corea. They are armed with the newest weapons. • EGYPT.—THE FINANCES OF THE COUNTRY. CHOLERA. TRIESTE, OCT. 24.—Count von Beast, the eminent Aus- trian statesman, who was Chancellor of the Empire from 1867 to 1871, and for several years subsequently held the post of Austro-Hungarian Ambassador in London, died in this city to-day. A Reuter's telegram, dated Suez, Sunday, says :—Her Majesty's Indian troopship Eaphrates passed Parim yester- day, homeward bound. Four deaths from cholera have oc- curred on board. THE CAMPAIGN IN BURMAH. RANGOON, SUNDAY.—The forces in Upper Burmah out- side of the Chindwin valley are divided into six brigades, bold 78 posts. The strongest brigade is that at Mandalay, which numbers over 6,000 men. The 6th brigade, at Pagan, which has charge of the country ravaged by Boshway, is nearly 1,000 strong, and the weakest brigade is that at Rhatiia. The Chindwin force, under Colonel Toker, 900 strong, forms an independent command. The Irrawaddy has fallen considerably and heavily. Oar scouts report that Boshway is at Napeh (25 miles to the west of Minba), a fort in the Yomadung mountains. A large British force is now available at Minbu, and active operations with cavalry and mounted infantry will probably be immediately commenced against Boshway. CALCUTTA, BllNDLY.—General Sir F. Roberts will sail for Burmah on the 4th November, accompanied by General Sir T. D. Baker, Adjutant-General. News of successful operations against the insurpents at Tutnmu has reached India. PREPARATIONS FOR A COMBINED ATTACK. RANGOON, WEDNESDAY. Intelligence from Myingyan states that the rebels are increasing in number in that dis- trict. The mail proceeding to Yemethen has 1).-en attacked and looted by the insurgents, who killed all the men of the native escort. The Memboo district is being harrassed by the rebels under Boshway. It is proposed to attack the latter next week. The Ist Battalion of the Beloochees will leave on the 4th prox. to join the company of the 21d Bat- talion of the Queen's Liverpool Regiment stationed at Tonghoo, whence the combined force will march in the direction of Myingyan, with the object of engaging the rebel leader, Buda Yen. THE INDIAN VICEROY ON TOUR. SIMLA, THURSDA.Y.—The Viceroy started on his tour this morning. His Excellency will visit Bhawulpur, Lahore, Baroda, Goa, Hyderabad, Bangalore, Madura, and Pondi- cherry. and will reach Calcutta on December 13. FRIGHTFUL MASSACRE IN CENTRAL AFRICA. The Church Missionary Society has received letters by the Zanzibar mail, on Tuesday, giving painful details of the massacre of native Christians in Uganda, by order of King Mwarga, telegraphic intelligence of which was re- ceived on September 23. The persecutions broke nut in June,in consequence of a Christian lady, one of the King's pages, refusing to commit an abominable crime. Many were tortured, mutilated, and speared, and 32 were burnt alive together. The intercessions of the missionaries were of no avail. Most touching accounts are given of the steadfastness of the victims, and the massacres seem to have quite failed to intimidate the candidates for baptism. Within a week or two after several converts were baptised at their own earnest desire.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. A meeting of this Council was held in the Council Chamber on Tuesday evening for the purpose of winding up the business of the municipal year. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were also present—Aldermen Crosfield, Holmes, Davies, Webster, Burgess ; Councillors Broadbent, Barker, Dixon, Mackie, J. rierpoint, Brown, Dakin, Hutchin- son, Greening, Sutton, W. Pierpoint, Francomb, Roberts, Litton, Bolton, Wight; Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), and Peter- son (gas manager). THE SANITARY WORIC.—A SATISFACTORY LETTER. The MAYOR said he had a communication from the Local Government Board, which, he thought, would be gratifying to every member of the Council, and especially so to Alder- man Burgess and the Sanitary Committee, over which he presided. The letter was as follows :—" Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., October 25, 1886. My dear Sir,— I was sorry to be obliged to leave on Friday before the in- spection of the satttary works was ended, but having on the previous day examined the I.49ngford works with Mr. Long- din, I have really seen all the arrangements for carrying out the pail system, and the disposal of the town refuse at War- rington. The new intercepting depots seem to provide for the reception and emptying of the pails without offence, and the application of Shone's ejectors to the transmission of the contents to Longford appears to be perfectly successful. At Longford the manufacture of the crude excreta into a p3rt- able and saleable manure by evaporation in vacuo by means of steam generated by the destruction of the house refuse appears to be effected economically and with as little offen- sive smell as can be expected. I think that Warrington is to be congratulated on the success which has attended the labours of the Sanitary Committee, and on the skill of Mr. Longdin in devisinv and carrying out the new works.—' am, dear sir, yours very faithfully, THOMAS CODRINGTON. John Burgess, Esq." He thought the letter justified the eulogiums that were made on the previous Friday, and he begged to move that the letter be entered on the minutes of the Council. (Hear. hear.) Councillor GREENING seconded the motion, which was

carried. WATCR COMMITTEE.-THE CHIEF CONSTABLE'S REPORT. At a meeting held on the 30th September, the Watch Committee passed the following resolution :—"Tliat the Committee wish to express their great regret at the death of Inspector Berry, and their sympathy with his widow and family in their Bed bereavement. The committee regarded Inspector Berry as a most efficient and praiseworthy officer, and they feel that the borough has sustained a great loss by his death." It was resolved that a gratuity of £93 12s be granted out of the superannuation fond of the borough to the widow of the late Inspector Berry, being the maximum amount allowed by law.—At a meeting held on the 7th October, it was resolved that the sum of £6 85 be granted out of the borough fund to the widow of the late Inspector Berry, making with the amount voted out of the superannua- tion fund the sum of £lOO. It was resolved that Police- Sergeant Cox be promoted to the rank of inspector to fill the vacancy occasioned by the death of Inspector Berry, and that Police-Constable Cheeney be promoted to the rank of sergeant, to fill the vacancy occa- sioned by the promotion of Sergeant Cox. et a meeting of the committee held on the 21st October, the annual report of the Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) was ap- proved, and ordered to be entered on the minutes. We give the following extracts from this report :—" One thousand three hundred and sixty-one males and 403 females were apprehended, and summoned for offences dealt with sum- marily, of whom 1,143 males and 288 females were con- victed, and 218 males and 120 females discharged. 'The offenders summarily dealt with consisted of 68 male and 11 female known thieves,' 92/emale bad characters,' 56 male and 10 female tramps,' 336 male and 72 female suspicions characters,' 29 male and 6 female habitual drunkards,' 538 male and 142 female good characters,' and 334 male and 75 female characters unknown.' The num- ber of persons proceeded against, residing in the borough, is 1.003 males and 336 females; non-resident,' 356 males and 74 females. 798 males and 180 females being English, 551 males and 232 females Irish, and 6 males and 2 females Scotch. Their degrees of education are 407 males and 270 females none,' 920 males and 139 females 'imperfect,' 26 males and 6 females well.' and 1 male 'superior.' 34 per- sons were apprehended for 64 indictable offences, 29 being males and 5 females; 5 were attempts to murder,' 1 wounding with intent to do bodily harm, 1 for defilement of girls under 13 years of age, sec.. 4, Criminal Law Amend- ment Act,' 9 for breaking into shops and warehouses, &c., 5 for horse stealing, 3 larceny from the person, 6 simple lar- ceny, 1 receiving stolen goods, for fraud 1, perjury 1, and neglect of family 1. The total number of indictable offences and petty larcenies is 155, property stolen valued at £2lB 14s lop, recovered £127 3s id, not recovered £9l us 91-d. Lest year the figures were, reported 158, value stolen £279 16e 7d, value recovered £lBB lie 9,1, value not recovered £9l 45 101 In addition to the 1,803 borough cases 15 per- sons were locked up for offences committed in <Aker towns, 64 by the adjacent Lancashire County Police, and 30 from the Warrington County Court. For non-payment of rates 205 persons have been summoned and dealt with. Pedlars certificated 92, chimney sweepera 11, value £24 12s 6d, which has been duly accounted for. There are probably 24 children detained in reformatory and industrial schools, for whose part maintenance the sum of £67 2s has been col- lected and duly remitted to the Government Inspector of said schools. Under the 'Crimes Prevention Act,' chap. 112, 8 persons on ticket of leave and 9 under police super- vision have reported themselves at this office during the year, passing through the town; two of the latter class remain on our books as residents. The number of tramps booked is 5,811, against 6,294 last year. The reports of sudden, violent, and unaccountable deaths are 72, as last year, 27 being referred to the registrar, or certified by doctors after inquiries by the police, and inquests held on the remaining 45, verdicts being, natural causes' 14, acci- dental causes 22. found dead 2, found drowned 4, suffoca- tion 1, and misadventure 2. There are 87 licensed public- houses, 48 licensed beerhouses, and 71 off-licensed houses ia the borough ; 4 beerhouse-keepers were proceeded against, 3 being convicted and 1 dismissed. The area of the borough is 1,442 acres; population in 1881 41,456, and present estimate 45,000. The police establishment consists of 42 members, viz :—Chief-constable, chief inspec- tor—who is also police clerk ; 2 uniform inspectors, 4 sergeants, and 34 constables, one of the latter acting as Resistant clerk, arc, and another as police messenger, The salaries and pay amount to £3,311 lie 84, clothing and accoutrements to £217 5s 2d, total £3,528 165 104 ; £4B 03 lid more than in 1885. The sickness in the force from natural causes extended over 340 days, 30 days being allowed to constables hurt upon duty. Leave of absence for relaxation and recreation amounted to 265 days, and, taking sickness into the account, was an average of 14 days each during the year. It is now my painful duty to refer to the sad death on the 29th ultimo of Inspector John Berry, who was drowned in the river Mersey at Fiddler's Ferry, by the upsetting of a small boat he and Mr. William (Captain) Mather had gone down the river in to shoot wild birds, dtc. Berry joined this police force on April 28th, 1866, and on date of his death had served as constable, ser- geant, and inspector 20 years and 154 cl,ys. He was 'a good officer in every sense of the term, being courteous, truthful, sober, honest, induetrious, fearless of danger in the execution of his duty, and straightforward in all his transactiens for or against those with whom he was brought in contact when discharging such duty. I have no doubt he will be long re- gretted by his fellow constables, and the public of Warrington generally. The Town Council, on the recom- mendation of the Watch Committee, has granted his widow the sum of £93 125 from the superannuation fund, equal to one year's pay, Inspector Berry having subscribed thereto for 20 years and 5 months. The variations in the force have been :-2 resigned, from continued illhealth and in- disposition to the service, respectively ; the first (Hitch• mough) has died since; 2 dismissals; and the drowning fatality to Inspector Berry ; the lattlik has necessi- tated promotion in the force, viz : Sergeant , George Cox, with 14 years and 173 days' ser- vice, to rank of inspector; and P.C. Henry Cheney, with 4 years and 68 days' service, to rank of sergeant. The length of service of members of the police force on the 20th September last was—under one year, three constables ; between one and two years, two constables; between two and three years, six constables; between three and four years, four constables; between four and five years, two consta- bles; five to six years, one sergeant and seven constables; six to seven years, four constables; seven to eight years, one sergeant and one constable; nine to ten years, one con- stable; eleven to twelve years, one constable; 14 to 15 years, one sergeant and one constable; 15 to 16 years, one sergeant; 16 to 17 years, one constable; 20 to 21 years, two inspectors; 21 to 22 years, one inspector; .22 to 23 years, chief constable; and from 26 to 27 years, one con- stable."
