SOUTH AFRICA. PIETERMARITZBURG. WEDNESDAY.-Sir A. Havelock, Go- vernor of Natal, to-day announced in the Legislative Coun- cil that the Secretary of State had declined to accede to the Proposal of the Colony te undertake the government of Zululand. The Governor having refused to give particulars of the recent negotiations with the Zulu Republic, the Council adjourned until to-morrow, when a resolution will be introduced practically declining to Tote supplies until the Council are acqnainted with the nature of the ne- gotiations. This action of the Council is generally approved here. - -

THE STATE OF IRELAND. At the fortnightly meeting of the National League in Dublin, on Tuesday. it was reported that £1,155 had been received since the last meeting for the Irish Parliamentary fund. Father Fahy writes from Galway Gaol declining to ac- cept anything but an unconditional release. He repudiates the action of those who are seeking to secure his liberty by other means. General Buller has been engaged at Killarney in arrang- ing with Mr. Murphy, the Crown Prosecutor, as to the Moonlighting prosecutions, which are to be brought on at the next assizes. Archbishop Croke has received from Sydney £209 for the fund subscribed for the widow and children of the late A. M. Sullivan. in recognition of his unswerving fidelity to the cause of Irish Nationality in its darkest hour. Lord Lansdowne has written to Mr. Townsend French, the agent on his Kerry estates, giving the reasons which have determined him to offer his Kerry tenants a reduc- tion of 20 per cent in case of judicial rents, and 25 to 35 per cent where the rents have not been fixed by the Land Court. A proposal that the amalgamation of the British Home Rule Association with the United Kingdom Home Rule League will be considered at a meeting of the council of the associati n, next week, at the Palace Chambers, West- minster. The Recorder of Cork, in charging the Granel Jury at the Quarter Sessions on Saturday, referred to the war which was made on the landlords by the National League, and tenants backed by the League, and said that unless the landlords were prepared to be snuffed out they were bound to bring their ejectments. The city of Derry is profiting by the sad experiences of Belfast. Fearing that the result of the election petition trial might cause irritation in certain quarters, the magis- trates have issued a proclamation prohibiting party proces- sions, and warning the people of the peril they incur by assembling in numbers in the streets and open spaces. A Londonderry correspondent states that another large scheme of farmer proprietary has been successfully nego- tiated, the Skinners' Company having agreed to sell their estates in Londonderry at something under eighteen years' purchase, under Lord Ashbourne's Land Purchase Act. The estate contains nearly 1,000 tenants, and needy 35,000 ;acres. The instalments for the next 49 years will be 25 j per cent less than the present rents. Payments will then ' cease. Preaching on Saaday on the Belfast l'llots Commission, pr. Hanna said that Catholics had entered into a conspiracy, aided by the police, to stop Loyalist processions in Ireland ; while the civil magistrates had been trying to evade their duty by attempting to suppress the Loyalists ant encourage sedition. The present Commission had not got at the root of the complaint against the police, and consequently there was a want of confidence on the part of the Protestants. The constabulary force was degeneratiog, being contamina- ted by seditious sentiments. THE IRISH DEFENCE UNION.—Last year the Irish De- fence Union was organised in London. It is composed of a numerous and influential body of gettlemen—English, Scottish, and Irish—of various creeds and politics, associa- ted for the purpose of aiding persons suffering from illegal coercion in Ireland. In many Irish counties Local Defence Unions have been formed, and the work of the London branch has been to collect and transmit funds to each of these societies. Arrangements have been made to provide a special fund, to be administered by the Cork Defence Union, to assist boycotted persons in Counties Kerry and Limerick, in which no Defence Unions have as yet been organised. Great efforts are being made to fertn a Defence Union in County Nerry, and it is hoped that within a week or two it will be in full work. Tun DERRY PETITION : THE TORY UNSEATED,—On the resumption of the Londonderry election trial, on Saturday, c. Lewis, the sitting member, withdrew his defence of the seat, and the court then proceeded to consider the claim of Mr. Justin McCarthy, the petitioner. In the course of the subsequent arguments the judges expressed the opinion that no legal evidence of bribery had been produced.—Mr. Justice O'Brien ultimately announced that in the interests of she peace of the city, and the security of life arid pro- perty, the delivery of the formal judgment would be postponed until Monday. The result, however, is that Mr. Lewis is unseated, and that Mr. McCarthy obtains the seat. Great excitement prevails. Mr. Justice O'Brien has formally delivered judgment in the case of the Lon- donderry election petition. He declared Mr. Jestin Mc- Carthy duly elected by a majority of legal votes; those of the minors and of Samuel McDermott and Robert Neely be- ing disallowed. The Court held Mr. Lewis guilty of illegal practices, through his agent, and ordered him to pay the petitioner's costs ; the Crown to pay the Attorney-General's costs. Counsel for the petitioner offered evidence in their Possession to the Crown. Tans MOONLIGHTERS AT WORt.—WHOLESALE ARRESTS. —A Killarney correspondent telegraphs that late on Mon- day night, 14 yoang men, of the farming class, were arres- ted while in bed at their homes, in the parishes of Milltown Kealhill, Tallagh, and Castlemaine, and were immediately taken to MilltoWn Bridewell. The names of six of them are Moriarty, Counihan, Kelliher, Fitzgerald, Prendergast, and Sheehy. It apPears that on August 11th last, when a large number of police were engaged at the annual fair, known as "Puck Fair," at Killorglin, the absence of police from certain localities was taken advantage of, and a raid was made on the house of Mr. Haggard, magistrate's secre- tary at Milltown. and arms carried off from the police pro- tection post. A doctor and three others are also awaiting trial charged with firing on the police on the same night. Three men, named James Corn, William Cullen, and Pat- rick Herron, were arrested at Donaghmore, county Tyrone, by District-Inspector McGavern, of Dungannon, on a charge of having attacked a house on Saturday night, and, after threatening to shoot the occupier, thrown a large stone through the window. One of the men admitted the of- fence. THE BELFAST RIOTS COMMISSION.—The rebutting evid- ence of the constabulary was taken on Saturday. It had reference mainly to the charges of misconduct made against individual members of the force by witnesses of the Loyal- ist Defence Committee. The printipal witness was a dis- trict inspector named Taylor, who stoutly denied having been drunk while on duty during one of the August distur- bances, as was alleged against him. Other officers denied having beaten innocent People with their batons and sticks. One of the charges was that by the Rev. Dr. Hanna of in- solence from a man whom he took to be a policeman, and who had told him that if he and Dr. Kane made less noise in their pulpits there would be less rioting. It turned out that the man was a commercial traveller. Father XleGeea, a Falls Road Priest, admitted having advised the

Councillor ROBERTS moved That the Watch Com- mittee be requested to furnish to this Council a full state- ment of the circumstances attendant upon the dismissal of Joseph Neill from the police force." Mr. Roberts thought ' he should be able before he finished to show by the state- ment of facts that had been submitted to him that there was a very serious cause for a further inquiry into the mat- Ur. He should like to say that he had heard with consi- derable regret that the Chief Constable considered that his (Mr. Roberts') action was in some sense or other a reflection upon him and upon the police force, but he wished to repudiate any such suggestion. For his own part be had a high opinion of Mr. Hunt and of the police force. (Hear, hear.) He knew nearly every member of the force, and a finer set of men he did not think existed in Lancashire. The fault he had to find was not with the Chief Constable or with the police, but with the Watch Committee. He must say that he had had considerable difficulty in ascertaining the facts of the case. for in the first place there was nothing on the minute book of the Watch Committee, and he had applied to the Chief Constable for a copy of the report which he presented to the Watch Committee, but the Chief Constable declined to give him that report. without giving any reason for so declining. He was perfectly at a loss to know why that information was withheld from him. Councillor Roberts then referred in detail to the action of Neill in connection with the prisoner Smith, whom he ap- prehended at Ashton on the 20th July, and he (Councillor Roberts) strongly reprobated the conduct of the officer. He submitted that Neill had been guilty of something more serious than an irregularity, and he held that in the in- terests of the police force itself the case should be further investigated, because if incidents of that kind were allowed to go on it was a direct incitement to acts of a similar char- acter on the part of members of the police farce; and the interests of the public also demanded further investigation. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR poieted out that Neill was not now in the employ of the Corporation, and asked what possible good cocld come ot requesting the Wateh Committee to furnish the Council with a full statement of particulars. He also remarked that the Watch Committee were not amenable to that Council. • tleAlderman BURGESS seconded the motion,and said that that Council could not afford to refuse the inquiry asked for, and it would never do to say that the Watch Committee was not amenable to the Council. Alderman CROSFIELD thought with Councillor Roberts that they ought to keep up the character of the police force in Warrington. He must say that he respected the police very much and thought them an admirable body of men, and for the sake of the character of the police he was of opinion that something ought to be done in this case. The MAYOR: You cannot do anything with him. Councillor BOLTON did not think it fair for a member to get up there and make an attack upon a man who wal absent and had his living to get. He thought the matter had been brought forward for purely vindictive motives. Alderman WEBSTER and Councillor BROADBENT defended the action of the Watch Committee, and Councillor SUTTON, Alderman DAVIES, and Alderman HoLarEs advised the with- drawal of the motion. Councillor ROBERTS, in replying, repudiated the assertion that he had pursued that matter from vindictive motives, and said he had done so at the stern call of duty. After the explanatiens given he was quite prepared, for the moment at aay rate, to withdraw the motion. The discussion then ceased. VOTE OF THANES TO THE MAYOR. Alderman HOLMES in very complimentary terms moved: —" That the best thanks of the Council be presented to Joseph Harrison, Esq., Alderman of this borough, for the able and satisfactory manner in which he has discharged the responsible duties devolving upon him as Mayor and Chief Magistrate of this borough, during this his third year of office, and for the unvarying courtesy, kindness, and impar- tiality displayed by him when presiding over the delibera- tions of the Council and in his intercouse with its members." (Applause.) Alderman WEBSTER seconded, and Alderman DAVIES sup- ported the proposal, after which it was put to the meeting by Alderman Crosfield (Deputy Mayor), and heartily carried. The MAYOR having acknowledged the compliment, the meeting terminated.

Mr. BLUNDELL MAPLE had placed on the agenda a resolutions favouring combinations for thrift among tin=mhers of clubs in the National Union ; but in his ab- sence, Mr. BIEO,II HEED read Mr. Maple's resolution and speech.

- Colonel MALLESON (City of London Carlton Club) moved —`‘_That this Con'erence has confidence that Her Majesty's present Government will pur,ne the patriotic policy of Lord Beaconsfield in vigilantly guarding British interests in the East from the aggression of Russia, and that they will es- pecially guard the independence of Constantinople."—Col. INlalleson was speaking to his resolution, when Lord Ran- dolph Churchill entered the room. The delegates rose in a body, and cheered his lordship with enthusiasm ; the demon- straiion having ben preceded but a few minutes by a cor- dial welcome to Mr. Chaplin. . .

Quiet having been restored, Co). MALLESON argued that if a strong maritime power obtains: possession of the Darda- nelles. and cons,quently control of the Mediterranean, it would be an exceedingly serious matter for the interests of this country.

Lord R. CnuecteiLL, in his reply, said there could not be the least doubt that the policy which had animated Lord Beaconsfield would be the policy which would amuate the present Government abroad, so far as the change in circum- stances in Europe would permit. (Hear.) No one would have been more ready than Lord Beaconefidd to adapt his policy to the changing state of affairs in Europe. (Hear.) A pacific policy might be the best for our intereational welfare, and for out. foreign interests. He advised them to study closely our relations with foreign powers, and said they must always be the subject of anxiety; but he believed they might have coredence in the present Government. (Cheers.) Having congratulated the delegates on the success Of the meeting, and the value of their organisation, Lord Randolph urged them to keep the Parliamentary leaders well informed of their desires end wishes, and asked them to hold many meetings in their own localities, rather than great demonstrations at which Cabinet Ministers were ex- pected to attend. Large meetings involved a certain tax on Cabinet Ministers, and the present Government desired to be rather a working than a talking Government. (Cheers.) One other matter he desired to refer to. The speakers of the Separatist Party had constantly attempeed to cultivate the idea that the alliat.ce between the Conservative Party and the Unionist Libera's was but of a fleeting and transi- tory charactee, and that it suited for the last election. They were patting tte idea about sedulously, and were trying to impress upon the Liberal Unionists that they had better come back to the fold. That, however, was an un- scrupulous and dangerous argument, and one upon which Conservatives ought to be on their guard against. The alliance existed from certain defined and important objects, namely, the maintenance of the Union, but subject to that, and the restoration of order in Ireland, and the return to a satisfactory mode of procedure in the House of Commons, nothing further was involved in it (Hear, hear.) These were the main objects of the alliance, and it was perfectly certain that on these lines it would last be- cause Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain bad declared that so long as Mr. Gladstone remained wedded to his present policy of repeal, so long would they do all they could to prevent his return to power As long as they had the support of those statesmen with them, so long would the Union be preserved; and he hoped they would bear that point in mind. In everything they did, he desired them to give the Liberal Unionists the same sup- port as they did at the last election, so long as the circum- stances of the time demanded that there should be a common bond between the Unionists and the Tory party. I (Cheers.) Other resolutions concerning the affiliation of Conserva- tive clubs, organisation of the party in the Radical divisions of Yorkshire, the unsatisfactory position of the law relating to the lodger vote, and the depressed condition of the hop industry inconsequence of foreign competition, were chiefly debated; but were either withdrawn or referred to the Coun- cil for consideration. Tne Conference in each case refrained from expressing a decided opinion. The Conference closed with the usual votes of thanks. THE NIGHT'S MEETING. SPEECH BY LORD R. CHURCHILL. On Tuesday night St. George's Hall was crowded with an immense multitude of people, who displayed the most en- thusiastic interest in the proceedings and in the speakers. They were kept in good humour with vocal and organ per.- formances during the hour which intervened be- tween the opening of the doors and the appearance of Lord R. Churchill. When he was conducted on to the platform he was hailed by the audience with repeated rounds of cheers. Amongst those en the platform were Lord Windsor, Lord Dunraven, Mr. A. K. Rollitt, M.P., Mr. A. L. Cohen, M.P., Mr. Stuart Wortley, M.P., the Earl of Dartmouth, Mr. R. G. Webster, M.P., Mr. Trotter, M.P., Mr. Tomlinson., M.P., Mr. Henniker Heaten, M.P., Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, M.P., Mr. H. Chaplin, M.P., Jets Lord L'ncleshorougb, who was expected to preside, was unable from ill-health to be present, and the chair was therefore taken by Mr. Ashmead Bartlett, M.P.

On the motion of Mr. H. BYRON REID, seconded by Mr. HENRY MITCHELL, a resolution was enthusiastically Passed congratulating the Government upon the great Unionist victory gained at the general election, and expressing com- plete confidence in them. Lord K CHURCHILL, who received an enthusiastic recep- tion, spoke to a resolution expressing the gratification of the meeting on the great Unionist victory gained at the general election and confilence in her Majesty's Ministers. The noble lord said the accounts which reached Ministers as to the social condition of Ireland and as to the prospects of the restoration to tranquillity were encouraging. There had been a marked recovery of prices, and, from all the 1 Government could learn, rents were being fairly paid all over the country. He thought the Irish landlords had a claim upon their consideration. They had justified the con- fidence reposed in them by the Government by granting liberal reductions of rent, and so lessening the difficulties of the crisis by which they were surrounded. The Irish tenantry had co-operated in a signal and marked manner to- wards restoring tranquillity and order. There were some districts where disorder still lingered, and they might have to be specially treats]; but there bad been a marked de- crease in crime and outrage, the returns of which for the last month were lower than they had been for the last five years. There was no doubt that the Irish people had already appreciated or were rapidly appreciating the fell significance of the resolutions of the last general election. He thought if the Unionist party held together and took proper precautions for the future the question of the maintenance or the repeal of the Union was settled for at least two generations. In his reference to foreign affairs the Chancellor of the Exc'eequer said he had reason to know that the opinions he expressed at Dart- ford represented fully, accurately' and fairly the minds of Lord Iddesleigh and of Lord Salisbury. Dealing with the present position of his political opponents, he described them as being sick unto death. He expressed his belief that the country was fairly well satisfied with the Government's programme. On the question of Home Rule. the Light hon. gentleman said the present Government did not intend in any shape er form to grant Home Rule to Ireland, nor to be responsible for any legislation which could by any reason- able person be supposed to contain the germ of Home Rule, but they did intend to deal with the question of local government in Ireland, they did not mean to be hurried or hagy in that dealing, and the proposals of the Government would be drawn upon lines analogous to those upon which they hoped to build up a systen of local government for Great Britain. Lord Randolph then proceed to discuss the question of Parliamentary procedure.

THE NATIONAL UNION OF CONSERVA- TIVE ASSOCIATIONS. LORD R. CHURCHILL AT BRADFORD. The animal conference of the National Union of Conservative Associations commenced on Tuesday, at the Technical College, Bradforl. Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett, M.P., presided, and amongst those present were Sir Albert Kay Rollett, Mr. Stuart Wortley, Mr. Gratrian, Mr. J. W. Plunkett, Mr. Byron Reed, Mr. W. H. Houldsworth, Mr. Hayes Fisher, Mr. Seagar Hunt, Mr. F. S. Powell, Mr. W. a. Long, and other members of Parliament. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report and balance sheet, congratulated the delegates on the remarkable attendance. The conference had a twofold purpose—to re- joice over their glorious victory, and to take council to- gether, so as to make that victory secure and its consequence immutable. Sir ALBERT ROLLITT warmly seconded the motion, wh:ch, after some discussion, was carried. The Conference, which is being held with closed doors, subsequently proceeded to the election of the Council. After the ballot for the election of the Council had been completed, the Conference proceeded with the consideration of a proposition by Mr. SEAGAR HUNT, M.P., that it should be a recommendation to the Conference to empower the members of the Council o act as an Executive Committee until the first meeting of the Council, which should be sum- moned within the first 14 days of February next, and giv- ing power to Mr. Bartlett and the hon. secretary to call the meeting. Mr. GEORGE IRWIN (Leeds) seconded the motion, but little discussion followed, the Conference agreeing to the suggestion of the Chair, that the matter should Ise left in the bands of the Chairman for the time being. The next business introduced was a motion by Mr. BYRON Ruin. M.P., that triennial elections of future Coun- cils were undesirable, and referring the matter back to the Council. Mr. Reed urged that to elect members of the Council for three years was very undesirable, is members of the Council might not be in agreement with the general body of the Union. A rather lively discussion followed, but the Conference adopted the suggestion. The Conference then unanimously elected the Right Hon. Lord Londesborough as president for the ensuing year. The first subject for discussien outside the general busi- ness of the Conference was the following resolution by the Hon. GEORGE CunzoN, M.P.:—"That the Conference of the National Union, recognising the supreme importance of the question of Imperial Federation, impresses upon Con- servatives the desirability of its universal adoption as an article of Conservative faith." Mr. COUTTS STRICKLAND, of the Cambridge Canton Club, seconded the resolution, which was supported by Lord Dux- RAVEN, Under Secretary for the Colonies, who said there were now two alternatives before the country—either to adopt Imperial Federation or increase our military and naval forces. He could not exactly say what scheme could be propounded, but he infinitely preferred feieration to an in- crease of the military and naval forces. The resolution was carried amid loud cheers, and the dele- gates adjourned for luncheon. The Conference resumed its sittings at two o'clock, when Mr. Wainwright (Blackpool) declined to move a resolution in his name, in favour of Women's Suffrage, as it might lead to a division in the party, but another delegate moved the resolution. The proposal in favour of Women's Suffrage was disposed of, after a lively discussion, by a delegate moving the pre- vious question.

Before leaving Bradford on Wednesday Lord Randolph Churchill attended a meeting in the St. George's Hall, at which he was presented with about 400 addresses from Con- servative organisations in all parts of the country. In re- plying, Lord Randolph said he took these abundant ex- pressions of devotion to a great political cause as being in- tended not so much for himself as for tie Government col- lectively,and he was sure those expressions would serve as encouragement in the hard work lying before tbem. One important address came from Scotland, sand his lordship commended the energy and zeal of the men who had created so large a body of Conservative feeling, especially in the West of Scotland. That growth of opinion led him to believe that Lord Beaconsfield's predictions as to the future position of the Tory party in this country were almost realised, and he much regretted that that great man had not lived to see his declarations verified in the present day. Referring to the presence of a deputation from Ireland, Lord Randolph said that unfortunately, through the work of native agitators and some leading men in England, constitutional principles bad not been very popular in that country. All that was wanted in order to make those principles popular was to give Ireland the bene- fit, from which England had gained so much, of strong, orderly government; that the government of Ireland should no banger be the sport and Playground of political parties, and that the great mass of political influence should coin- bime to give to the Irish people those blessings which we in England had for so many years enjoyed. The Chancellor of the Exchequer afterwards paid a brief visit to the works of Messrs. A. and S. Henry and Co, and then left Bradford for Newmarket.

Berystide, near Windsor, the mansion of Mr. Henry Standish, was almost totally destroyed by fire on Wednesday morning. The Prince of Wales was recently a visitor at Berystide, and Mr. and Mrs. Standish were to have Visited His Royal Highness at Sandringham within the next few days. ALLEGED BIGAMY AT BOLTON.—A STRANGE CASE.—At the Bolton Borough Police Court on Monday, Daniel Par- kinson, collier, of Chow bent, was charged, on remand, with committing bigamy on the 16th August, 1885, by inter- marrying Martha Rawsthorne, his wife being then and now alive.—May Markland (formerly Brooks,, wife of James Markland, stoker, Albert.p.lace. Farnworth, stated that she was present at the marriage of Daniel Parkinson and her sisten, Elizabeth Brooks, at the Parish Church of New Bury, near Bolton, on the 11th July, 1876. Her sister was now in court. They lived together until her sister found out that prisoner was going with another woman, and in the month of October, 1877, they separated. Since the parting her sister had had a Chita by another man.—Martha Ravrs- thorne, residing at the Waggon and Horses Inn. Farnworth, stated that she went through the form of marriage with the prisoner at the Wesleyan Methodist Chapel, Bolton, on the 16th August last year. She knew from the first that be was a married man. He had been very kind to her, and she ' had had one child by him.—Prisoner said. in defence, that , his wife baying had a child by another man, and they hav- ing been parted for eight years, he considered there was ' nothing wrong in getting married again.—Prisonor was committed for trial at the assizes.

div.head: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.
div.p: CEMETERY COMMITTEE.

At a meetina of the above Committee the Registrar re- ported that the interments for the past four weeks were : Adults 30, minors 47, stillborn and premature 10; and for the corresponding period last year, adults 31, minors 25, stillborn and premature 13. The receipts for the past four weeks were reported to be £6B 53 9d, and for the correspond- ing period last year £56 Os 4d. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor Buows seconded, the passing of the minutes.—Carried.
TOWN HALL, PARK, AND BATHS COMMITTEE. The minutes of the above Committee were of a routine character.

The MAYOR moved, and Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of the Com- mittee. Councillor DIXON asked if any steps had been taken to prevent the nuisance occasioned on a Sunday afternoon by the pumping at the baths. Nothing was said about the matter in the minutes. Alderman WESTER: When we get new baths all this will
be done away with. (Hear. hear.) The MAYOR said that Councillor Dixon's observations would be attended to.
The minutes were agreed to.

MARKETS COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the above Committee, the total in- come from all sources was reported to amount to £290 17e 7d. Councillor LITTON proposed. and Cpuncillor HUTCHINSON seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BARKER suggested the desirability of altering the pavinv of a portion of the Market-place around the fish stall, as it was in a very deplorable state, and ttie stench that arose in consequence was very strong. Councillor I...rrrox : We have nothing to do with that matter. It belongs to the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee. Councillor BARKER thought it wag desirable something should be done. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were approved. GAS COMMITTEE. At a meeting of the above Committee, on the Ist October, the average illuminating power of the gas for the past fort- night was reported to be equal to 1713 candles at both works. At a meeting on the 15th October the average illu- minating power of the gas for the past :fortnight was repor- ted to be equal to 17.75 candles at both works. On the motion of :Alderman HOLMES, seconded by Coun- cillor WRIGHT, the minutes were agreed to. FIRE ENGINE COMMITTEE.

At a meeting held on the 14th October, the Superintend- ent reported a "run out," and the Borough Treasurer was ordered to pay the expenses, Ll Ss 3d. Councillor FRA.NCOMB moved, and Councillor WILLIAM PIBRPOINT seconded, the confirmation of the minutes. Councillor BOLTON asked for what purpose the superin- tendent had had a "run out" and why the expenses had amounted to £1 8.13 d. Councillor FruNcosts : I think notice should have been given of the question. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: I hardly think it requires that, because a specific sum is mentioned on the minutes. It would have been different if there had been some fresh expendi- ture, and you had had no opportunity of understanding how matters stood. Councillor Strrrort It is a proper question to ask, and I think we ought to know where the superintendent" ran out" to, whether the Chairman went out with him, and where they called at. (Laughter.) . L Councillor Fiascoms : We have a rule that if there is

div.head: SANITARY COMMITTEB.
div.p: SANITARY COMMITTEB.

This Committee met on the 20th October, when it was recommended that the Corporation undertake the paving of Hardy-street, from Lythgoes-lane to the eastern boundary of the intercepting dep6t; and Norman street, from Hardy- street to Orford-lane; and resolved, "That the best thanks of this Committee be tendered to Mr. Alderman Burgess for his able and valuable services as Chairman of the Commit- tee during the past year." Aldertnan BURGESS, in referring to the paving of Hardy. street and Norman-street, said the Council were asked to do what seemed an irregular thing, but as these streets had been put into their present bad elate ny Corporation vans, and as nearly all the traffic was in connection with the Corporation, he thought the Council ought to do the paving. It was estimated that it would take £3OO to do this work. _ _
Councillor SUTTON seconded the proposal, which was supported by Councillor MACKIE and Alderman DAVIES, and carried.

Tlig COST OF STET CONSTRUCTION. At a meeting of the Paving and Sawerage Committee, held on the 4th October, it seas resolved that notice be given to the Gas Department and the Warrington Waterworks Company, Limited, requiring all gas and water mains to be laid at a depth of not less than two feet six inches below
the surface.—At a meeting held on the 18th October, it was resolved "That a footpath be made co-extensive with the

Conservative Club buildings in Winmarleigh-street ; that the tenders of Messrs. Hough and Son for the labour re- quired in forming and paving part of Son, Glad- stone-street, Glazebrook-street, and part of Paul-street, at the following prices, be accepted :—Eustace-street (part), £22 lOs lid; Gladstone-street, £66 2e ; Glazebrook-street, £3l 3s 10d; Paul-street (part), £l5 95 scl; and that the tender of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway, for 1,000 tons of bur stone, at the following prices, be accepted :—At Whitecross Wharf, 23 5d per ton; at Glazebrook-street, 3s 90 per ten; at Gladstone, Eustace, and Paul-streets, 3s 50 per ton.— It was further resolved that the tender of Messrs. Walton

Brothers for 750 lineal yards of 12in. by 51n. curbs, at 25 83 per yard, be accepted; that the tender of Messrs. John Nunnerly and Ce., Limited, for 400 tons of granite setts. f.o.b. Liverpool, at. 163 per ton, be accepted; and that the

tender of Air. William Bennett, for 50,600 c'hequered tiles, at 693 0d per 1,000, be accepted. Alderman DAVIES, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, alluded to the notice which had been given with regard to the laying of gas and water mains, and said this was done to prevent injury to the pipes, especially in streets over which the steam roller passed. Councillor BROWN seconded the motion.
Alderman HOLMES said that as to the general question of laying the pipes at a depth of two feet six inches, he could . . _ _

promise en behalf of the Gas Committee that they would be as good boys as they could—(laughter)—and wherever it was possible they would put the pipes in at that depth. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CROSFIELD wished to call the attention of the

Chairman of the Commiitee to what he thought was a foolish expenditure of money. He thought that the streets of War- rington generally were a credit to the towf. (Hear, hear.) In streets where there was a heary traffic it was siise to get a good foundation before the setts were put down, but he protested against a foundation of 18 inches of red sandstone with setts on the top of that in streets where there was no traffic beyond a cartload of coals once a week, and occa- . _ _

sionally a cab. He alluded to a street at the south end of Spring-gardens, that led nowhere, which had a foundation equal to that of Church-street, over which thousands of tons passed every week. A foundatien of a foot or 18 inches was being put in Arpley-street, but he contended that for the next 50 years there would be no heavy traffic over that road. (Hear, hear.) He really thought the time had come when they should begin to diminish the rates in the town. (Hear, hear.) They had got up to seven shillings in the pound, and in his opinion the rates ought not to be more than five ehillings. (Hear, hear.) Now that the Sanitary Committee had got through their expenditure, and would re- quire no more money to speak of, it would rest with the Paving and Sewerage Committee to get the rates down. He hoped Alderman Davies would take those remarks in the spirit in which they were made. He did not want to inter- _ _ _ _

fere unnecessarily with the work of the Cimmittee, but he thought it was ridiculous to make streets such as he had described where there was next to no traffic. (Hear, hear.) Councillor dom.; PIERPOINT agreed with Alderman Cron- field's remarks, and said that the making of many side streets over which no traffic could possibly be expected to go for the next 50 years or century was enormously costly, and he hoped that the question would be taken up by the Com- mittee and reconsidered. He (the speaker) moved an amendment at the time Suez-street was being laid that the maximum depth of the foendatione in side streets should be nine or ten inches, but he now believed they were getting back to 15 or 16 inches. (Irear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS thought that if Alderman Crosfield had inquired into the merits of the case he would hardly have ventured to make the suggestions he had. (Hear, hear.) All their streets were made according to an order of that Council made 16 or 20 years ago, from which the committee could not deviate. In that rule it was laid down that the foundation should be a certain depth- Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT : What was that? Alderman BURGESS: Nine or twelve inches. Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT : But that was altered. Alderman BURGESS : It was never altered from the time it was entered on the minute book to this day. The com- mitter have never deviated from a rule laid down by the Council. Alderman CROSFIELD : IS there not a foundation of 18 inches in Church-street? Alderman BURGESS: I believe not. Councillor JOHN PIERPOINT : There are 18 inches in Suez- street. Alderman BURGESS contended that if they wished the committee to. make an alteration in their system they must first of all rescind the order ef the Council. (Hear, hear.) He thought when they came to examine the question they would not be led away by a little claptrap about ratepayers and property owners, and all that sort of nonsense. (Laugh- ter, and hear, hear.) He thought they would adhere to their common sense in these matters. (Alderman Crosfield : " We shall.")

Councillor ROBERTS said he could testify that the foun- dations in all the streets which had been made during the past five years were 9 and 12 inches. The foundation in Arpley-street was nine inches, and in Froghall-lane there was one of 12 inches, in full compliance with the regula- tions of the Corporation. The expense of making streets, however—and he spoke from a practical knowledge of the materials—was not so much affected by the character of the foundations as by the quality of the setts placed upon them. They were now using the Irish sett, which cost them four shillings per superficial yard. He maintained that this was a much too costly sett. They ought to use the Rawtenstall sett, which would not cost them more than 2s GI, while it would last almost as long as the most expen- sive kind. (Hear, hear.) It was a waste of money to put down the best Irish or Welsh setts in streets which were only cu lde sacs. (Hear, hear.) Councillor BOLTON said that the question was one which oueht to be looked at from a ratepayers' point of view. He held that if their streets were made in a superficial manner the ratepayers would be called upon to keep them in repair very frequently, while if they were made substantially their cost for repairs would be very little. The ratepayers were bound to protect themselves by seeing that after a street was made it was worth banding over, and that it would not re- quire repairing every other week. (He*, hear.) Councillor Dr. MACKIE was sure that he had been the re- cipient of more complaints in connection with the extrava- gance in the making of streets than upon almost any other subject, and he most earnestly hoped that at an early date the Council would consider the question de novo. (Hear, hear.) Certainly they made some streets which they could see were intended to last almost until the crack of doom. (Hear, hear.) If it was a Question of Irish stones versus Rawtenstall, he would say that in that case the Irish must stand aside. (Laughter.) It was evident to him that what Councillor Bolton had said should not be received as the purest gospel, because if the owner of property was com- pelled to put down streets costing a very large sum of money he simply added it to the rent. (Hear, hear). Councillor Fnmecoun said that they had already begun to use the Rawtenstall setts for side streets, and he thought it might have been done some years ago. The red sandstone foundation was the cheapest material they could get for street foundations. He believed it was actually cheaper than carting the refuse from the different ironworks of the town. Councillor SBTTON said, whilst agreeing that it was very desirable that they should put owners of property to as little expense as possible in making side streets, it after all became a question of policy whether it was not better to make them well than imperfectly. For instance, they knew that it cost less to make a street in the way suggested by

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 30, 1886.

THE Liberals must look to their laurels. Ths Conservative party, after their wont* abused the Caucus in the most vituperative fashion' and have ended not merely by adopt- ing it, but by enthusiastically putting it in practice. In proof of this, we have only to turn to the record of the proceedings, at Brad- ford, of the Union of Conservative Associa- tions. Then again, as to a programme; there is not a single article of faith (except opposi- tion to Home Rule) which is not put forward by the Tories as essential to political salvation that the Tories themselves have not pre- viously denounced as revolutionary or vision- ary. It is true there are some of the old- fashioned sort who are not prepared to swallow, all at once, what Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL has set before them; but they will come roundto a profession of faith when, as they will probably find, profession is all that is expected of them. Lord RANDOLPH is, for the moment, very much in earnest—in his way. The Tories are in office, and his lordship is now the recognised leader of the Tory party in the House of Commons. It is natural that he should like place and power, and, as he has an unnatural readiness for doing anything, however inconsistent, to pre- serve both, he is juggling at present with the Liberal Unionists on the one hand and with the Tories on the other in order to keep the two Parties together. Nobody knows better than he that the Tories are in a minority, and that they can hold office only by "union with the Unionists." How long This unholy alliance ' will last it is impossible to say; but mean- time it is a reality, and, having to humour such Liberals as Lord HARTINGTON and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, Lord RANDOLPH must needs have a Liberal programme. He does not, of course, give it that name; it would not be accepted by his followers if he did, for, as it is, there are some who kick against it. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER is very em- phatic in declaring that "the Government do not intend in any shape or form to grant Home Rule to Ireland, nor to become re- sponsible for any legislation which could by any reasonable person be supposed to con- tain the germ of Home Rule." This may be taken as a pledge to the Liberal Unionists, and as a challenge to the Liberals as a party. It is, however, admitted that the Tories "intend to deal with the question of local government in Ireland ;" and it will therefore be interesting to examine the kind of abortion which does not contain even so much as a " germ of Home Rule." It will, further, be interesting to observe the attitude of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN in face of such a Bill, seeing that he has publicly declared himself in favour of the principle of Home Rule. Will he "jump Jim Crow," or will it be Lord RAN- DOLPH who will again turn about?

The new leader of the Tory party in the House of Commons , has familiarised the public with " Lessons in Political Lying," or the national mind would be shocked at his latest illustrations; but, however indifferent we may, unfortunately, become in a matter of this kind it is none the less immoral. His lordship, with the accustomed face of brass,

div.p: I help may set a man on his legs again, and enable him to keep clear of "the House." The people who imagine that they can do away with outdoor relief have possibly some specific tor driving poverty out of the land. But until they disclose their new social cure- all, we may be forgiven for exercising scepti- cism when they prophesy beneficent results from givinz poor men but one step between independence and the workhouse.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

So the Municipal Elections in Warrington have passed off without the disruption which seemed imminent last week. Even "James," who thought to have a " Cave " to himself, has been " Whittled " away. This is as it should be. All's well that ends well.

Alderman Joseph Harrison, thrice Mayor of Warrington, has well earned the vote of thanks which was accorded him by the Town Council on Tuesday evening. He has been exceedingly courteous and obliging—always ready to lend a helping hand to a good ob- ject. They do say that he was a bit too fluent, especially on the bench.

There is a story told of a darkey who was ordered to be flogged. His master pro- ceeded to lecture him on the enormity of his offence, upon which Sambo exclaimed— " Oh ! massa, if you preachee, preachee, and if you floggee, floggee ; but no preachee and floggee too." The coming Mayor is also something of a preacher, but a word to the wise is sufficient.

The Nonconformists of Widnes have been walked over in the matter of the School Board Election, having returned one only of their three candidates. It is not that they haven't voters, but the voters are not brought to the poll. There is too much apathy, and a lack of organisation. They must fight again on the next occasion, and be prepared for the fight.

The Irish Nationalists are justly proud of their victory in having unseated Mr. Lewis for Londonderry, and put Mr. McCarthy in his place. It is not that they have any special grudge against Mr. Lewis, .who has held the seat for i 4 years, but they rightly conclude that when they can thus win in the heart of Ulster they will soon win all along the line. .

Shakespere couples lunatics and lovers, and there is a young man at St. Helens whose conduct would seem to justify the connection. Having quarrelled with his sweetheart, he got into the house where she lived and burned her dress. Love always was a consuming passion; but Byrnes has cooled down since the magistrates called upon him to pay igs. 6d. for his escapade.

Who says there is no spare cash in the country, when over one hundred millions are offered for shares in the new firm of Guinness and Co? Oh, the power of drink—Oh, the faith in "stout," when the capital required is subscribed a score of times, in as many hours! But brewers do make enormous sums of money; they pay so little for labour in pro- portion to the turn over—a fact which ought to set workingrnen a-thinking.

Let not the Manchester Ship Canal Company despair, now that they have evidence of the scores of millions that are seeking for a profitable investment. But they must con- vince the public that it will be profitable ; they must down with the trump cards them- selves if they would have others follow suit. The hunt is still up, for the latest report is that surveys are now being made in the meadows at Barton and Eccles. But what else is being done?

It will be seen from another column that two Warrington exhibitors of note decline to accept the medals which have been awarded them by Ole jury of the Liverpool Exhibition. It is a thousand pities that a doubt should have crept in as to the awards being given in all cases for merit pure and simple. The Exhibition Committee owe it tothemselves and to the public to carry out a most searching investigation into the alleged dishonourable touting for gold medals.

The Rev. H. Elwell Smith, late curate at Earlestown, has been for some time under the ban of his bishop. He has been appeal- ing to have the inhibition withdrawn; and, failing this,, he intimates his intention to iqnore ecclesiastical domination in his lordship's diocese." The Bishop's secretary retorts by calling attention to the fact that Mr. Smith was "defendant in the case heard before the county magistrates" in November last. The Bishop seems to think that if the inhibited curate leaves the Church it will be for the Church's good.

James Concannon, of Widnes, would seem to be a "chartered libertine" in the matter of ferocious dogs. An order was made upon him in November last to keep one under con- trol; and his idea of obeying the order seems to have been to turn out with this and two other ferocious dogs—all on the loose. A constable saw the dogs run at people and at- tempt to bite them; but the magistrates did not go beyond their fotmula of making an orcter. Tames Concannon will now feel at liberty to parade the town with six ferocious dogs, and when they have worried a magis- trate he will perhaps be dealt with according to his deserts.

At an inquest held on the body of Patrick Ryan, who lost his life at St. Helens through falling into a chemical pan, the jury seemed to think something, should be done to prevent such an accident for the future. Her Ma- jesty's Inspector of Factories, however, says it was "a most dangerous and unnecessary proceeding" for the man to get on the edge of the pan. This would appear to be a case in which the man had it in his Dower to pro- tect himself; and the lesson to be learnt is that workmen should not incur unnecessary risk.

The fatal accident to a carriage washer at Bank Quay .Station, Warrington, was of a different character. From the inquest held on Tuesday, it seems that the victim ran risks which were unavoidable. He had to use a brush which was seven feet long, while, when a train was passing,there was "only three feet between the footboard of one train, and the axle box of the other." The jury did well to throw blame on the Railway Company "for allowing carriages to be washed in such a dangerous place ;" and the Coroner was quite justified in complaining that the Com- pany had treated the case so lightly that they were not even repiesented by their solicitor.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 30. 1886.

THEATRE ROYAL, RUNCORN.—Miss Maude Branscombe terminated a three days' engagement at this theatre on Wednesday night. The building was crowded to the door lon each evening. On Thursday, Miss Gertrude Norman's Company opened with "Her Atonement." RESISTING THE POLICE AT WIDNES. A youth named Thomas Walsh appeared at Widnes Petty Sesaions, on Thursday, to answer a charge of resisting P.C. Heibrook in the execution of his duty. On Saturday night, the 16th, the constable arrested the defendant's sister on a charge of disorderly conduct in Sankey-street. The defendant at- tempted to rescue his sister, and was with great difficulty got away,—A line of 5s and costs or seven days' hard labour was imposed. THEFT OF A WATCH AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, John Smith, a tramp, was charged with stealing a silver Waltham lever watch, worth 101 ficl, the property of Alfrsd Brouchernite. landlord of the Model Lodging-house, Lugsdale-road. A woman named Mary Seed was charged with complicity in the robbery. While in the dock the female produced the watch from her pocket, and stated that it was given her by Smith. Both prisoLere were re- . minded to Monday. CLOSING OF A WELL AT NORTON. Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Ses- sions, on Monday, Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, applied on behalf of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority' for an order ender the Public Health Act, to close a well on the Manor Farm of the Norton estate, belonging to Sir Richard Brooke, Bart. Mr. Farrington, the nuisance inspector, stated that the Manor Farm was occupied bv Captain Bagu- ley and described that the well was surrounded by privies, cesspools, and pig styes, from which filth liquid percolated through the poreus soil into the well. The water was drawn through an old "pump tree." There had recently been a case of typhoid fever at the farm. Dr. Carter Bell, the county analyst, had analysed a sample of the water, and cerified that it was "a very bad water and not fit for do- mestic use." The Bench made an order that the well should be cloel until the owners could show that the water was fit for domestic use. AN Ex POLICEMAN CHARGED WITH THEFT AT RUN- MEM—More Mr. J. Brupdrit, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, Joseph Foulkes, until recently agent for the Singer Manufacturing Company, at Runcorn, was charged with stealing a chair, worth 6' the property of Mendel Blank, a Jew furniture dealer, Ellesinere-street, Runcorn, On Thursday Foulkes obtained Blank a customer for a wringing machine, and the latter promised to give him 23 for his 2ood offices. After the machine was delivered Blank declined to pay the commission until he had received the first instalment from the purchaser. Foulkes was not satisfied with this, and in the evening Blank missing a chair from a truck, suspicion fell upon the prisoner. who was ap- prehended by P.C. Milliagton. At that time be was muddled in drink, and admitted that he had "taken the chair for his money." He took the constable to the Old Q lay, where he had thrown the chair, hut would not ac- company the officer to the police station until he had had a 1 pint of bear. The witnesses were cross-examined by Mr. J. W. Knowles, of Widnes, who defended. The magistrate , did think thare was sufficient evidence to remand the pri- soner. Mr. Knowles said the prisoner was a man with an excellent character. He had been a water bailiff at Chester, and for sortie time was in the Warrington borough po:ice force. Mr. Brundrit said it was evidently another case of drinking, which was the curse of so many people. He warned the prisoner to be careful in future, and dis- charged him. THE WIDNES COUNTY COURT.—The Registrar has taken an office in St. Paul's Buildings; and the sit- tings of the court will commence next year, and will be held once a month, the sittings already , fixed being Friday, January 28th, February 25th, , and March 25th. The office for entering plaints will probably be opened next month.' The district of this court will include Widnes, Appleton, Pam- worth, Cronton, Ditton, Hale, Halewood, Speke, and Much and Little Woolton. Courts will be held at St. Helens once a fortnight as usual. LIBERATION SOCIETY'S MEETING AT MANCHES- , TER.—The annual meeting of the Manchester and District Branch of the Liberation Society was held on Tuesday at Manchester. Mr. J. H. Crosfield pre- sided. In the report, which was read by Mr. J. F. , Alexander (secretary?, the committee said that they had never before had to deal with the work of two general elections within one twelve mouths, and scarcely ever had had to record such scanty legis- lative results as to their own movement; yet they recognised the signs of• some progress. The agricul- tural householders had disappointed the hopes of the Tories even more than the committee had anti- cipated would be the case. The counties appealed to on the cry of "The Church in danger," gave a large majority to the Liberal party and to the Liberationists within that party. The classes who knew most about the Establishment pronounced its doom. The Establishment men were convinced that disestablishment was the inevitable battle- : ground of the near political future. Trim HOME IRON TRADE.—After the depression i which has hung over the English iron market these 1 many months past, it is a positive relief to be able to chronicle that the improvement which has been coming so slowly and for so long has assumed a definite shape. Notwithstanding what croakers' and doubters may say to the contrary, there can now no longer be any doubt as to the reality of the better prospects of the English iron trade. Steel may be said to have given the impetus, and the re- newed activity in that branch brought with it first a revival in the hematite and now also in the ordinary pig-iron business. We note with equal satisfaction that the better turn shipbuilding is taking has re- animated the finished iron trade. The reports re- ceived from our correspondents this week may be I described as uniformly cheerful and cheering. The 1 North of England pig-iron market has been quiet, but this is due chiefly to the reluctance of makers to conclude coiitracts on present terms, which, although better than a few months back, are still thought by them not to be sufficiently remunera- tive.—lron. A ST. HELENS DIVORCE CASE: SCENE IN COURT.— In the Divorce Court, on Friday, before Mr. Justice Butt, the case of Thompson v. Thompson, in which I the wife, Mrs. Annie Thompson, sought a judiciul separation on the ground of her husband's adultery, came on. The marriage took place in November, 1883, and the petitioner afterwards lived with her husband, Frederick Thompson, an analytical chemist at St. Helens. The petitioner ultimately found upon inquiry that her husband had been in- timate, and continued such relations, with a young lady named Jessie Stewart, living in Crosfield-street, Liverpool, and presented a petition. --Whilst the evidence in proof of petitioner's case was proceeding, the respondent, who for some time had evinced premonitory symptoms of a fit by great agitation and shaking of his clenched fists, suddenly uttered_ a series of piercing shrieks in court, which necessitated his hasty removal and the temporary adjournment of the case until his recovery. Later on he was sufficiently well to be examined; and whilst admitting adultery with Jessie Stewart before his marriage, he denied that anything improper had afterwards taken place. He admitted, in cross-examination. that the lady was a person of loose character. In the result his lordship considered that the charge of adultery had not been established, and dismissed the petition. MARRIAGE OF A DAUGHTER OF THE REV. J. CAL- VERT. Says, in one portion of his Bradford speech, that "nothing whatever has been added to the programme which we put before the country in November and in January last ;" and then, with characteristic inaccuracy, pro- ceeds to name, as two things which have been added, the proposal to deal with the Payment of tithes, and "the conclusion that there must be some power adopted by Parlia- ment for closing debate." Then there is what is generallf spoken of as "the three acres and cow' question. It is a simple matter of history, that the Tory Government were turned out of office on a motion of Mr. JESSE COLLINGs relating to this subject. But Lord RANDoLpH ignores history, for he now appropriates Mr. JESSE CoLLINGS and his theories, while impudently declaring that nothing whatever has been added to the Tory programme, But, worse still, this " Po- litical Welsher," as Mr. PARNELL not in- aptly designated him, completely shuts his eyes to the main feature of " the pro- gramme of the z6:h January." That was described by the then leader of the Tory party (since ousted) as "the policy of the suppression of the National League." We hear nothing of that to-day; Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL knows perfectly well that it .would not go down with the Liberal Unionists, upon whose Miles he depends for his official existence, and yet he can prate of consistency while his conduct makes a mockery of the word! Lord RANDOLPH, to crown his topsy-turveydorr., would, having "changed his mind," enforce the most strin- gent closure on the House of Commons ; it is a pity the closure cannot be brought home. There would be less heard of the lying spirit which is abroad if the closure were applied to him.

THE project of a church House, by way of commemorating the QUEEN'S Jubilee, is an untimely piece of ecclesiastical display, which is calculated to injure the Church in the eyes of its best friends, and to set in a more glar- ing light the abuses in the Establishment which still call for a remedy. We do not want better backing for this opinion than the letter which an " East Anglian Rector " sends to the " Standard." " Sir," he says, , "The income of my living last year was I twenty-three pounds ; this year it may be sixty pounds. My parishioners, many of them, stand on the village green with their hands in their pocket and starvation in their faces, while Bishops with five thousand . pounds a year press us both to give to the Church House. Of the above twenty-three pounds, Queen ANNE'S Bounty desire to have ! twelve pounds as first fruits, to augment small livings ! I shall have to pay it." What our "East Anglian Rector" says scores and hundreds of poor curates can repeat, and i no one with the most superficial knowledge of the distribution of Church endowments I can deny. When the Church has set its , house in order, it can build a great Temple to celebrate is triumphs and give evidence be- fore all men of its strength and virtue. But at present it is in no condition to do anything 1 of the kind. However, even if he affairs of the Church were in a more satisfactory condition than they are, it may be doubt- ful whether it would be well to focus, as it were, the bad taste, the want of origi- nality, the poverty of design, of our architects in a building which cannot be anything more than a pretentious imitation of a style which is as dead as the men who originated it. Mr. RUSKIN has shown us very clearly why men ; do not build such churches as Notre Dame or Westminster Abbey nowadays. We have lost the 'spirit out of which these beautiful thoughts in stone grew. If we build anything now ; with a will, it is an hotel, or a railway station, ; or an exchange. Nothing is more beautiful than to observe, in the decorated style of Gothic architecture, the intense love that the artist took in his work, and the delight which it gave him to adorn it with representations of all that was most delightful in the heavens and the earth and the waters that are beneath the earth. Not the most enthusiastic believer in the virtues of the nineteenth century will ! pretend that any such spirit exists now. If , we build a great Church Temple it will be ; from a kind of vague sense that we ought to do what our fathers have done, and that the men who invented railways and telephones are bound to show that they are not to be beaten by ignorant ecclesiastics who lived in the "dark ages." Well, the light that shines on us is not the "light of other days." It may be just as radiant, but it takes a difErent direction. If the Church desires to do some- thing worthy, there are still, we should say, plenty of poor about her lands, plenty of ignorance which she does not enlighten, plenty of vice which she does not redeem, plenty of lives that derive no help from her services andieher counsels. Let her take ac- count of them instead of building a Church House which, after all, cannot turn out to be anything more than a kind of sanctified Crystal Palace.

A CONFERENCE of Poor-law officers no doubt represents a great body of collective wisdom. Guardians of the poor are men of business, and they do their work conscienti- ously in nearly all cases, and mercifully, we hope, in a good many, but when they meet in solemn conclave they do not, we think, do entire justice to themselves. Mr. SCLATER BOOTH seems to imagine that the main use for Poor-aw conferences is to secure " con- tinued watchfulness over out-door relief." In this spirit of watchfulness, accordingly, the Rev. B. HALL BUCKLE read a paper and moved a resolution to the effect that "out- door relief, being the chief cause of pauper- ism, should receive the urgent attention of guardians, with the object of reducing it to a minimum." One might gather from this that the whole duty of the watchful guardian was to keep his watchful eye on outdoor relief, combined of course with the general duty of forcing everything—including the pauper's subsistence—down to a minimum. We con- fess that we regard this as a somewhat res- tricted view of Poor-law guardianship. On the other hand we fear our minds are not sufficiently expansive to endorse so very sweeping a generalisation as that outdoor relief is the chief cause of pauperism, the corollory of which is we suppose, that if you abolish outdoor relief you will also do away with paupers. It would, we submit, be just as fair and as accurate to say that outdoor re- lief is a prevention of pauperism. The sys- tem, of course, is far from being a good one, and the abuses of it are occasionally flagrant. But it may be questioned whether as a rule guardians are the easy dupes of imposture which in their conferences they represent themselves to be. They are as a rule hard- headed, and not always too soft-hearted men of business, and it is by no means easy for the professional pauper to pasture on their tender mercies. It is undoubtedly true that indiscriminate outdoor relief may sap the energies of the idle and the unreliant among the poor. But it is also true that temporary

Sweeney. " Ihe Union, its effect, and remedy," is the subjecteand Englishmen "who want to hear the cause of Ireland tally and fairly stated, are cordially invited." Worsley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Bull's React public-house, on Monday, upon the body of William Moores, 73 years of age, an old employee of the Bridgewater Navi- gation Company, who fell down dead on Friday under cir- curnseanc,s already reported. A. verdict was returned that death was die to natural causes. WIDNES C:E.T.S.7-The usual weekly meeting was held on Thursday evening in the National Schools, under the presidency of the Vicar. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—At this court on Wednesday, Samuel Gregory was convicted of having, on the 21st June, trespassed upon land in the occupation of William Bradbury, at Norton, in search of game. A fine of 10e, and costs 18s, was imposed and paid.—,For sleeping in an unoccupied house in Penketh-lane on Tuesday night, Mary Ann Walsh and Margaret Martin were, on the evidence of Inspector Millington, sentenced to 21 days' hard labour. CAMDEN IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN. At the weekly meeting of this class on Friday evening last, Mr J W Woodland read a paper on " The disesteblishment of the Church of England." A friendly discussion aftemards took place, which was taken part in by the Rev T B Bell and Mr W H Rogerson, of Holy Trinity Church (who were present on invitation), and Messrs John Moulton and H D Kitte. The debate was adjourned for a fortnight on the motion of Mr Kitto. Mr liandle presided, and there was a fair attendance. DYSON'S DIORAMA. AT RUNCORN.—The pictorial and mu- sical entertainments provided by Mr. Joshua Dyson, in Run- corn Public Hall, during the present week, hava been an unqualified success. There have been crowded audiences each evening, and those present have manifested their de- light in an unmistakeable manner. The dioramic views have embraced many quarters of the civilized globe, and with Mr. Dyson as guide, pleasant and profitable evenings have been spent. The musical performance of the gipsy choir is an undoubted attraction. FEROCIOUS DOGS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, James Concennon, formerly a noted foot racer, was charged with using the owner of three ferocious dogs, without having them under proper control. tie was also charged with keeping a dog without a license.—P.C. Thomp- son stated that he was in Widnes-road on the 18th October, and saw three greyhounds belonging to the defendant "run at people" and attempt to bite them. The defendant had only two licenses. Inspector Wood said that on the 4th November, 1885, an order was made upon the defendant to keep a ferocious dog under control. The same dog was in- cluded in the present charge. The Bench made an order upon the defendant, who did not appear, to keep the dogs under proper control. He was also fined 7s 6d and costs for not having a license. NARROW ESCAPE OF AN EXPRESS TRAIN AT DITTON.— One night last week the Chester express bad a narrow escape from being wrecked near Ditton Junction station. A tree had fallen from a goods train that had passed shortly before the express was due, and, unperceived by any of the officials, it lay directly across the line. The express rushed through the station at a tremendous rate, and the life- guards striking the tree, it was dashed down the line a con- siderable distance. The engine wheels, on coming in con- tact with the trunk again, smashed it to pieces, and the train proceeeded safely on its way. Both the life-guards in front of the wheels were broken, but beyond that no damage was done. The train from which the huge log fell was bound from Garston to Wigan, the timber being for use in the collieries. Several of the props came loose, and con- siderabte damage was none, some bricks being knocked out of the bridge, a trespass board destroyed, and a lamp slightly injured. The line, however, was not blocked. MR. SPURGEON ON WIDNES —ln connection with the Widnes Baptist Chapel, a bazaar is to be held in the Baths Assealbly-room, on Tuesday and Wednesday next. Fell particulars will be found in our announcement column. The proceeds of the affair are to be added to the fund for the erection of a new chapel. The trustees have a capital site in view, and it is hoped that a sum eufficient to complete the purchase and transfer of the land will be realised. The Rev. R. Yeatman, the pastor, has received the following letter, dated October 25th, from the Rey. C. H. Spurgeon, of London have often heard of the inconvenience of the Baptist Chapel at Widnes. Now Widnes itself is not pre- cisely paradise, and a place of worship stuck down in the worst part of Widnes is • badly placed indeed. What with smells and gases the friends at times have a hard time of it, and it will be a real act of charity to. help them to worship in a little better air, if there be any better air in such a chemical town. Mr. Yeatman is doing well and deserves the favourable regard of all his brethren. The church also is helping itself, therefore may look to be helped by others." RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fort- nightly meeting was held on Tuesday, under the presidency of Lieutenant-Colonel Ashton. Present—The Revs J W N Tanner and John Lockwood, Messrs J Weir, Aaron, Lewis, Whitlow, Brandreth. Hadfield, Mclntyre, Knowles, Hall, Percival, Moanfield, H Linaker (clerk), W H Linaker (assistant clerk). and James Farrington (nuisance inspec- tor.) The Medical Officer (Dr Adams) reported a case of typhoid fever at a cottage in Sandy-lane, Weston, the patient being a young man aged 22. The man came home from Coventry a fortnight ago on account of illness, and he soon showed symptoms of typhoid fever. The case was therefore imported. He was unable to find any sanitary de- fects about the premises, and the water was from the com- pany's main. The usual precautions had been taken, and he trusted there would be no extension of the disease. The condition of the roads at Weston Point was a disgrace to any township, and it was really time public opinion should be exerted in the proper direction. It did not appear to him that the Sanitary Authority could undertake the duties of a highway board. There was no other business of im- portance. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.—The fortnightly meet- ing of the members of this Board was held on Thursday, at the Workhouse, Whiston, Mr. John Lowe presiding, and there were also present—Mr. R. Neilson, J.P. (ex officio), Rev. Thomas Chambers, Messrs. J. W. Wareing, J. Fisher, J. Jackson. W. Middlehurst, J. Buckley, W. G. Ashton, J. Whalley, J. Burchall, W. Gerard, W. Tyrer, E. Syder, C. B. Johnson, J. Ranson, J. Ellison, Thomas Heald, Joseph , Griffith, and P. Longton. A lettet was read from Mr. j Henry Sumner, architect, Liverpool, accepting the cheque for £2OO in settlement of his account for professional ser- I vices.—The Clerk (Mr. Hartley) said he had received a I pamphlet entitled, "The Child of the English Savage " (laughter).—Mr. Johnson asked what was the drift of the pamphlet P The Clerk said he did not know, as be had not read it. Any Guardian could read it if he liked, but as it was sent to the Union it must be included in the official documents. (Leughter.) The pamphlet was laid on the table.
