div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting s";a-s held on Thursday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P. Present— Revs. J. Clarke, T. Finegan. Messrs. Bradshaw, Deacon, Iniison. Glover, and Dr. O'Keefe, with G. U. Danby (clerk). • _ _

div.head: YEAR'S EDUCATIONAL WORE,
div.p: A YEAR'S EDUCATIONAL WORE,

Mr. H. W. Deacon, chairman of the committee, presented a report of the work of the District Education Committee during the past year. It appeared that there bad been 4.176 cases summoned before the committee, as compared with 4,051 in 1885. In the present year these cases repre- sented 2,035 persons, lest year 1,783 persons. There had been r,213 persons before the committee for 2.658 offences against the Education Act, whilst in 1885 there were 1,164 persons who had to answer 2,634 complaints. 823 persons made 1,518 applications for the payment Of school fees, and the fees were paid in 1,400 cases. In 1885, 619 persons asked for the payment of school fees in 1,417 cases, and the fees were paid in 1,306 cases. There were 394 persons prosecuted before the magistrates, and BTh were convicted and fined as compared with 559 prosecuted and 537 fined in 1885. In 1885 there were six children committed to industrial schools, this year 11, end at present there were 40 children in those institutioes. Tne evereee number on the rolls was 5,957.5, average attendance 4,909 2, per centaire 82'3. In 1885 the figures were ever Age on the rolls 5,7371, average attendance 4,752 9. 'pt.:- centage 83.—Mr. Deacon, in com- menting upon this report, drew attention to the increase In the applications for echool fees. There were fees paid for 1 7,8 children to each persen, whilst last 'year there were 2 1-3 children t each person. The payments varied throughout all the year, but he could not explain why they should vary so much. It looked as though the fami- lies were smaller this year than formerly. There had been 163 fewer p osecntions this year than last, and as the committee hed acted on the same basis this year as in other years, this was a matter for congratulation. (Hear, hear.) He should like to say a word or two with regard to the state of things that existed six years ago when he and Father Clarke were that appointed en the committee. They had at first Mr. Hartland as a colleague, and for the last three Tears Mr. Glover had been their coadjutor. In 1881 the average percentage of attendance was 71.2, this year it was 822, an increase of 11 per cent. It might be con- sidered that this result was o,etained by forcing the children into the Beerd schools and neglecting the voluntary schools. The average attendance in the volun- tary schools had, however, also considerahlv increased. In 1881 the average attendance in voluntary schools was 657; this year it had increased to 79 8, an increase of 14'1 net cent. This was an indication that the committee had done its work fairly and impartially. In 1881 the average attendance in the United Kingdom was 711; in Widnes 778. In 1885 the average for the United Kingdom was 764; for Widnes 85.9. (Hear, hear.) In voluntary schou:s the average for the United Kingdom in 1881 was 70 6 ; in Widnes 651. In 1885 the average for the United Kingdom was 763; in Widnes 799; that was 3.6 above the average. He (Mi. Deacon) thought the committee could claim some credit for this improved state of the attendance, though he might mention the Council of Education as an important factor. These figures, be thought, showed not a bad increase for the six years. (Applause.)—Mr. Mover referred to the children in industrial schools, and said it ought to be clearly understood that great disgrace attached to an able bodied father who lost the control of his child.—The Chairman remarked that the report was very gratifying, and he moved its adoption, accompanied with a vote of thanks to the , cammittee‘ and especially the chairman of the committee. ' (Hear, hear.) He adverted to the immense amount of work the committee had to perform, and said the warmest thanks of tke Board were due to the members.—The motion was carried unanimously.

div.head: ADMIRAInE RESULTS.
div.p: ADMIRAInE RESULTS.

On the recomMendation of the School Management Com- mittee, it was decided that a bonus of £5 be paid to Mr. E. Robinson. assistant master in the senior boys' department of the Simms' Cross Schools, in recognition of his success as a teacher during the past year, he having passed the whole of his class at the recent Government examinations without a single failure in any subject.—The Chairman said the result betokened A great deal of hard conscientious work on Mr. Robinson's part.
CHANGES.
Numerous changes in the teaching staff were made on the recommendation of the Management Committee.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Accounts amounting to £984 were passed for payment. Since the last meeting the following same had been received —Fees from Simms Cross £6l Os 7d, Warrington-road £27 Os 4d, West Bank 445 18s id, from overseers on account of precept £l,OOO, small 'items £1 2s 6d, total £1,135 17s 6d.
VOTES OF THANES.

The Rev. Father Clarke, as one of the oldest members of the Board, proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman for the eminently able manner in which he had presided over the affairs of the Board during the past three vears. (Hear, hear.) Every member bad admired the dignity and firm- ness which Mr limmis had brought to bear upon his du- ties, and at the same time bad experienced something of the kindness which be had on all occasions exercised towards the Board.—Mr. H. W. Deacon seconded the motion with pleasure, and observed that Father Clarke had expressed the views of the members.—The Clerk, in putting the mo- tion to the meeting, said he had the utmost possible pleasure in bearing his testimony to the ability Mr. Timmis had dis- played in conducting the business of the Board, and to the courtesy which he had exhibited towards all with whom he was brought in contact. (Hear. hear.) The vote was unanimously carried.—The Chairman expressed his heart- felt thanks for the vote which they had been pleased to pas 4 so unanimously, and also for the kind words the proposer and seconder had been good enough to use, He could not for one moment take to himself the entire credit for the un- animity and harmony which had prevailed at the Board. He rather attributed it in the main to the courtesy dis- played by every member of the Board, and the desire which all bad evinced to carry out the work speedily and without indulging in undue controversy. Upon all matters brought before the Board there had been fair criti clam, but generally the conclusions of the committees had been accepted, a circumstance due to the fact that all their matters had been well fought out before being brought to the Board.—Mr. Imison moved, and Mr. Glover seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr. Bradshaw, the vice-chairman.—The Chairman, in supporting the motion, said he was sorry that that Board would be deprived of the services of some of the old members. Two gentlemen had retired voluntarily, while a third had been defeated at the poll. He referred to Mr. Joseph Robinson, and he regretted that a gentleman who had joined them so recently, and who gave such pro- mise of bane- a useful member had not been returned to the Board. (Hear, bear.)—The motion was carried unani- mously, and Mr. Bradshaw having replied, the meeting ter- minated.

MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, WIDNES. A sale of work in aid of the funds of this chapel was held in Mali's Temperance Hall on Thursday. There were two stalls tastefully decorated and laden with a capital assortment of useful and fancy articles. The former were by far the most numerous, and represented the industry of many a busy hour: The ladies who presided over these stalls were—(l) Mrs. G. Rae, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mrs. Dorn- ing, the Misses Warne, Miss TravN, and Miss Doming; (2) Mrs. Chapman, Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Philips, Mrs. Lewis, and Miss Thomas. There was also a refreshment stall, from which the good things were dispensed by Mrs. and Miss Hodgkinson, Mrs. McCririe, Miss Baron, and Miss Hirst. The opening ceremony was performed by the Rev. R. G. Hughes, the pastor, who said the articles they saw on those beautiful stalls represented the labours of seven or eight ladies of the church who had been meeting once a fortnight for the last five months, and he thought they de- served a high compliment. (Hear, bear.) Mr. Brock, when he opened their last bazaar, stated that the efforts of the working classes were far greater, far higher, and far nobler than the special giving or bestowment of money by rich and wealthy gentlemen—(hear, hear)—and they saw before them that afternoon the results of the self-sac,ificing labours •of the wives of working-men. It was in their soul to work, and he hoped they would continue for evermore to do that' which was good.—The Rev. R. Burdon (Wesleyan superin- , tendent) also spoke. He was sure they had a very able and 1 a very devoted pastor in Mr. Hughes, and if they would help him with sympathy they would find their church the centre of holy light and mighty power. (Applause.)— The Rev. J. Bryant (Wesleyan) held out the right hand of fellowship, and expressed his pleasure to find the spirit of unity amongst the various churches in Widnes. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. R. Yeatman expressed his cordial syni- p i lthy with Mr. Hughes and his congregation in the work n which they were engaged.—The sale was then proceeded with. In the evening various amusements were provided for the visitors.

HAWKING BAD RABBITS AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Robert Swift, of St. Helens, and Alexander Murray, of West Bank, Wid- nes, were summoned on a charge of having offered for sale on Widnes market ground, 19 rabbits which were unfit for the food of man.—Mr. Eccles, of St. Helens, defended Swift —Mr. Dickson, inspector of nuisances, said on the 9th Oc- tober he saw the defendants on tha market ground offering the rabbits for sale. The rabbits were in an advanced state of decomposition, and the Medical Officer of Health (Dr. , Cooper) certified that they were quite unfit for human food. A justice of the peace gave an order for their de- struction. He afterwards found 40 other bad rabbis in the hack yard of Murray's house.—Mr. Shepherd, assistant inspector, corroborated. He also proved that both men were in charge of the rabbits.—Mrs Murray said Swift brought a quantity of rabbits to her house. on Timrs-lay night, and another late on EcidaY. The last lot turned out very bad. Swift skinned them on Saturday nimning. He urged her son to go out with them, but he said he would see Mr. Shepherd lirst.—Mr. Eccles, for the defence, stated that Swift was in the employ of Nickson, a fish and game dealer in a large way of business at St. Helens. On Thursday, the 7th inst, Nickson told Swift to find a customer for two boxes of rabbits, and Swift sold them to Murray. He denied that Swift had ar*thing to do with them. If the rabbits were bad when sent off to Widnes by Nickson, it was im- possible to find words strong enough to characterise Nick-

I son's character, and be was deserving of the most severe ceesure.—Benjamin Anders, porters at St. Helens railway station, deposed to Nickson consigning the rabbits to Wid- nes.—Francis Swift, brother to the defendant, stated that on Friday, the Bth inst. Nickeon told him he had sent his (wit- ness's) brother to Widnes to sell some rabbits. Nielson had refused on the previous night to come as a witness.—The defendant Murray stated that on Thursday, the 7th, he was in a beerbouse at the "Snig," when Swift entered and said if he would let him put his rabbits on his (Murray's) cart, he would pay him 4s per day. Swift sold the raboits, and he "shoved the cart.' On Saturday he went away without paying him his 3 days' wages, and also without paying • a , shilling for a "night's doss" at his mother's house. The • Bench fined Swift 20s and costs 17s. or one month's hard • labour; and Murray was mulcted in a penalty of 103 and costs, or 14 days hard labour.

THE IXCAVATIONS IN BRIDGE-
STREET.

The search after relics of the ancient Warrington friary is still being carried on with successful results in Bridge-street. The entire chancel has now been uncovered, and it is found to he 60 feet 6 inches in length and 20 feet 3 inches in breadth, this being a very large size. The wall at the east end of the chancel is 4 feet 7 inches in solid thick- ness and supported by massive buttresses. On the south side, at the entrance into the chancel, a door-. way has been discovered, the stonework upon the west side of which is very elaborate. Beyond-this doorway, and continuing to the south, tiles have been fond in position, and it is extremely probable that this doorway would .lead into the cloister. Further excavations may disclose the sacristy and chapter-house on the east cloister walk, the fratry, or refectory,.kitchens, and offices surrounding the. south and west sides, above some portion of which .would be the dormitories. Excavations beyond the doorway leading from the chancel are now being commenced. The fine line of• pillars down the nave has not been explored beyond the first two on the south side. There is no doubt that those on the north side exist below the little lane leading to the site of the present excavations, and that the west front, which would most probably be a very fine one, will be discovered at the termination of this line of pillars. Tiles of various and beautiful de- signs are being unearthed, amongst which are some of older appearance, and these are supposed to have belonged to an even older building. Amongst the most recent discoveries the stone lid of a coffin has been found, but the coffin itself has not been disclosed. The work has been to some extent im- peded by pools of water forming in the working places, and yesterday the fire engine was used to pump the water out.

div.head: ASSAULT ON A WIRE -WITH A POKER.
div.p: ASSAULT ON A WIRE -WITH A POKER.

Yesterday morning, at Warrington Borough Police Court, a respectable looking elderly man, named Timothy Ashcroft, was charged with assaulting his wife, on the 12th September, at Latchford.—Mr. Robert Davies, who prosecuted, said that unfor- tunately defendant had given himself up to drink- ing habits, which had undoubtedly been the cause of that Complaint. Defendant and his wife for some time after marriage got on uncommonly well together, until he gave way to the weakness of drinking. Mrs. Ashcroft dared not live any longer with him. She was willing to overlook the assault to some extent, but she wished the magistrates to grant an order for judicial separation. On the day in question defendant came home and had some words with his daughter, whom he knocked down. Mrs. Ashcroft threw her arms round him to prevent violence. Defendant then got a poker, and beat Mrs. Ashcroft upon the hands to make her loose her hold. Mr. Kerr, a neighbour, came in and separa- ted them. After he had left a married daughter came in, and, a quarrel having commenced again, the defendant threw a heavy kitchen poker at his wife. It struck her on the jaw, and also caused considerable loss of blood. Had it struck her on the temple fatal consequences might have ensued. Mrs. Ashcroft then went to Mr. Kerr's, and afterwards to Kenilworth, to a family in whose service she formerly was. Mrs. Ashcroft asked for a separation, but did not desire her husband punished. Evidence having been given, defendant said that since he. failed in busi- ness his wife had continually "nagged" him, which drove him from home to the public-house. He had sought employment in vain. He asked the magis- trates not to separate him from his wife.—Captain Reynolds, who, with Dr. Gi-ornall, occupied the bench, said they thought an aggravated assault had been committed. He felt sorry to see defendant, whom he had known to have been better off, placed in such a position by giving way to drink.—Mr. R. Davies said that he felt the same feeling, but thought it possible that further violence might have happened had not proceedings been taken.—Defen- dant was fined _EI, including costs, and an order for judicial separation was granted, without mainten- ance.

AND THE LIVERPOOL EXHIBITION AWARDS. Mr. ',Thomas Fletcher has addressed to the Chairman of the Jury Committee of the Inter- national Exhibition, Liverpool, a letter worded as follows:—"The Chairman of the Jury Committee, Liverpool International Exhibition.—Sir,--I regret to be compelled to decline to receive the gold meda/ awarded to me, and to ask that my name shall be erased from the list of awards. The shameful revelations in connection with these awards render this course imperative. I have no desire to have my reputation brought into question by the pos- session of honours ' from such an exceedingly doubtful source, although I am assured on the best possible authority that the award was actually de- aided by the jurors on the merits of the exhibit, and has not been interfered with either by the Jury Committee or by the exhibition agent who professes to assist In obtaining gold and silver medals for a consideration in money.--Yours truly, THOMAS FLETCHER.—Warrington, 26th October."

THE WHITECROSS COMPANY. The following letter has been forwarded to the Chairman of the Liverirmol Exhibition by the Whitecross Company, Limited, Warrington :—" The Chairman of the Liverpool International Exhibition. —Sir,--We are favoured by your official notification that we have been awarded a bronze medal for wire ropes and a silver medal for wire-. We notice in the list of awards that the gold medal for wire has been adjudged to a firm who have never manu- factured wire, and who have neither shown nor catalogued wire in their exhibit. We, on the other hand, showed the whole processes of manufacture as carried on by ourselves on the largest scale in this country, from pig-iron to the finished product, and are awarded a silver medal. We respectfully refuse to accept the award of the jury upon any of our products, because, whether from negligence or otherwise, we consider their judgment is dis- credited for the above reasons. This discredit ap- plies in an equal measure to the award for ropes, and we cannot accept it. As original guarantors of a considerable sum, we regret that we conceive it due to ourselves to refuse to be mixed up in any way with the memory of this Exhibition.--:-Yours respectfully, THE WHITECROSS COMPANY, LIMITED. (Signed) Wm. Carson, Managing Director."

"Truth" says :—There were about 2,600 exhibi- tors at the Liverpool Exhibition, and upwards of 0,000 medals have been given. Would it mit have been simpler to have given a certificate of his hav- ing exhibited to each exhibitor? Obviously, medals, distributed with such reckless profusion cannot be regarded as distinctions.

MR. S. SMITH, M.P., AT WIDNES.

Widnes Volunteer Hall was well titled on Monday even- ing nith an audience assembled to listen to a concert arranged with the object of raising funds to liquidates debt of £l2O upon Hartland Wesleyan Chapel. Mr. S. Smith, M.P., of Liverpool, who presided, was introduced to the assembly by the Rev. R. Burdon, and in opening the pro- ceedings made a brief speech. Atter a humourous reference to the absence of the picturesque in Widnes, he congratula- ted the Wesleyan Chapel on only having a debt of £l2O. He hardly knew a chapel that got off with so small a debt. (Laughter.) He got gentle reminders about once a day that there were large delve still extant upon chapels. His Welsh friends had given him much valuableinformation upon that subject during the present year, and he really thought that most of them would consider it infra dig to make a fuss about such a small debt as £l2O. However it proved to him that they in Widnes must be a more than ordinary honest population that their cansciences should be troubled with such a small debt (Laughter.) He only wished that this peculiarity of IVidnes wAs largely extended all over the United Kingdom, for one of the cry- ing evils of the day was the gigantic debts into which all religious bodies seemed to be in, which at the present time it was extremely difficult to pay off. He did not think he had ever, is his experience, come into contact with so much difficulty of maintaining the religious and the benevolent work of this country as there was at the present time. Speaking for that small village of Liverpool—(laughter)— with which be was connected, he dared say that he had never known such depression of trade in his experience,such general poverty, and such difficulty of raising the money requisite for the wants of the society. He believed that Widnes was not altogether exempt from the calamity that bad fallen upon them in Liverpool. He did not know much of their affairs—they did not seem to grumble so much— hut he thought they were sharing the general poverty over the kingdom. However, he ,was glad to tell them that there were signs of improvement in trade showing them- selves. (Applause.) He really ventured to think that they might congratulate themselves now that the worst of this terrible depression was past. America had at last started on a career, he thought, of solid prosperity, and they knew that whenever that great country became prosperous some drop- pings fell upon this side at the Atlantic. (Applause.) He hoped that these droppings would increase, and that they would soon have a great broad stream of prosperity passing over the country. (dear, bear, and applause.) It greatly needed it. The mass of the population had had a hard time of late years, but they had borne their sufferings very pa- tiently and very bravely, and for their sakes he felt a great desire to see happier and better times. (Applause.)—The concert was then proceeded with. The principals were Madame-Laura Smart (Liverpool). Madame Emilie Young, (Manchester), Boa Morlais (Swansea), and Mr. Josef Can- tor (Liverpool). The enjoyment of the audience may be measured by the fact that each vocalist was recalled, a honour which was merited by the excellency of their per- formances. The Soap Works Brass Band, and the vocal union also added to the evening's pleasure.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD ELECTION.

The triennial election of the members of the Wid- nes School Board took place on Saturday. There had not been a contested election since 1877, when the Catholic party and the Church party each re- turned four ct.ndidates, and the Nonconformists three nominees. Up to the present year compromises have been arranged upon these lines. The Church organisation on this occasion was unable to control affairs within its own ranks, and it being evident that a contest must occur, there were 21 gentlemen nominated. By withdrawals the number was re- duced to 16. Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Union, had made very complete arrangements for taking the poll. The following were the voting s6ations —Farnworth district, No. 1, Farnworth girls' schocl ; presiding officer, Mr W. T. Husband. Appleton district, No. 2, St. Bede's school, Appleton; presiding officer, Mr. Richard Whiteside. Simm's Cross district. No. 3, Simm's Cross Board schools; presiding officer, Mr. C. H. Lewin. Albert-road dis- trict, No. 4, Albert-road Wesleyan school ; presiding . officer, Mr. John Goff. Warrington-road district, No. 5, Warrington-road Board school; presiding officer, Mr. J. W. Knowles. Newtown district, No. 6, St. Mary's Catholic schools, George-street; presid- ing officer, Mr. 11. B. Shores. Victoria-road district, No. 7, Lacey-street Wesleyan School ; presiding officer, Mr. M. Hale, Prescot. Waterloo-road district, No. 8, National schools, Waterloo-road; presiding officer, Mr. Thomas Peters. Mersey-road (No. 1 district, No. 9, West Bank Board school; presiding, officer, Mr. T. C. MacKenzie, of Prescot. Mersey- road (No. 2) district, No. 10. Oakland-street Wes- leyan school; presiding officer, Mr. A. W. Dennis, solicitor, Prescot. There was an utter absence of excitement over the election caused to a great ex- ter.t by indifference as to the result, and the poll was a very light one. Many persons were under the impression that voting papers would be distri- buted at each dwelling, and were waiting for the familiar policeman with his bag of papers to appear as in an election for guardians. The poll closed at 8 p.m., and the ballot boxes were then conveyed to the police station for safe custody until Monday, when the votes were counted at the offices of the Local Board. About 3 o'clock in the afternoon the returning officer declared the result as follows:— Rey. George Bond 3186 ' Mr. J. B Imison 1584 Rev. James Cie rke 2816 Mr. J. W. Wareing ... 1545 Rev. Thomas Finegan 2744 Mr. R. H. Davies 1430 Dr. J. M O'Keeffe 2583 Mr. J. Robinson Mr. R. Bradshaw Mr. F. HeTes Mr. H. Wade Deacon... 2070 Mr. S. K. Muspratt BO Mr. T. S. Timmis ...... 1916 Mr. G. Prvde The first eleven gentlemen are elected. The Rev. George Bond. who "came out " in defiance of the Church organisation to winch he belongs, heads the poll with a majority of 370 votes over the next candidate. He probably occupies this position owing to plumpers, as each ratepayer can give eleven votes, and distribute them as he pleases. The Catholic Association and the Church party have returned the whole of their nominees, whilst the Nonconformists have the poor record of ending the list of elected with one suc- cessful candidate. They thus lose two seats upon the Board. That this is the true representation of nonconformity in the town the most rash partisan would not openly affirm. The unsatisfactory result has been brought about through indifference and a want of efficient organisation, a state of things which it ought to be the aim of the Nonconformist leaders to remedy before another election arrives. The religious representation on the School Board is now five Catholics, five Churchmen, and one Non- conformist.
On the proposition of the Rev. George Bond, seconded by the Rev. James Clarke, a vote of thanks 'MIS accorded to the returning officer, when the de- claration of the result was made.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, and Councillor Greening. DuusitENNEss —James Tracey was fined 53. including costs, for being drunk in Orford-street on Saturday night.— William Cunr.inghans was similarly treated for being drunk in Union-street on Saturday night.—Michael Duffy, Thomas Broderick, Alfred Potte, and a man named Connor were also fined for drunkenness. NEGLECT OF F illiam Kelly was charged with neglecting to maintain his wife and children.—Mr. Shearer proved the case, and said that the prisoner's wife was ad- mitted to the Workhouse on the 13th of the present month. As long as prisoner had been married he and his family had lived with his mother, and that was the cause of all the disturbance.—Prisoner promised to take a house of his own, and the case was adjourned for 14 days to see what steps he would take. WIFE ASSAULT.—SamueI Clifton was charged with being drunk and disorderly in James-street on the previous night, and with assaulting Mary Ann Clifton, his wife, at the same time and place. The wife appeared in court with a face shockingly disfigured, but she said that her husband when sober was very kind to her. The magistrates con-1 sidered that the assault was of too serious a nature for the infliction of a fine, and sent Clifton to prison for fourteen days. OESTRUCTION.—Georg. Jackson was fined 2s 6d and costs for causing an obetruction on the 16th instant by allow- ing two ladders to remain an unreasonable time in the street. YOUNG GAMBLF.RE.—John Fallon, Michael Hughes, Thomas O'Brien, and Patrick McGrath, lads,were summoned for gaming, and, after being severely admonished, they were dismissed. WHEELING A COAL WAGGON ON THE FOOTPATH. Elizabeth Pass was charged with this offence, and was dis- missed with a elution. STONE THROWING.—Ten boys were tiach fined is, with- out cus's, for stone throwing. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks and Councillor Broadbent. A STRANGE PRISONER—Thomas Makinson was brought up on a charge of being drunk and disorderly in Bridge- street on the previous afternoon. Prisoner was apparently in an unsound state of mind, and all the reply he made to questions was—" Pay me, and I'd go." He was re- manded. WEDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Davies and Mr. John

_ Fairclongh. THE STRANGE PRISONER.—Thomas Makinson was again brought up on a charge of drunkenness. The constable who proved the c-tee said that prisoner behaved like a madman. As there was no alteration in his condition, he was remanded to the Workhouse to be taken care of. THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton, Alderman Webster,

and Mr. T. Sutton. AssAuvr. Robert Forbes, Bostock-street. who was charged with assaulting Henry Jones on the previous day, was ordered to find two sureties of £5 each to keep the peace for six months. or go to prison for a month. DItrNICENNESS.—John Rooney, who made is 85th ap- pearance, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bank street. He was dismissed on payment of one shilling, the lock-up fee.

div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TrESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall, R. Pierpoint,Neild,

and Jones. MISCELLANEOUS.—F. Marshall, J. Ford, and J. Hassan were each fined 53 and costs for having been asleep whilst -in charge of horses,—Philip Tideswell was ordered to pay the costs for a like offence.—Thomas Hatton, for having al- lowed a cow to stray on the highway at Appleton on the 21st October, was fined 2s 61 and costs.—Richard Ilignett and S. Hignett were each fined 2e 6d and costs, the former for having moved two cattle through an infected area at Appleton, and the latter for haying caused the cattle to be so moved.—William Ashton was fined is and costs for hay- ing allowed two dogs to be at large at Little Leah on the 4th October.—Thomas Lech, teamsman, Moore, was sum- moned to show cause why he should not contribute is 6d per week towards the support of a daughter in an industrial school. RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY. Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley. PERMTSSION.—James Caseells was granted permission to sell at the Brunswick Inn, Brunswick-street. ASSISTANT OVERSVER.—The magistrates approved of the annoietment of Mr. Joseph Acton as assistant overseer for Sutton. A rate of 9d. in the £, to realise £271 13s 2d, was also signed for that township. WATCHFUL NEIGHBOURS.—Ann Limb was charged with assaulting Sarah Houghton. The complainant lives in Lock-street and the defendant lived in the same neigh- bourhood. On the 20th October the complainant noticed a sailor go into the defendant's house, and afterwards observed that it was not prudent to have a sailor in the house four hours and a quarter while her husband was at work. Next morning the defendant struck the complaisant on the hand and arm with a bucket. By Mr. Lake (who defended): She did not know whether the sailor was a relation or not. Annie Hammond deposed to seeing the blow struck, as did Sarah Ashbrook, who, however, contradicted the other wit- nesses in important particulars. Without hearing the de- fence, the Bench dismissed the case. MISCELLANEOrS.—John Ea3tun, a boatman, was fined 23 6.1 and costs for keeping a dog without a license. For al- lowing two calves to stray on the highway at Stockham, on the 6th October, Andrew Stormont was ordered to pay the costs. Louisa Spencer was convictEd of fighting in Fryer-street, and she was bound over to keep the peace. Assatur ON A WOMAN. Mary Ann Walsh, a young woman was charged with assaulting Louisa Spencer.—The complainant said she was going over Top Locks with a young man, when the defendant struck her on the back of the head and she became unconscicue. The defendant also kicked her on the body and limbs, and she was covered with plaister. The defendant admitted that she struck Spencer on the left side of the face, but it was in self defence, as she tried to do her (the defendant) some bodily harm. She called Mary Wilson. who stated that Spencer was drunk. She was told that—Joe Woodhouse was going with "Polly Walsh," and she then "ground her teeth" and threatened to split them open with a glees in the first public-house that they went into. Spencer struck the first blow.—Joseph Woodhouse, a sailor, also gave evidence. The Bench bound the defendant over to keep the peace six months, and pay 13s 61 costs. NEIGHBOURS AT WAR.—Janm Clark was summoned for assaulting Alice Bothwell. The women, who are married, live in Cooper-street. On the 18th October they had an altercation, and the defendant struck the complairnnt on the face. Bothwell was charged with using threatening language towards Mary Ann Fish, the daughter of Clark in the last case.—The Bench bound each defendant over to keep the peace. Is A RREAR.—Edwin Lewis, a labourer at the old Quay, was summoned for arrears of contributions towards his son's maintenance in Stockport Industrial School. The defen- dant was £5 lOs in arrears, which had accumulated at the rate of is per week.—An order of 2s 6d per week was made, to remain in force until the arrears are paid off. Ac OLD OFFENDER. Catherine McCann, for being drunk and disorderly, was fined 203 and costs, or a month's hard labour.

Golding, Davies,and Co., on Saturday night, Michael Timmins was sentenced to seven days' hard labour.—Mary Ellen Royle, Ellen Fenlon, Margaret Burgess, and Mary Ford, girls, were convicted of having on Friday last stolen a quantity of timber from the Connubia Copper Works. A fine of 53 was imposed upon each prisoner.

THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. 11.-G-a..1-k-ell,-seaior, and F. H. Gossage. DRUNKENNESS AND DISORDER.—Richard Connolly (35th appearance) and Sarah Ann Taylor, Litton (23rd appear- ance), were fined 103 and costs for being drunk and disor- derly.—Martha Jane Whelan was tined 5s and costs for a like offence.—John Conlon was fined lOs and costs on a similar charge.—For creating. a breach of the peace, Eliza- beth Whelan was bound over.
