WARRINGTON EXCELSIORS V. HOWLEY ROVERS —Re- suit: Excelsiors, ona goal, tett) tries ; Rovers, one try, two minors. FRODSHAM -ROVERS V. SANKEY (A. TEAM).—This match was playel at Frodsham on Saturday, and after 20 minutes' play the score was Sankey one minor, Froclsham nil. Sr. PAULS V. FARNWORTH (" A " Teams).—Played at Farnworth on Saturday last, and resulted in a victory for the home team. Score—Farnworth, one goal; St. Pants, one try. COCKHEDGE MISSION STAR OF HOPE (2ND TEAM) WARRINGTON RECREATION. Played on Saturday, the " Stars " winning easily by 1 goal, 2 tries, and 9 minors to 2 minors. SANKEY 2ND V. SUTTON FREE WANDERERS.—PIayed at Sutton on Saturday, and after a very hard fought game victory rested with the visitors by 1 try (by Bate) 1 minor to 1 minor. SANKEY RANGERS V. FROGIIALL 'WANDERERS.—Piaved on the ground cf the former on Saturday, and after a rough game ended in a win for the Wanderers by one drop goal, two points, to one try, one point. Sr. PAULS V FARNWORTH (ISt Teams).—This match was played at Warrington on Saturday, and resulted in an easy victory for the home team. Eyres, Barlow, and Grounds were the best of the home forwards. Evres, and Lingard each obtained tries. Score—St. Pan's, 1 goal, 2 tries, and 3 minor points ;Farnworth, nil. WIDNES V. WALKDEN ("A" Tnaats). Played at Wid- nes on Saturday, and after a very evenly contested game ended in a draw. the Wi,ines scoring 4 minor points to Walkden 1 minor point. Parkinson early in the game had a good opportunity of scoring for Widnes, but unfortunately mulled the ball. For Widnes, Gandy (forward) played a strong game, and at back T Wilkinson was very safe. WARRINGTON "A" V. MANCHESTER RANGERS 2ND.—A match between the above clubs was played at Warriisgton on Saturday, and resulted in the home team winning by two tries (Nevins and Boardman) and six minors to nothing. The game was a very quick one and most exciting, and the visitors proved themselves no mean foemen by the dashing; rnannr in which they played against their formidable op- ponents. WIDNES RECREATION V. Sr. BARTHOLOMEW'S, SALFORD —Played at Widnes on Saturday, victory resting with the home team by one try and four minors to nil. Broome ob- tained the try, Grundy failing to increase its value. The game throughout was a forward one, but lacked interest owing to the visitors continually falling on the ball. For the visitors Kennedy and Chadwick were the best of the division, while the brothers Sixsmith were the pick of the forwards. The Recreation were best represented by Grundy and Broome behind, and Tonkies, and Flynn for- ward. RUNCORN HORNETS V. HALTON.—This match was played at Halton on Saturday, and ended in a win for the Hornets by one goal (disputed), one try, and 10 minor points to one try. The Hornets kicked off uphill, and against a Wight breeze, and at once began to press the Hal- tonites, and at half time the score stood—Hornets 6 minors, Halton 1 try. In the second half the game was all in favour of the Hornets, who added 1 goal, 1 try, and 4 minors to the score, and eventually won a 3 above. For the Hornets the whole team played capitally, while Ashley, Snake, Cook,

and Collis played best for Hilton. BOOTLE WASPS V. RUNCORN (2ND TEAM).—Played on the ground of the former at Bootle on Saturday, and after a very one•eided game the visitors won by four goals, six tries, and six minors to Bootle nil. The tries were obtained ey Davies (3), Andrews (2), Dunbavand, Abrams, Stubbs, Whinyates, and Lunt (1 each). Brazendale kicked the goals. The visitors plqed a splendid combined game throughout. Teams :—Bootle: J. Balmer, back; H. Lloyd, S. Lever, and J. Whittaker, threelnarter backs; J. Little and F. Hind, half hacks; H. Boustead, D. Burns, W. Bryce, C. Haslett, E. H. Jattes, H. Thomas, J. Currie, H. Lever, and J. Snodgenns, forwards. Runcorn : J. Brazen- dale, back; E. Lunt, T. Davies, and T. Whinyates, three• quarter backs ; G.Whitly and A. Clare, half hacks; W. Dun- bavand, R. Dolan, W. Jones, P. Riley, E. Andrews, T. Abrams, J. Ford, and J. Gittins, ferwards. COCEPIEDGE MISSION STAR OF HOPE V. WIGAN ST. Jamvs'.—The fixture for the former club on Saturday was the Wigan Rovers. Two members of the team went to the station to meet the four o'clock train from Wigan. The train arrived, and with it the St. James' club. The horns members then took them to their club room, thinking they were the Rovers, It was not until after stripping that the mistake was found out, as the Wiganers had come to play the Warrington Ringers' second team. However, being ready for action, the visiting captain decided to play a friendly game with the "Stars," and arrange other dates with the Rangers. It was truly a curious mistake. Landed on the field, the home captain won the toss, and the visitors kicked off, when Miles nearly succeeded in crossing their Hues, a minor resulting. After some hard play the home forwards worked the ball over the line, and Hope falling on it gained a try. The kick at goal was a difficult one, and proved a failure. From a scrimmage the visitors' half back attempted to pass to the centre. but Scarisbrick secured the ball and dropped a nice goal. The visitors objected on a plea for off side, and the home team gave way. After some fast play the home forwards again worked the ball over the line, this time Shaw being successful in scoring a try. Towards the finish of the game the visitors gained a try, leaving the home team winners by two points to one. WARRINGTON HORNETS V. HIGHFIELD (IST TEAMS).— The return match between these two teams was played on Saturday last at Highfield, and resulted in a drawn game. On account of the late arrival of the visitors, two half hours were selected to be played. The home team won the toss, and decided to play with the wind in their favour. The visitors captain kicked off, and no return behag made several tight scrimmages took place in the home team quar- ters. Nothing of importance took place until about five minutes before half time, when the home team forwards dribbled the ball down the field and scored a try, which was objected to by the visitors on the ground of foul play, and for the referee giving his decision before he was appealed to. Half time was shortly afterwards called. After the usual interval, the home team re-started, the ball falling into the hands of Wright. That player carried it back to the centre. Again some good dribbling on the part of the home team took place by taking the ball into the visitors quarters, but it had not been there long when the visitors, by a combined rush, tooke the ball ep the field, and from a scrimmage it was passed into the hands of Joe Pritchard, the little centre three-quarter making a grand attempt at goal, the ball just going wide. From this point up to the finish the game was in the visitors' favour. At the call of time tile score stood :—Warrington Hornets, 3 minors: Highfield, 1 disputed try and 2 minors. Teams :—Highfield: Full back, J. Glover; three-quarters, Joe Forster, T. Berry (captain), and J. Wood; half backs, T. Pennington and W. Pennington •, forwards, 'l'. Gee, Pickering, Waterworth, W. Forster, Walsh, Melling, Bryant, Whittaker, and R. Wood. Warrington: Full back, W. Hibbert ; three-quarters, W. Wright, Joe Pritchard, and E. Lawless; half backs, T. Catterall and W. Graham; forwards, Donhue' Atherton, Dobson, F. Cooper, W. Catterall, H. Roberts, T. Forster, H. Williams, and J. Mather (captain). RUNCORN V. BIRKENHEAD PARK.
This match took :place on Saturday at Runcorn in fine
weather, aladin the pi.:esence of upward;of 3000 spectators.

After very exciting game Runcorn retired the victors by one goal, two tries, an four minor points, to Birkenhead one dead ball. W. Hughes started the ball, when some very quick play ensued in the centre of the ground. After some good passing between Spence, Holden, and Black, the ball was gradually carried into the Park half, where, after a few lines out a scrimmage was formed. H. Hughes very adroitly got away from the pack, and dodged through his opponents, crossing the line close to touch, scoring the first try for Runcorn. W. Hughes made a good attempt at goal from a difficult place. Resuming play, Black again got the ball, but still an opening was denied him, and Wright, who was next to move in an opposite direction, made a good rush through. Wright losing the ball, Campbell secured it. and kicked to Wood, who put it into touch at mid-field. From this point, Andrews made an effort, but was tackled by Hol- den and Spence. A screw kick by H. Hughes gained further ground, but this was quickly neutralized by Holden passing to Black, whom Johneon and Riley stopped very cleverly. Stoddart followed up this effort, and punted the ball dead over the home line. Succeedine, the drop out, Faulkner, playing a sterling game, started a movement which was taken up by the rest of the pack, and a general rush was made to the Park line. A clever pass by Stoddart relieved, and Spence gave further relief by kicking the ball into touch. The Park forwards then made an effort, Cowen and Dun leading the movement, which was followed up by Holden. who passed to Davies. A run was made for the line, but 'Cawley was safe, aed the at empt was checked. Broady got back towards mid-field, and Black returned, and getting to Woods the latter held him tenaciously, the ball getting free. When half time was called the score was—Runcorn one try, to a minor point for the Park. After the usual interval Cowen started the ball, which was not returned, and pliy ensued in the home half, where Faulkner stopped a dangerous rush by Dun and Cowen. Hostilities were soon removed to the Birkenhead half, and a long kick by Riley caused Campbell to touch down. Ho had to 'resort to a similar etep as the result of a dribble started by Andrews, and carried on by Wright. In response to Black's drop out, Broady returned the ball to Campbell, who kicked hack to Woods, the latter sending it in touch. Spence for the Park and Hughes and Andrews for Runcorn tried hard to get away, and a moment later a touch-down was conceded to Runcorn. Following the drop out, an effort was made by Clarke, ably seconded by Broady and Faulkner. Spence retaliating looked like getting off, but Riley brought him down, and the home forwards took the ball into the Park quarter. Gatley very smartly charged Campbell's kick, and H. Hughes got possession of the ball and made tracks for the line, and succeeded in adding another try to the score. The kick at goal by Lewis failed. Black dropped the ball into play, and Faulkner returned to Davies, who kicked into touch at mid-field. Hence the ball travelled across the field, when eventually it got to Black from Holden. Black ran very strongly until well checked by W Hughes, who ran acress to meet him. Some smart play followed on the Part of Spence, Holden and Black. but Faulkner and Lewis, ever ready, stopped the movement a few yards from the home line, when an effort alas again made by Spence, who

slipped, thus losing his chance. W. Riley relieved the pressure. kicking to Campbell, who returned in touch. A lot of wild passing was indulged in by the Birkenhead backs, which cost them a try, for Black pass,Kl as he thought to Holden, but Andrews snapped the ball and galloped away over the line between the posts, Lewis landing a goal from the place. The home players, encouraged by their success, p;ayed up, and continually pressed tbe visitors, but to call of time were unable to score any more points, Runcorn win- ning a fine game by five major points to none. The teams were as follows: Birkenhead Park: F W H Campbell, back; JI a Black. C Holden, and E 0 W Davies, three- quarter backs; F W Spence and L D Stoddart, half backs; G Cowie (captain). F Dun. P A Williamson, W H Atkinson, J Cowen, C L Williams, T Wood, R P Moodie, and R W Williams, forwards. Runcorn : T Woods, back; W Riley, H Cawley, and T Johnson, throe-quarter backs; H Hughes and H T Andrews, half backs; W Wright, W Hughes, J Lewis. J Barnes, J Gatlev, F Joule, W Faulkner, W Broady, and J Clarke, forwards. WARRINGTON V. MANCHESTER RANGERS.

The Warrington team journeyed to Manchester on Satur- day to play their fixture with this rising young team. It will be remembered that last season this club played one of the best games witnessed on the Warrington ground, and Saturday's match was not one to be laughed at, as it took the Warringtonians all their time to win, the score being— Warrington, one goal and five minors, to one try and four minors. The weather was fine, but, owing to the heavy rains of last week, the ground was found to be very heavy and detrimental to fast play. Accustomed a.s the visitors were to a good ground, they did not seem to be at home here, the ridges very often interfering with the runs of the backs. H. Ashton won the toss, and elected to play with the wind slightly in his favour. The home captain kicked off, Dillon returning. Frank Turner charged down eeabin's counter re- turn, and the visitors looked like scoring. The ball, how- ever, was worked a short way up the field, and Frank Tur- ner took it with a rush to the line. Again the home for- wards worked the ball up, but Gilbert passed the ball to Barnes, who, in turn, passed to Jolley. who almost got over. H. Radcliffe. however, was on the alert, and removed play by a nice run and kick to the half-way flag. A fine pass was witnessed between Parkinson and Barnes, the little centre three-quarter gaining ground. Some tight scrim- mages now took piece in the centre of the field, but Dillon and Ashton broke through, Sabin returning with a run and kick to touch. Hayes next stopped a dangerous rush, and Fair. Turner had a eallop to the home 25; but Sabin was equal to the occasion, and smartly returned. The home forwards, headed by Haselham, Galley, and Pollard, next broke away. hut Walsh stopped their career in grand style. Jolley shortly afterwards got in a nice kick, and following well up prevented a return. Again he punted, but Harrison put in a long kick to touch. From the line out Parkinson got hold, and gained a lot of ground by a well-judged kick. Some good play was next witeessed between Gilbert, Par- kinson, and Speakman, the result being that play for some time settled down in the visiters' quarters. The full back on the visitors' side now mulled the ball, and Barnes from pass by eirilbert took a drop at goal, a minor resulting. From the kick out H Haselham came out with a beautiful dribble, being only stopped in the Warrington 25. Speak- man gained ground by a kick to touc‘i, but Parkinson afterwards replied with one equally good, and further bet- tered this by another kick to line. The Warrington for- wards relieved, but H Ratcliffe returned to the charge, and play for some time raged furiously in the visitors' quarters. Frank Turner now broke away, but was collared by Sabin, and Gilbert would have scored had he not had B Parkinson to contend with. Good play was next witnessed between Barnes and Jolley, and then Haselham broke away with a splendid dribble to the visitors' lines, the Warrington men being to blame for not making the ball dead before dis- puting any point, Jones scoring a try chiefly through the aid of Sabin and Haselham. The latter failed to kick the goal. This brought about half time with the scor e—Ran- gers one try. Warrington ens minor. Frank Turner re- started, and there being a poor return the first scrimmage took place in the home quarters. Tbe first to show up was Parkinson, by a good kick, and then followed Gilbert with a neat pass and rue. Again H. Haselham dribbled finely, Haves saving shortly afterwards in good style. The War- ringtonians now gradually worked the ball to the home quarters, but some good passing and play by the brothers Ratcliffe was instrumental in taking play to half-way. Some good scrimmages followed, and the home forwards carrying one of these took play to line, but Massey put in a strong kick, and W Dillon and Fair Turner improved mat- ters still further. Barnes shortly afterwards made a bold bid at goal, the ball striking the outside of the post, but in a minute or so Gilbert gave him another chance, and this time he popped the oval over the crossbar amidst a shout of applause. From now entil the end ef the game the visi- tors seemed to have the best of it, as the play was confined to the home quarters, although the home team played Pluckily until the end. The game at the call of time stood —Warrington one sreal five minors, to one try four minors. It need hardly be said that the game was one of the hardest, if not the fastest, ever played by the Warringtonians. All the backs on the Warrington side played a good game, es- pecially Barnes, Gilbert, and Jolley. Speakman also did the lion's share in stopping rushes. The forwards were divided into two clams—Ashton, Hayes, Hughes, and Dil- lon played well in close quarters, and Davies, F and Fair Turner were effective on the loose, The Manchester backs were best represented by Parkinson, Sabin, and the brothers Ratcliffe. Harry rfaeelham was the best forward, his drib- bling being a treat to witness. His best supporters were his brother, Galley, and Pollard. Teams :—Rangers: Back, Harrison ; three-quarter backs, Sabin, Parkinson, and H. Ratcliffe; half-hacks, F Ratcliffe and S Taylor; forwards, Jones, Mee, H B Haselham, H Y Haselharre Pollard, Cox, Dodds, Galley, and Hammett. Warrington: Back, Walsh ; three-qnarter backs, Jolley, Barnes, and Massey ; half- backs, Gilbert and Speakman; forwards, Fairfield Turner, Frank Turner. Hayes, Hough, Davies, Povey, Hughes, and Ashton. Umpires, Messrs Harden and Barns ; referee, Mr W Dale.
THE EXAMINER, SAT r'PIiAY, OCTOBER 30, 1886.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

A Frodsham correspondent, signing himself "Fair Play," sends a complaint. We give the purport of his letter, but wish it to be understood that these columns are not open for the discussion of disputes between clubs. The letter is in reference to a football match between Frodsham and Sankey Ist, played on the ground of the former on the 23rd ult., and says that Sankey from the commencement of the game played foul until the Frodsham captain protested, and finally called his men off. The Sankey men, it adds, then made a disturbance.

div.head: WARRINGTON BO A_RD OF
div.p: WARRINGTON BO A_RD OF
GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this B3ard was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present—the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Woods, Clark, Jolley, Eckersley, Isherwood, Black- hurst, Greening, Wright, W. Houghton, Humphries, Grange, Owen, Brown, Balharry, Llibbert, Harrison; Broadbent (ex-officio), J. C. Sutton (clerk) and S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

div.head: SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

This committee's minutes stated that the chaplain had reported that he had made an examination of the girls' school and had found their work generally well done. The doctor reported the schools to be free from disease, and the superintendent that the children were well with the excep- tion of a few chi!blains on the younger children, and that Mr. Stevens, sub-inspector of the Local Government Beard, had visited the schools on Monday, the 25th inst. It was recommended that the wage 3 of 'Mrs. Smith (mother of No. 4 house) be increased to the rate of £7 yearly, in lieu of £6, on the discharge of her eldest bov.—On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. WOODS, the minutes were passed. •

div.head: SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: SCHOOL FEES.
The School Fees Cemmittee reported that fees had been allowed in 95 cases, 79 of which were old and 16 new cases. —On the motion of Mr. BLACBHURST, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minutes were passed.

SALARIES. An application for an increase on her present salary, which is £2O a year and rations, was read from Ann Langley (assistant roafron at the workhouse), but as it was explained that the application was too late in being sent in, it could not be dealt with this year.—On the motion of Mr. HARRI- SON, the following increases of salary were granted, viz. : Miss Garner, school mistress, £2 ; Miss Spittle, nurse, £3 ; Miss Scott, porteress, £5. A COMPLAINT.

The following letter was read from Mr. Curry, the porter :—" As I have experienced some difficulty in getting away from the workhouse at convenient times, I beg to ask you if you would be kind enough to make some regu- lation for my doing so. I have to go to town to purchase rations for myself and family as they are required. and my duties are of such a nature that it is impossible for me to say in the morning what time it will be convenient for me to go away. My reasons for troubling you are that I have receiven the fAllowiug Memorandum of order" from the master which I find it impossible to comply with :—" That all the workhouse officials requiring temporary leave apply personally, or in writing, to the master or matron before ten o'clock a.m., stating the time they wish to go and return.— G. Mackey."—A somewhat prolonged discussion took place upon this letter, and both the workhouse master (Mr. Mackey) and the porter were called before the Board. It was ultimately decided that the order of the master should stand with the exception of the words "before ten o'clock a.m.," which were ordered to be struck out. It was also directed that at each meeting of the Board a list showing the absence from the workhouse of the various officers dur- ing the previous fortnight should be presented. It was also agreed, on the motion of Mr. W. HOUGHTON that a re- turn showing the absences of the officers daring the past six rn.9nths should be presented to the Board.

GIFTS, The WomcaorsE MASTER acknewledged the gifts to the inmates of a number of periodicals from Mrs. Jack, and a number of books and tracts from Mr. E. Bolton. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

MILL FIRE NRAR BOLTON.—The Bagley Mills, near Bolton, were entirely destroyed by fire on Thursday morn- ing, the damage being estimated at over forty thousand pounds. Many hundred workpeople will be thrown out of employment.

Official reports published by the Bengal Government show that, in spite of the difficulties thrown in the way of trade with Sikkim and Thibet, it has trebled in the last two years. The opposition to Mr. Macaulay's mission appears to be confined to the Lhassa monks.

ILOCAL WESLEYAN METHODISM. On Tuesday the Wesleyan Methodists of the War- , rington centre of the Liverpool District, which com- prises Warrington, Widnes, Runcorn, Frodsham, St. Helens, and Wigan, held several meetings in Bold- . street Wesleyan Chapel, Warrington, with the ob- ject of promoting the work of God. The first meeting commenced at seven o'clock in the morning, and the last at seven o'clock in the evening, : and all were presided over by the Rev. W. Wilson, ; chairman of the district. They were well at- tended, the large chapel being filled at the evening ' gathering.

div.head: MORNING MEETINGS.
div.p: MORNING MEETINGS.

In the morning there was a meeting at seven o'clock, which was followed by a meeting for prayer at ten o'clock. An hour later there was a gathering of ministers, office bearers, and members called for testimony and devotion, and to hear an address by the Rev. J. Chalmers. Supporting the chairman on the platform at thks meeting were the Revs. G. E. Young (superintendent Warrington cir- cuit), G. E. Cutting and J. 11. Jones (Warrington), J. Chalmers, M A., (Waterloo), E. Mosscrop (Frod- sham), J. Kent (Earlestown), J. A. B. Malvern (Wigan), Simpson Johnson (Liverpool), and Mr Swales (Widnes). The Rev. J. CHALMERS, in the course of his address, which was mainly directed to the younger people present, said that the principle of Christian life was faith. By some the Chris- tian life, that was the happiest, was looked upon as the best. That kind of experience was looked upon by many people as showing a high state of Christian life; but it did not follow that it was so. In that happy state of religion there was something very subtle, something that had laid hold of the people in a very subtle way. If it was cherished, it would breed in them a feeling which would be found not to ba joyful. It certainly gave a stimulus to Christian life; but that was not the main thing. If it were, Christian life would not be strong. Wise Christian people did not make too much of a happy experience; and when they found that their happy experiences had gone,. they dis- covered that they had not lost a great deal. There were people who checked such feelings, and they were no great losers by it. AFTERNOON CONFERENCE.
A united conference of workets was held in the afternoon, when addresses were given on different subjects, a hymn being sung between the delivery of each address.

, The Rev. G. E. CUTTING (Varrington) gave the first address, his subject being " Fitness for Service." What, he asked, constituted fitness for service ? It was spiritual Sonship. He exhorted them all to commence to work for God, for Christ said "Son, go work to-day in my vine- yard." Those who never entered a pulpit had to preach Christ by the daily sermon of a Christly life, and by efforts to bring their friends and relations to His feet. The Rev. E. Mossceems (Frodsbam) spoke on "Family Religion." They bad reason to believe, if every Methodist father and mother did their duty, they would soon see a very large increase in their Methodist churches, and in the number of Christians in the country. Christianity exer- cised a blessed influence on family life.. It threw a safe- guard round the home, and invested the name of father, and ,of mether, with a better and richer meaning. Family re- ligion implied a wise administration of family government. The father should not only command, but see that he was obeyed ; should not only forbid sin, but punish it. It was the daty of parents to bring their children as early as pos- sible under proper discipline. They must avoid,.however, the severity that inspired hatred, as much as the leniency which fostered dieobedieace. Family religion also implied conscientious observance of family prayer, careful instruc- tion in Christian knowledge, and the influence of parental Christian example. Let them direct the way to Heaven be- cause they knew the way themselves, and let their families be pervaded by religion. The Rev. J. KNNT (garlestown) then gave an address on the "Daily reading of the word of God." It seemed strange, be said, that if the Bible was such a wonderful book there should be, as he feared there was, lamentable neglect of it—neglect, he was afraid, amongst those who acknowledged it to be the book of God. Without habitual companionship with the Word of God the soul would be insufficiently nourished, and they could not without it have a ripe Christian experience and perfection of Chris- tian character. Without habitual study of the Bible th eir Christian armour would be incomplete and vulnerable. The Rev. G. E. YOUNG (Warrington) speaking on "House . . .

. . to house visitation," said that he attached great importance to the work of the pulpit, as he believed that the principal means that Gad had designed for the salvation of the people was the preaching of the Gospel. He did not think that the power of the pulpit was decreasing, but that it was increasing. There was, however, considerable importance to be attached to. tbe work of endeavouring to preach the Gospel from house to house. It was the daty of a minister to Lake a prominent and leading party in such a work but it mast not be confined to them. The officers and members must do what they could in house ts house visitation. Whenever people would not come to them they must go to the people. They were losing thousands every year from their societies. House to house visitation would not do everything, but it would do a great deal to stop the leakage. Last year they had 45,000 new members of the society ad- mitted, and yet had the humiliation at the conference of re- porting a decrease of members. What had become et the 45,000? There were upwards of 27,000 persons returned as "ceased to meet," and there were 13,000 lost through re- movals. It was time they were wide awake. He believed one way of filling their chapels was by house to house visita- tion.

_ The Rev. J. A. B. MALVEMN (Wigan), in an address on "Mission bands," said that they came on the heels of house to house visitation. They should keep up the pioneer ele- ment in their churches, and in mission bands they had that element in 8 most practical and useful form. Every Methodist place should be a centre of pioneer work. If mission bands were established all ever the circuit, the Wes- layans could raise a Salvation Army in a week,—Mr. Swales (Widnes) also spoke on the same subject, after which the conference concluded.

div.head: EVENING MEETING.
div.p: EVENING MEETING.

Another meeting, commencing at seven o'clock, was held in the evening, when the chair was again occupied by the Rev. W. Wilson. There was a large attendance. In open- ing the meeting the chairman remarked that the idea of holding those central meetings was inspired, he was per- suaded, by Divine wisdom and understanding. One had been held in Liverpool, one in Chester, and that was the third of the series. The sight of the large congregation filled him with gratitude, and inspired him with hope re- specting the grand work in the Liverpool district. He was sure that if all would do their duty as one army, great as were the mountains of difficulty that lay before them, they would be able to cvercorne them.

The Rev. S. JouNeme spoke on "Entire consecration," which he said meant entire devotion to the service of God. There was a difference between entire consecration and en- tire sanctification. The former was something that people did for themselves, when they surrendered themselves fully to God ; the latter was something that God did for them the moment that surrender was made. Entire consecration meant the complete devotion of one's life to the service of God. People, he went on to say, were very variously gif- ted, some being more richly endowed than others, but if such gifts as one had were devoted to the service of God then they were consecrated, whether these gifts were many or few. As an instance of this be referred to the death in Liverpool of the evangelist known as the cabman's bishop, who, he said, was not a learned man. If that man, whose funeral the day before had been attended by thousands, in- cluding the most prominent citizens of Liverpool, had been measured by his gifts, it would perhaps have been found that he bad but one gift—that of personal appeal. But that one gift was consecrate.l, and when he saw that funeral he felt that a consecrated life was a beautiful one. In conclusion

he remarked that entire consecration was the only way to bring about the entire conversion of the world. The Rev. I. E. PAGE (Chester), in the course of an ad- dress on "Christian fellowship," suggested that they should introduce more Bible reading into the week-night services. If they ministers would give and expound a Bible reading, he thought they would find an added interest in the ser- vices. Anokher important part of Chnstian fellowship was the holding and conduct of class meetings. At the recent Church Congress in Wakefield, he remarked, one of the clergymen present spoke of the class meeting as a grand thing in Methodism, and there were clergymen who were starting similar classes. The Wesleyans already had class meetings, and they must stand by them. Mr. Page also re- ferred to the partaking of the Lord's Supper and the holding of the prayer meeting, and said that in all these things they must try and have fellowship, partnership, awl participation all round, and try always to cultivate a friendly feeling amongst themselves. The Rev. FORSTER CROZIER was the next speaker. His subject was "Aggressive work in circuits." The first essen- tial thing in that work was, he said, a deep sense all round— from the superintendent ministers to the other preachers, and the offic3 bearers, down to the Youngest and last received member—of personal responsibility. If they could get the sense of personal responsibility to extend the work of God, there would be no poorly attended class meet- ings, no empty chapels, even in the large towns, and the whole church organisation would go with a swing that would delight all their hearts. They were told again and again, and were generally led to believe, that as soon as a man found Christ his instinctive desire was to at once bring some one else t 9 Christ. That should be the case, and generally it wee so if there was real life, but some people cooled down and lost their sense of personal responsibility in respect to the work. He proceeded to urge more extended

aggressive work in connection with the ordinary agencies of the Wesleyan connection, and there were none of those agencies, if the matter was looked at properly, that had not an aggressive side. If all would labour earnestly to bring people into the house of God, their congregations through- out the connexion would be double what they were to-day. If people would do that they would find that their labour would bear fruit. There was also aggressive work to be done in the class meeting, in the prayer meeting, in tract distribution, and other ways. They wanted to put good, strong, common sense in all the departments of their work. There were mines of Christian usefulness nnworked in the Methcdist,Cburch, and if they would work them with all their heart and soul they would see the membership doubled
and trebled, and spiritual life thrilling the church through and through.
'IOM The ReV:.As WAUGH then delivered a stirring ad- dress. his subject being, "The young people of Metho- dism."

SANITARY WORK IN WAR- RINGTON. LUNCHEON IN THE TOWN HALL, After the inspection, on Friday afternoon of last week, of the Longford and intercepting depots re- cently built, by the member of the Warrington Town Council and other gentlemen (a report of which we gave in our last issue), a luncheon was held in the Town Hall, at which several toasts were., proposed and speeches made. The chair was filled by the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) who in well-- chosen words gave the toasts of "The Queen '• and ' "The Prince and Princess of Wales and the rest of the Royal Family." Alderman DAVIES next proposed "The health of the Mayor of Warrington: During the past three years, he said, the Mayor had filled his office with credit to himself anl advantage to the town, and he , was to be congratulated on having been successful for so long a period. (Hear, hear.) The hearty thanks of the town were due to any man who had the trouble,the assiduity and the art to maintain the affections of the people for three years. The Mayor had done that, and he had also been of some advan- tage to the town. (Applause:), The toast was cordially honoured. • The MAYOR, in responding, could not say that he had succeeded, but if there was any credit in trying to be successful, he could claim) that whatever he had done, had been done with an honest desire to make himself as useful as possible, and to- ungrud- gingly devote as much time to the duties of his office as he possibly could. (Applause:) Alderman WEBSTER proposed the' health of Mr. Bearaont. As he stood there he said: his memory . went back 40 years to a time when Mr. Beamont was foremost in the struggle which took place for a most important improvement, that was the in- corporation of Warrington. (Applause.) Those who recollected the circumstances would remember how keen and severe was the contest that took place between contending parties at the time. There were gentlemen who thought the incorpora- tion of the borough would'he prej udicial,but he was happy to say the majority led by Mr..Beamont was of a different opinion, the result being that that most important change took place. (Hear, hear.) Since that time numberless changes-had taken place in the government and social arrangements of the borough, but he thought that, next to the incorpo- ration of the borough, the one they had witnessed that afternoon would be the most important. (Ap- plause.)

- The toast was honoured with much heartiness, and on rising, Mr. BEAMONT was received with loud applause. All that had been done in Warrington, he said, had been carried out in a spirit truly worthy of this ancient town. There had been a great number• of things besides those mentioned by Alderman Web- ster. They were the very first to inaugurate a sys- tem of licensing lodging-houses, and many a time had it not been for that they should have had infec- tious disease in the town. There had a great number of things taken place in Warrington, and it made• him ashamed that he had been behind the time in not thinking of some of them sooner. (Applause.) Alderman PICKMERE proposed the toast of "Suc- cess to the scheme." The experiments with regard to sewage in Warrington had certainly cost a great deal of money, but he could honestly say from what they had seen that day that the present experiment so far as it had been carried on had proved a great success. (Hear; hear.) He congratulated the chair- man (Alderman Burgess) and the Sanitary Commit- tee on the success that had been achieved. (Ap- plause.) Dr. MACKIE said be had much pleasure in seconding the proposition made by Alderman Pickmere. He had known Alderman Burgess for 33 years, and he had had the pleasure of fighting for and against him again and again, and after all these experiences, and many intervening ones, he could most heartily second the vote of thanks as a recognition that, although he (Alderman Burgess) might not always have been in the right, he had always, in his own estimation, believed that he was in the right, and that was all he could expect from their common humanity. (Applause.) Twelve or 14 years ago Alderman Burgess and he discovered in the streets that they had been rather surly to each other for some Years, bat they crossed and shook hands and remained good friends. He could appeal to Alderman Burgess that he had never been his opponent in Longford matters. (Hear, bear.) They had differed about urinals—(laughter)—but on more important questions they had been at one. When the chair- man of the Sanitary Committee was deposed by his own prime minister and the other members of his cabinet, he was the one who came to the front and proposed an act of obli- vion and restored him to his bishopric. He had never re- gretted that act. (Applause.) The toast was drunk with musical honours and with cheers for Alderman and Mrs. Burgess. Alderman BURGESS, in acknowledging the toast, said they must bear in mind that what had been submitted to their notice was the result of 14 years' labour. (Applause.) He was sorry to say that he feared, owing to the lapse of time awls other causes, he was the only member of the Sanitary Committee who, 14 years ago, had the honour of bringing before the Council the proposal which had resulted in the , scheme, the completion of which they had seen that day. The work had been to him a labour of love, and if he had had ten times the amount of opposition the result would have been precisely the same that day. (Applause.) He might say that it was never intended that his work should develop into that of a manure manufacturer. He never dreamt of such a thing when he undertook the work com- mitted to his charge. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Burgess then referred to the report to the Local Government Board of Dr. Ballard, who in 1871 held an inquiry into the sani- tary condition of Warrington. That report contained several recommendations, and a copy of it was sent by the Local Government Board to the Warrington Corporation, and soon after a resolution was submitted to the Council authorising the Sanitary Committee to undertake to carry out the whole of the recommendations. That resolution, he believed. was passed in 1872. With regard to the midden-steads which then existed, the committee arrived at the conclusion that there was no such thing as remedying the system, and that the only remedy was the entire sweep- ing away of the middens. (Hear, hear.) They paid a visit to Rochdale, and they found there a system adopted which the committee recommended to the Council, that that was known in Warrington as the pail system. That was the commencement of the work. The Paying and Streets Com- mittee had assisted the Sanitary Cemmittee in their work by being instrumental in bringing about a better state of things as to the residences of the people; and the Water- works Co. had assisted them in no inconsiderable degree by giving them for domestic purposes a supply of water far superior to anything they had had before. (Hear, hear.) The result of all these various causes was that the death- rate of Warrington had been brought down from 30 in the 1.000 to 18 Der 1,000. (Applause.) The question they soon found they 'had to deal with was that of the disposal of the sewage. There *as an insuperable difficulty in the way of introducing water closets into the town, because the only water they then had was from Appleton, and they did not know then that they should have a better supply. They had therefore had many difficulties to encounter, and these had not easily been got over. Alderman Burgess then re- ferred to the methods at first adopted to get rid of the sew- age, and said that at length it was suggested to them by Mr. Milner that they should take counsel with Mr. Fryer, who had devised the destructor they had that day seen in operation, and Mr. Fryer unfolded to them the present scheme with the exception of, the finishing opera- tion. The Council in the generous manner in which it bad always dealt with the Sanitary Com- mittee gave them without stint all they asked for. They gave them authority to spend £12,000, which was also agreed to by the Local Government Board on the re- commendation of their engineer. The work had now been accomplished and the obligation entered into by the com- mittee was cancelled. (Applause.) They had that day been shown the work in a state of completion, and he was pleased to find it had commended itself to their judgment. He believed that the pledge which had been given to the town that the £12,000 would be well. spent had been re- deemed. (Hear, hear.) The result of the work that had been going on for the last 14 years was a diminished death- rate of a marked character. To reduce the death-rate in a town like Warrington from 30 and over 30 to 18 in a 1,000 was no slight thing, and was indeed a work that no gentleman in that room had formed any idea of. Taking the population at 46000, they would find that it resulted in preventing 550 more persons dying and being taken to the cemetery every year; they had 1,100 fewer people laid on a bed of sickness, and, besides that, what must be the improvement in the general health of the town. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Did it not rise higher and higher as the death-rate became less and the number of sick less? Was it no advantage to a large employer of labour that he could depend on the service of healthy people ? And there was besides the question of the value to Warrington of the lives that were saved by the improved unitary conditiens. (Applause.) In conclusion Alderman Burgess thanked those present for the manner in which they had honoured the toast.

Mr. BEAMONT remarked that the death rate of 18 per 1,000 was one of the most remardable of the many facts that had been brough out that day, because it was well known that the death rate of many villages was higher. (Hear, hear.) Alerman CROSFIELD proposed the toast of "The Rural Sanitary Authority." Having declared that he knew no- thing of the Rural Sanitary Authority or the work they did but which he boned they did well, he felt proud to sit at that table that day and also' to observe the result of the ef- forts of the Warrington Sanitary Committee. He said without hesitation that the efforts of the Committee were worthy of the highest commendation, and he felt proud as an Englishman, as a Lancashire man, and as an inhabitant of Warrington, that they had a chairman like Alderman

Lord and Lady Rosebery left London on Thursday morn- ing for Tilbury Docks, where they embarked forlndia. DR. PARKER AND THE CITY TENTLE.—The Rey. H. R. Haweis, vicar of St. James's, Marylebone, was announced to occupy the pulpit of the City Temple on Thursday morning. When the time arrived for commencing the ser- vice, Dr. Parker stated from the pulpit that he had received a letter from Mr. Haweis saying the bishop had forbidden him to preach in that church. At this there were cria of "Shame," and Dr. Parker resumed his seat to allow those who came to hear Mr. Haweis to withdraw if they wished. At the close of his sermon Dr. Parker commented on the action of the Bishop of London. He thought that after what he had announced, infidels would look on with won- der and amusement.

GENERAL NEWS. The Cabinet' will meet for the first time, since the Proro• gation of Parlianent, probably on November Bth. In deference to. the representations of his friends Lord 114rtinE.,,ton has finally decided not to go to India this winter.
Early on Saturday morning the communion service, valued at fAct, was stslen from Whitwell Church, near 'Worksop. _
The death is announced of Lord MonkswelL who was better known before his elevation to the peerage as. Sir R. P. Collier.

A Dublin telegram reports the arrest at Denbigh of a per- son passing as" the Rev. Jahn Jones," said to have been concerned in another "clerical imposture in Ireland, Lord Hartington returned to Devonshire House, Picca- dilly on Saturday, from Hardwicke Hall. His lordship, with the Earl of. Fife, will leave for India almost imme.. d lately.
Two members of the Royal Engineers were drowned las the Meroey on Wednesday afternoon through the capsizing of a punt. They belonged to a surveying party engaged on the defence works.

At Glasgow, on Tuesday afternoon,, two children, William Pollock and Clara Black, found a boa's of vitriol on the staircase in their house, and drank the contents. The latter died almost immediately, and Pollock is not expected to live

At an intsrview, on Monday, betvteen the Serviatt Minister for Foreign Affairs and the new Bulgarian Agent, an understandivg was arrived at regarding the resump- tion of friendly diplomatic relations between Servia and Bulgaria,

AT serious fire broke out on Monday on the National steamer Queen, lying in the Alexandra Dock. The Queen' arrival in Liverpool on Saturday evening, with a cargo of' cotton, lubricating oil, and general merchandise, from NM' York. Considerable damage was done to the cargo and the vessel.

The London and North-Western Railway Company have. opened for traffic two- extensions of their system in the neighbourhood of Wigan, consisting of connecting lines, which have been constructed more especially with the object of relieving the passenger traffic on the main line at Wigan. Canon Body writes that the statement that the Arch- bishop of York has prohibited him from taking part in a mission in his diocese is inaccurate. His Grace has.simply refused permission to his preaching at a mission in his diocese when that permission was sought by the Vicar of the parish.

DOMESDAY CPumsnAmox.--About 400 visitors went to the Public Record Office, London, on Monday, and inspected the ancient documents known as the " Doomsday Book." this being the 800th anniversary of the completion of tbe original book. An interesting paper was read by Mr. Et übert Hall, of the Public Record Officeron the official custody of the book since 1076. THE FT:LRAM TRAGEDY 1 RECOVERY OF THE Bony.— The body of a woman answering to the description of Mrs Leader, who is supposed to have drowned her four children in the Thames at Fulham, and then committed Aticide, tan days since, bas been picked up in the river off Mort- lake. The husband has been communicated with, and has proceeded to the spot to see if he could identify the body. Sir Wilfrid Lawson, Bart., M.P.,. was, at a general meet- ing of the North Cumberland Liberal Association, held at' Carlisle, on Saturday, elected chairman of the association, in the stead of Mr. Geo. Howard resigned. Sir Wilfrid referred to the position taken up the Dissentient Liberals. He said the Liberal party was immortal, for the Gladstonians' i would never go "cap in hand" to those who had placed Lord Salisbury in power. .._.

_ FIRES. - Pulteney Town Royal Hotel was burned to the groan,l on Monday. The flames spread so quickly that there was no chance of subduing them. The inhabitants of the back portion of the hotel and of adjoining houses had to escape by the upper windows, only partly dressed.—Thatch House Tavern, Tweedmouth, was destroyed by fire on Sun- day niaht. The cause of the fire, which originated at the back of the house,is unknown; but the premises are fully insured.

POISONING (2sl3.—The Wandsworth cook, Emily Parry, was cnarged on Wednesday, at the Central Criminal Court, with administering poisosi to her mistress, Mrs. Rose Dar• hog, with intent to murder her. She was found guilty of the minor offence of administering the poison with intent to annoy. The prisoner had no defence to offer ; but Mr. Jus- tice Smith, taking into consideration the feelings of remorse expressed by the prisoner, sentenced her to only three months' hard labour.

DISESTABLISIIMENT. Addressing the members of his Diocesan Conference on Wednesday, the Archbishop of York expressed his firm conviction that the issue of the struggle of the next few years as to the union of Church and State would depend upon the amount of agreement within the Church as to what they desired to defend. If they were cordially united, he questioned whether there was any antagonist without who was powerful enough to enforce disestablishment. A CLERGYMAN SENT TO PRISON.—At Carlisle ASSiZeS on Wednesday, the Rev. John Henry Latrobe Bateman, vicar of Haile, Cumberland, was found guilty of having feloni- ously solemnised a marriage in his church between Robert Little, a youth of 18, and Mary Jane Cockburn, without license and without previous publication of banns. There was another charge of falsifying the register in regard to the same ceremony. Mr. Justice Day sentenced the prisoner to eighteen months' imprisonment with bard labour. THE SENTENCE 017 A TOWN COUNCILLOR.—At Longford Quarter Sessions, on Tuesday, Joseph Wilson, a town coun- cillor, appealed against the decision of the magistrates at the petty session, where they sentenced him to a month's •

imprisonment for an assault oaa fellow councillor, named, George Lemon, age 70 years. The Bench, after a lengthened consideration, confirmed the decision made at the petty sessions. Mr. Wilson is chairman of the Long- ford Geardians, and vice-president of the local branch of the National League. Mr. Lemon is a Conservative. The assault took place after a heated argument during a meeting of the Town Commissioners. THE FEMALE PORTER.—The young woman Lois Schwich, who assumed the garb of a boy, and as a porter obtained employment at several West-end shops in London, was on Wednesday again brought up at the Marlborough-street Police Court on charges of theft. It was stated that the police bad ascertained that the conduct of the prisoner was not a freak, but formed part of a series of deliberate thefts.. For the defence it was urged that she was the victim of persons by whom she had been led astray, and a General of the Royal Artillery was willing to become bail to the extent of £1,000; but the magistrate declined to allow bail, and committed the prisoner for trial. POOR LAW ADMINISTRATION. Mr. G. Sclater Booth, M.P., presided on Monday at a conference of poor-law offia cers in London, and urged upon the delegates to hammer away persistently at the right administration of outdoor re- lief, urging that a too liberal and unprincipled administra- tion of it tended to diminish the thrift which they were all anxicus to enconrage. The right bon. gentleman said he should regard with suspicion anything which tended • to absorb in the county government that which it had hitherto been the duty of the guardians of the several unions to perform • and he contended that the poor-law system should not be sacrificed to the local government in the counties.

M. GLADSTONE STUNG BY A WASP. is There was a numerous attendance of visitors at Hawaffen on Sunday, some of whom had travelled long distances in the expecta- tion of seeing Mr. Gladstone. The route to the parish church along which Mr. Gladstone usually passes was lined with an expectant crowd just prior to the commencement of the service, but they were disappointed in this desire. A messenger arrived about this time with the news that Mr. Gladstone intended to remain indoors. A correspondent was informed on inquiry that the reason for his absence was due to a misfortune which befel him the previous night. He was out in the park felling a tree, when a wasp or some other stinging insect flew up and stung him upon the eyelid, of his right eye. SIR CHARLES DMUS AND POLITICAL LIFE. Sir Charles Dilke, in a letter to the President of the Chelsea. Liberal Association on a second vote of the Council naming him as a candidate, persists in the answer he had given after the first vote in his favour, to the effect that he will not re- enter public life until circumstances have reversed in the opinion of his countrymen the moral effect of his country- men the moral effect of the verdict in the Case of " Craw- ford V. Crawford, the Queen's Proctor intervening." Sir Charles adds that when the gross calumnies with which he has been assailed have been disposed of to the public satis- faction, as he feels sure they one day will be, he shall be. free, if he thinks fit to resume a political career. His pre- sent duty, he says, is to devote himself to the work of re- moving the unjust prejudice from whioh he suffers. AFFRAY WITH CROFTERS.—At Kelmure, Skye, on Mon- day, while a sheriff's officer, named Grant, from Inverness, was proceeding to the house of a Crofter at Bomaskitag, to serve a writ for arrears of rent, he was met by a crowd of people who appearectdetermined no to allow him to ap- proach the house. Grant was escorted by .a number of police- men, who endeavoured to disperse the crowd. A conflict ensued, the police using their batons freely, and the mob using sticks and stones. A detachment of marines were close at hand, and were ordered to disperse the crowd at the point of the bayonet. No resistance was offered the mili- tary. Six men were afterwards. arrested and taken to Por- tree on board her Majesty's ship Seahorse. On the arrival of the vessel the prisoners were landed and removed to Portree gaol, under a strong escort of military and police. THE ANTI-TITHE AGITATION IN WALES.—In the course of an interview with several Flintshire farmers, Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P., said that after the next session of Parliament it was very likely that tithes would be transferred to the landlords, and as the landlords' friends were in power lust now, it was quite possible that a revaluation would also be made. Beyond this they could not hope to go for some years. But nothing but the disestahlishment of the Church in England as well as Wales would finally settle the matter. —A meeting of the larrcers of the parish of Llantysilie, in the Vale of Llangollen, was held in Llantysilio schoolroom on Saturday evening last, under the presidency of Mr. T. M. Shaw, who read letters from the tithe owners expressint regret that tbe farmers had resolved to resist the tithe charge unless an abatement of 25 per cent. was granted. The tithe owners offered to make a reduction of 1.0 per cent. on the past two half years, or an abatement of 20 per cent. on the half year tithe rent now due. A heated discussion ensued, in which the farmers expressed their de- termination net to pay any tithe, and to suffer distraint rather than accept anything less than a reductien of 25 pez cent.

div.p: Bogess—(applause)—who had fought that battle against tbe most bitter oppositiot —(" oh, no," and " yes ")—outside the Council. (Hear, hear.) He was determined, however,' to carry the work through until it became a success. It redounded upon him the greatest credit, and he was glad he had stuck to Alderman Burgess on the Sanitary Committee against the most bitter oppoeition of some of the mem- bers who were uneducated on the question. They had oppcsed the scheme from sheer ignorance. (A Voice : "Because of the money it would cost.") Well, he would say because of the cost; and also from want of information. Laughter.) Warrington in his opinion that day stood fore- most amongst the towns of England. (Applauae.) It was the first town in the world in sanitary matters. It was an example to England. Ireland, Scotland, and Europe. The scheme had cost £l,soebut what was the money in compari- son to the health °Vie people? ( e ear, hear.) He had no patience with those people who condemned the Sanitary Committee because they had spent money for the benefit and the health of the people. (Hear, hear.) Who had been slandered more than Alderman Burgess? But what be had to saw to him that day was that he had got his reward. (Applause ) Tl4e great thing in this country to-day when competition was so keen was to manufacture without evaete, and he was delighted to see at Longford that they manufac- tured, without waste. (Hear, hear.) Let them think that- what they used to turn from the sewers to pollute the rivers and kill the fish was now being used for growing auger in Jamaica. Why, it was not only a benefit to Warrington, it ' was not only a benefit to Europe, but it was a benefit to the whole world. (Hear, hear) Warrington that day stood in a splendid position, and he was proud of the town. (Ap- plause)) They had differences outside the Council some- times, but he wanted to say to them as friends of Warring- ton, as friends of the Town Council—and he spoke without political prejudice, but as an independent man, for be did' not care for politics inside the Council —that if they were to govern the town they must have on the Council representatives of the large ratepayers. (Hear, hear.) They must get rid of these miserable political interferences with the Council, and he was delighted to think that when he stood up to second the nomination of Councillor Mackie on the 9th November he should be able to say then that they had commenced a new' era in the history of Warrington, and that from that day they would elect members to the Council irrespective of politics—men whey were most fitted to sit round that table. (Applause.) He hoped the leaders of the Conservative party and otheraof the Liberal party would join him to see that that arrangement waa brought about, as he was certain it would be bet,er for the town. (Applause.) Councillor BROADBMTE, in responding, concurred with Alderman Crosfield as to political interference with the Council. (Applause.), Mr. W. OWEN aleo responded; after which Alderman BURGESS, in very complimentary language, proposed the health of Mr. Longdin, the borough surveyor, to:whom, he said, they owed a debt they would never be able to repay for the services be had rendered in connection with that sanitary scheme.—Alderman HOLMES also proposed the health of Mr. Alliott, a member of the firm which supplied the machinery at Longford, who was present.—Mr. Alliott having responded, Alderman BURGESS said he had the re- quest to make that the Corporation would offer the scienti- fic world an opportunity of seeing the sewage works for the benefit of the human race. (Applause.) The proceedings then concluded.

div.head: COLLISION ON THE THAMES.
div.p: COLLISION ON THE THAMES.

A, STEAMER SUNK: SEVEN LIVES LOST. A collision resulting in A serious loss of life oc- curred on Thursday afternoon on the Thames near Grvesend. The cutward bound steamer Minerva was proceeding down the river when she came into collision with the steamer Borderer, which was going up stream. The shock was terrific, and the Minerva sustained such, injuries that she soon sank in the lower end of Gravesend Reach, and out of 23 men on board six were drowned. The remainder were landed at the pier by a tug, but one of them was so much injured that he died almost immedi- ately after being taken ashore. The Borderer, which is an iron screw steamer of 1,740 tons, belonging to Liverpool, and owned by J. Glynn and Sons, sus- tained considerable damage, but nobody on board was injured. Another account states- that the collisionoccurred about five o'clock at Higham Bight, about three miles below Gravesend. It took place between the screw steamer Minerva .of West Hartlepool, and the screw steamer Borderer, of Liverpool. The Minerva, which is 1,589 tons gross, was bound for Sunderland, and proceeding down on south shore, while the Borderer, 4,740 tons gross, was steaming ' up stream homeward bound from Boston. The Borderer struck the Minerva abaft the engines on the starboard side, and the vessel immediately .be- gan to sink. Some of the men jumped into the water and others mounted the rigging. The Red Rose (Captain W. Marsden) was waiting on the steamer Grecian, and on, witnessing the collision the captain immediately put off to the aisistance of the crew. They succeeded in picking up a number of men and three stowaways who had been on board the Minerva with a view of obtaining a passage to Sunderland, A coastguard skiff and other boats also went off, and the former rescued several men from the rig- ging. Six men, however, were drowned, and one named John Craig, engineer's steward, died on board the Red Rose while the men were being brought to Gravesend. The Borderer, it is stated, proceeded some distance up the river before she dropped anchor. Her stern is.severely damaged. The sur- vivors were conveyed to the Sailors' Home, Graves-- end, where they were provided with fresh clothing and. food at the expense of the Shipwrecked Mariners' Society. The names of the drowned are C. Steel, third engineer,. Sunderland; J. Mitchell, carpenter,. West Hartlepool; J.. Phillips, A. 8., Dun- dee; . D. Wells, A. 8., Dundee; W. Nelson, fireman, and T. Page, fireman, Whitby-. The Minerva had no I pilot, but the Borderer was in charge of a pilot from Dungeness. The Minerva sank in about seven I minutes after the collision in mid-channel off Ovens buoy, bottom of Gravesend Reach. The Borderer is anchored .off Powder buoy.

div.head: WIT AND HUMOUR.
div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

"Those who use our goods are very much attached to them," is what a porous plaster company advertises. She: "Why, Henry, what is the matter ?" He: "M' love—l—bit—lemon peel threw me down." She: "Lemon peel, yes; and what were the other ingre- dients ?" To be the sole possessor of a secret is frequently a source of unhappiness. For instance, a man knows he is a great man; no one else knows it, and he is miserable in consequence. THE LITTLE OlCES.—Harold, who wants to play in the garden, but is told that it is too cold, and is too proud to have anybody see him cry : "Oh, mamma, di* house is so hot—it des make my eyes sweat !" "Why, Laura, how tight you wear your corsets!" said one lady to another, as they were dressing for dinner. "I never could enjoy anything I eat if I wore mine as tight as you do." "Grace before meat," the other re- plied, as she laced herself in. One day the court marshal to the late King of Han- over came in bearing in his hand a large despatch with ft, broad black rim of deep mourning. It was the official announcement of the death of an old archduchess of Austria. The king, who had sent out cards for a court ball, declined to realise this interesting fact, and said, without breaking the seal, "There, there—take it away! I know all about it. Let her die next week !" COMPLIMENTARY TO THE LECTURER.—Hugh Stowell Brown used to relate how, on one occasion when he made his appearance at Edinburgh under the presi- dency of the Lord Provost of the city, a wealthy bailie rose with much empressement to propose a rather obse- quious "vote of thanks" to "his worship, the Lord Pro- vost, for the great sacrifice of his valuable time which he had made in coming out to attend this lecture." A VERY SUCCESSFUL CASE.—First Lawyer: " Ah, Dobkins, how did you come out of that case You were just beginning when I went out?" Second' Lawyer: "Gloriously. 'lt was a perfect success; created a great sensation; papers full of it; got lots of advertising out of it. I think it was the making of my future." "Good !" Glad to hear it, old fellow. .1 knew you had the stuff in you; and, by the way, what did they do with your client ?" "Oh, they hanged him." "One of my ancestors won a battle during the Cru- sades by his skill in handling his artillery," said the baron. "hut my dear baron,' said his friend, "at the time of the Crusades gunpowder had not yet been dis- covered." "I know that as well as you do, and so did my ancestor." "How did he win the battle then ?" "He brought his artillery to bear on the Saracens, and the stupid fools, seeing the guns, supposed that powder had at last been discovered, and fled in dismay." A man who had the gift of shaping a great many things out of orange-peel was displaying his abilities before Rufus Choate and Daniel Webster, and succeeded in carving a pig to the admiration of the company. Webster tried the same feat, and, after strewing the table with the peel of a dozen oranges, gave it up, with the exclamation, "I must give up the pig! I can't make him." "Nay," remarked Choate, glancing at the table; "you have done more. Instead of a pig, you have made a litter !" HE WAS A BOSTON Boy.—" Your little boy must be very intelligent," said a visitor to a Boston school- teacher, whose five-year-old son was forming Greek words with building blocks. "Intelligent !" exclaimed the proud parent. "He is phenomenally gifted. As an example of his early erudition, what do you suppose were the first words he ever spoke?" " Papa ' and 'mamma'?" "Stuff and nonsense !" ejaculated the father, in a tone of disgust. "Why, the day he was twelve months old he suddenly laid down his algebra and said to me, Father, the longer I live the more in- dubitable proofs I perceive that there is in Boston as much culture to the square inch as there ever was in the ambient area of ancient Athens' !" • The present Pope is an old gentleman with a keen sense of humour. Accredited to the Papal court is a functionary who represents the political interests of four Central American republics, and who is already bedizened with the stars of almost every order created by the Pon- tificate. Not long ago a fresh negotiation was concluded satisfactorily to the Mother Church, and the custom of giving a new distinction had to be observed; but what to do perplexed the Papal chamberlain. On application in the emergency to Leo himself, the latter said, "This time give bhim a snuff-box with my portrait." The diplomatist accepted the golden gift, aetached the por- trait therefrom, and appeared at the next audience with it hanging from his neck. Another state negotiation unexpectedly arose, and, when it was solved, there again came up the question of an honorarium. " This time," said Leo, "give him a marble statue, and see if he will wear that round his neck I" A RHETORlClAN.—Schoolmaster, to his wife: My dear, I wish you would speak more carefully. You say that "Henry Jones came to this town from Sunderland ?" Wife: Yes.—Schoolmaster: Well, now, wouldn't it be better to say that "he came from Sunderland to this town ?"—Wife: I don't see any difference in the two expressions.—Schoolmaster: But there is a difference—a rhetorical diriereLico. You don't hear me make use of such awkward expressions. By-the-way, I have a letter from your father in my pocket.—Wife: But my father is not in your pocket. You mean you have in your pocket a letter from my father.—Schoolmaster : There you go with your little quibbles! You take a delight in harassing me. You are always taking up a thread, and representing it as'a rope.—Wife :Representing it to be a rope, you mean.—Schoolmaster: For goodness sake, be quiet! Never saw such a quarrelsome woman in my life! A gentleman formerly a professor in Roberts College, Constantinople, records the following travesty of justice illustrative of the law in Turkey, where an accused man must prove his innocence, or else he is declared guilty. A convert to Christianity came to Dr. Lord, a missionary there, and asked if it was ever right to tell a lie. This was a staggerer for the doctor, and he said he would have to know the case before he could decide, although on general principles he did not think it was. "The case is this," replied the seeker after truth. "A Turk, a stranger to me, living in Rustchuk, accused me of buying and receiving from him one thousand sheep. I knew of no way of proving that I did not buy and receive these sheep, and the case must certainly go ' against me. It came up for trial to-day; and, after the charge had been made, I admitted that I had bought and received the sheep—which was a lie—and had at the same time paid for them in full. He couldn't prove that I had not, so the case was dismissed." The doctor thought that, if ever a lie was justifiable, this was cer- tainly the time. We read in "Personal Memoirs of the U.S. Grant" that on one occasion during the Civil War M the United States, when stationed at a post of several companies commanded by a field-Officer, General Bragg was com- manding one of the companies at the same time acting as Post quartermaster and commissary. He was first lieutenant at the time, but his captain was detached on other duty. As commander of the company, he made a requisition upon the quartermaster—himself—for some- thing he wanted. As quartermaster, he declined to fill the requisition, and indorsed on the back of it his reasons for so doing. As company commander, he re- sponded to this, urging that his requisition called for nothing but what he was entitled to do, and that it was the duty of the quartermaster to fill it. As quarter- master, he still persisted that he was right. In this con- dition of affairs, Bragg referred the whole matter to the commanding officer of the post. The latter, when he saw the nature of the matter referred, exclaimed, 44 Good heavens," Mr. Bragg, you have quarrelled with every officer in the army, and now you are quarrelling ourself!

THE CLERICAL IMPOSTER. On Monday, at Dublin Police Court, before Dr. Keyes, Q.C., the clerical iriaposter, Thomas Keatinge, alias Moreton, was charged in custody with having obtained money by false pretences from the Rev. Dr. Moffatt, of Milltown Church, Dublin; also with hav- ing failed to comply with the conditions of his ticket- of leave to report himself to the Dublin police in June last. The Crown Solicitor prosecuted by direction of the Attorney-General, and, having recounted the several convictions already standing against the ac- cused, said he would shortly examine the Rev. Dr. Moffatt, and identify the prisoner for the purpose of a remand. Mr. Murphy, solicitor, appeared for Keat- inge, who was attired in a heavy freise "dread- nought," with a cape, and was cleanly shaved, exoent his moustache. Keatinge kept his hand to his ear during the recital of his previous convictions, and complained of deafness. He asked the Crown Solicitor to raise his voice. His demeanour was quiet and subdued, and he calwly looked round him and scanned' the faces of the crowded court. Several members of his congregation were present, but none had a word of pity for him. They said they had never from the pulpit heard him speak against the Church of Rome, though he had frequently done so in private conversation. Dr. Moffatt deposed that the prisoner had received money for officiating for him. He was introduced by the "Priests' Protection Society," and the Archbishop of Dublin sanctioned his being employed. He repre- sented himself as having been a Roman Catholic priest, and said that re-ordination was unnecessary in joining the Episcopal Church of England. The prisoner, who interrupted with the remark, "Don't tell lies," was remanded, bail being refused. His wife was in court, and upon creating a "scene," was removed. Mrs Keatinge has written a letter in which she re- pudiates a number of statements made regarding her husband. She winds up the epistle in the following terms :—" It is not alleged even by his enemies that anything has been committed by him since 1879. In any other profession eight years' good character would cover a multitude of sins. Lord Plunket cannot allege anything against my husband's personal con- duct during the six months that he has been in Dub- lin, nor can anyone who has admitted him into the intimacy of their friendship. All right-minded per- sons must admit that it is my husband's great and ex- ceptional talents that have stirred up spiteful jealousy. He had a right to expect fair play from the public, to be treated as his conduct while under their eyes meri- ted ; and if they would even now, after his enemies have exhausted their malice, give him this chance, they would find him fully deserving their confidence." The Rev. E. L. Forster, of Holmer- road, Hereford, in a letter to the Dublin Express," gives a remarkable account of Keatinge's experiences in England. He says: The Rev. T. Hedge, of Helm- don, Northampt.n, was first brought in contact with him when on a visit to his sister in London. He was asked to visit a person in great poverty in an attic, where he found the impostor, who, it afterwards tran- spired, had just come out of Wandsworth prison, where be had served twelve months for obtaining money by false pretences from Mr. Remington Mills, then an M.P. Mr. Hedge invited Keatinge to his country house, and Mr. Mudie, the great bookseller, gave him money for an outfit. Keating went to Helmdon with Mr. Hedge, and afterwards filled a vacant pulpit at the Independent church at Brockley ; subsequently, under the name of Morton, Keatinge presenta himself at Mr. Forster's church and was allowed to preach. Mr. Forster, however, soon found him out. and they got rid of him. He then made his way to Bradford, in Yorkshire, where he put up at a lodging-house kept by a widow with three children. He soon married the widow, and went about asking for help for himself and wife and. children. He afterwards made his way back to Loudon, and wrote to his deserted wife stating that he could do nothing more for her, and that she had better look out for another husband as soon as she could.
