div.head: Tetteo to the i,ditor.
div.p: Tetteo to the i,ditor.
"A WARRINGTON HIGH RIP GANG."

Sir,—You will no doubt be surprised to hear that we have such a gang in Warrington. The members of it are loafers who usually block the corners of Bank-street and Hill-street (better known as Pig Hill). Any day, if you will take a look round, you will find them at one of the places men- tioned, chewing tobacco, cursing and swearing, and spitting over the footpath. This stops respectable people from coming up Buttermarket-street. Is this what we pay rates for? You might say what the policemen are doing to allow these ruffians to run sway with shopkeepers' trade, but then look what a glorious occupation we find our officers of the law—we have then watching a rubbish heap to see that children do not run away with the bits of fancy tiles they have found. And vet they allow people of the above class to block the doors of tradesmen and ran away with trade. Such is life."—Yours, REFORM.

div.head: SUNDAY SCHOOL AND THE THEATRE.
div.p: THE SUNDAY SCHOOL AND THE THEATRE.

Sir,—The devil is said to quote Scripture when he is 1 carrying out some of his most sinister designs. By the same token I conclude that your correspondent, "J. B. Isaac," has some uncanny and very crude ideas respecting the theatre; and I would ask him what he knows of it—. from experience, not hearsay. If he has been in the habit of visiting a respectable " home of the drama," he has a' brain of the shallowest if no good has accrued to him there; and if he does not practically know the theatre, he is utterly unsuited to express an opinion upon it, and is a very blind leader of the blind. In fact, he is a mere profess()), and realizes Thomas Hood's famous definition of one to a nicety :

" A mere professor, spite of all his cant, is Not a whit better than a Mantis— An insect. of what clime I can't determine, That ldts its paws most parson-like, and thence, By simple savages—through sheer pretence— Is reek, n'd quite a saint among the vermin."

All Shakespere's trandest inspirations are drawn from the Bible, and re-produced on the stage to do us good; but "J. B. Isaac," either through sheer ignorance, or (what is worse) narrow-minded bigotry, would debar our younger genera- tion from reaping any benefits there. I feel thankful indeed that my children are net under his spiritual mentorsbip ; and when such a Catholic-minded man as the late Canon Kingsley could write : " I have derived more practical Christianity from seeing Shakesuere's plays enacted on the stage than from any sermon I ever heard from tke pulpit," I do think that "J. B. I. " might with profit revise his posi- tion and rise above the level of "shop" before egotistically condemning so mighty a lever for good as the stage. And, above all things, let him avoid quoting Scripture—he isn't happy at it. GARRICK. 26th October, 1856.

div.head: SPIRITUALISM V. CONJURING.
div.p: SPIRITUALISM V. CONJURING.

Sir,—A lady who was present at the conjuring entertain- ment given at the Public Hall, on Saturday evening, told me, in describing the many wonderful things done by the performer, that he said in answer to the question, "What is spiritualism ? " that it was "humbug." Now, I have beard much of this subject lately, and a short time ago a trades- man in this town placed in my bands a copy of a spiritualis- tic journal entitled "Light," and on perusing the same I was surprised to find the names of a large number of scien- tific, literary, and other distinguished personages; also -ministers and MD's, all giving their testimony to the genuineness of certain phenomena said to occur in the presence of persons entitled "mediums," and in the light, and for which at present no cause could be assigned than that these phenomena are due to the operations of departed human beings. lithe testimony of these witnesses is genu- ine, our friend the performer at the Public Hall has made a grievous mis-statement, which calls in question the honesty and truthfulness of persons who have, as far as we are able to judge, always been of unimpeachable character. I really cannot bring myself to think that the persons whose names I saw in that journal, given in attestation ot the gerniness of the phenomena, and of the honesty of the " medium" in whose presence they saw these things, have been "humbugged "; which they must have been if what our friend says be true. I should be glad to learn through the columns of your paper, of which lam now a constant reader, if any of my fellow subscribers have had any per- sonal experience in this matter, and what they think of it. I have no doubt there are others who, like myself, are de- siring more " light" on this subject, and with the hope that we may receive the same from some able pen, I re- main, yours faithfully, Warrington, October 27th, 1886.
"BETA."

div.head: WARRINGTON WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVE-
div.p: WARRINGTON WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVE-
MENT SOCIETY.

Sir,—As one of the secretaries of the above society, I feel that I must ask permission to trespass on your space in ,answer to the remarkable effusions which have emanated from the pen of W.E.S." I do not intend to enter into any polemical discussion with this individual, who is screen- ing himself or herself, as the case may be, behind a hetero- geneous alphabetical combination which, up to the present, I have been unable to fathom, as to the right or wrong of theatre going. That is a matter, in my humble opinion, for a Christian, Methodistical or otherwise, to settle between his conscience and his God. But I must protest against the manner in which " W.E.S.'B" complaint against our Society has been brought forward. This individual, who 19 promp- ted, according to his own words, by the highest moral mo- tives, tells us "in a quiet way" that he "is sorry to have had to write upon the subject, but it is his only means of getting listened to." Now I must take exception to that statement, entirely. Had " W.E.S." looked around, he might have discovered many happier, and it may be, more effective methods of lodging his complaint. I will only mention one. It is dis- tinctly stated on the notice papers of the society, which are posted weekly in the porches of our chapels, that "Persons wishing to become members of this society will please communicate with the secretaries." Now, " W.E.S." cannot plead ignorance of the existence of sue 4 officials, although we are only "ambitious young men;" and as one of those humble individuals let me inform him that it would have been perfectly easy to have communi- cated with either myself or Mr. E. Plinston, who would have been only too delighted to nominate so worthy an indi- vidual for membership, even had we known that his first act would have been to impeach the secretaries of the society. Such a method of proceeding would, at least, have had the advantage of being open and straightforward. But" vtoE goes on further to make statements which ha cannot for one moment substantiate. He says" the Sun if superintendents to a man are against von." I think f " W.E.S." would "come out from among" the multitude of anonymous writers, I could prove that tbis is far from being the case. Then again, with regard to our members he writes—"Of whom many are not Metho4ists and the majority of the remainder only nominal ones." What are the facts of to e case? Lot me enlighten this unhappy individual, whose " facts " are as inaccurate i!s his charges are uncharitable and trumpery. 3be following statement falls far short of the actual stite of the case with reg.ard to members of society e--Total number of members 94, members of society 59. nominal Wesleyans 27, other denominations 8. Such is this society of ambitious young men of wor:Zly taste With all deference to '" W. E. 5.," I would ask, What about the ladies? As to the dramatic recitals which. have so agi- tated the mind of "W. F. 5.," and, I admit, of some few ethers, thc. secretaries, of course, are primarily responsible. We are quite alive to our responsibility, and if we have in any way forfeited the confidence which has been reposed in us ly the society, our duty is clear, and we shall not be slow to act accordingly.
Apologising for trespassing at such length, I am, yours, &c.,
JOHN E. RICHARDSON. Paddington House, Warrington.
"THE REVIVAL IN TRADE."

' Sir,—Your readers must not smile at the heading to my ! letter. I should in its place have writ en " Trade Depres- sion," but for two reasons. First, everybody (including I writers of trade reports) says that trade is reviving, even Lord Randolph is rash enough to tell a listening world that "Pepper is rising ;" and second, lam afraid your readers would not have taken any interest if I lead aeked them to reed a few remarks on the "Third Report of the Royal ! Commission on Depression of Trade and Industry." This I report, just issued, is interesting ; it places before the pub- lic a mass of information, and, by the way, I wonder what i percentage of the population will ever read it? The evid- ence eiven is so conflicting, that one can but pity the Gov- ernment whose duty it may be to reduce it to order, and render some return to the country for the large outlay. , I may tell your readers that the evidence is extracted by an elaborate system of cross.examination. The consequence is that the reader is often puzzled to know what conclusion the Commission will come to, and what the witnesses ex. amined really mean. However, sneaking for myself, I have come to this conclusion, that the sooner Englishmen take the land question in hand the better. There is not in the evideuce tendered, out point put forward but what if , logically argued out leads us to the source of all life, to the j centre from which all profit springs, and towards which we I all have to look for sustenance. Your columns, and the Liberal press of the country, have for a number of years I been open to those who have felt called upon to urge the , ,nd question upon the public notice. Associations have been formed of land reformers, men who have felt it their ! duty to think out, well and diligently, the questions that affected the well-being and prosperity of the people; con- clusions have been arrived at, years ago as to what caused our troubles. These conclusions, when'given to the world, brought to their expounders—what? The world's scorn and contempt. Those of your readers who are acquainted with the lives of our dead and gone reformers, know that years of their weary pilgrimages were spent in prison ; that with the aid of their inventive brains, and the blood from their veins enly, could they manage to spread their opinions. There is no doubt the world moves; but, oh, how slowly! Yet what can we expect when in Warrington a Liberal is opposed to School Boards, and workingmen vote for a man who, year by year. keeps adding acre to acre, and whose riches are in proportion to their degradation ? Sir, I could name half a dozen burning questions which, put forward within the last half century, had they been carried would to-clay have conduced immensely to the well being and stability of the kingdom. Who to-day doubts that if the "International Association of Workingernen " had been successful in its objects, we Englishmen, Germans, and Belgians, should not at the present time have been at one another's throats fiercely contending for the right to earn bread for our children? And yet it, like most other brilliant ideas, was born before its time, or shall I say the people, contented to be hoodwinked, allowed those who had the power to stamp it out? The Report before me contains evidence that the pros- pects of farmers are anything but reassuring; men farming as much as 16,000 acres of land complain that rent is being paid out of capital, in consequence of "the average reduc- tion in value of farm produce being from 30 to 40 percent" The price of woel 15 years ago was 20 pence per lb., now it is down to 9d, with no prospect of rising. When asked if there were ere, prospects of recovery in farm produce, a farmer (Mr. Rea) answered, " I certainly see no prospect of agriculture rising just now, but everything on the contrary is tending to bring us down to the level of the world. I think we are not down to the level of the world yet. The prospect is that as regards our workmen in towns who are not employed, and without the prospect of being employed that I can see, and in order to enable them to spend any money, naturally the produce of the land will have to be at a lower rare than it is now. Ido not think we are at the lowest ebb yet." ' Sir, if I were to add nothing to this statement, if all the land reformers were to stay their efforts and merely publish the above evidence and give it to the world, it should be enough to convince the most dense that our remedy lies in the land. But it does not even convince the man himself. Speaking against small holdings he said—" It is not a fortnight since we had an application to our Board of Guardians for relief from a person who was a tenant farmer occupying 10 or 12 acres. On principle I said "No ; you must go and get your rent reduced like other people." This he explained further by saying—" If the small farmer received outdoor relief the result would be that the union upon which he was a charge would indirectly be paying the man's rent." Of course; still, this farmer paying his own capital away in the shape of rent, states that he "should be very sorry to see the castles and mansions unoccupied." One of the good old Tories this, who would blindly rush on to perdition before giving a band to reform, who insists upon it that our present trouble "is a labour question, and that we must come to the starting point with the labourer, for he is the consumer, but we must all come down to the level of the world. Look at the perpetaal strikes that are going on. Working-men must be content with less, and be more willing to do the work when they have got it." I think if the people knew the kind of evidence that is being given before the Commissioners they would scarcely rest satisfied. This man can see nothing wrong in his landlord pocketing his capital, but he deplores the "expensive habits of working-men," and insists that "they should be content with such wages as the employers can afford to give them." Really, it makes one despair of things. The statement is made by this farmer that his own grown barley "was this year being consumed by his own stock," and that he had been told by a maltster, "You muit be content to take a low price for your barley this year, be- cause your barley will not at all compete with what we can buy from Seal, in Germany." With the farmer, as with us all, the railway question is an important item; he says, "It will cost me more to send cattle to Liverpool than it will cost to send them from Chicago or New York." Sir, there are forces at work that not even the stupidity of Tory farmers can resist. In this morning's paper is the following :—" On Saturday 282 a. Or. 29p. of arable pasture, and wood land, having thereon farmhouse, buildings, and four cottages, at Timberland, near Lincoln, was sold by auc- tion for £2,150. It was stated at the sale that a mortgage of £16.00 was secured on the estate a few years ago." October 27, 1886. CLIFFORD DIX.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTEI:.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTEI:.

LONDON, THURSDAY. Lord Randolph Churchill still keeps the ball rol- ling for the Conservatives in the country. His visit to Bradford was a great success, albeit there was no- thing particular in any of his addresses. But un- doubtedly he added fuel to the fire of provincial Conservatism, and that is more than some more finished orators can do. Lord Randolph has the gift, possessed by Mr. Disraeli, of exciting the en- thusiasm and drawing towards himself the personal adulation of the mob; but it was only in later years that this great gift was developed in the old leader. In his political youth Mr. Disraeli was laughed at. In his middle-age he was detested. It was only in his declining years, almost at the close, that he became the object of party adulation. To Lord Randolph Churchill this enviable condition has come at the very outset of his career. His youth, his audacity, his irreverence, and his utter recklessness have endeared him to a people who like "go," and who have reluctantly acquiesced in Sir Stafford Northcote's confession that he was lacking in that quality; Lord Randolph Churchill has been the Bad Boy of the Parliamentary school, and as often happens in schools, he is the prime favourite. What his colleagues in the Ministry think of it all it would be interesting to know. Lord Randolph Churchill eclipses them much as Mr. Gladstone loomed so large in the public eye that his colleagues found their personal influence wholly diminished. But there is a notable difference in the two cases. Mr. Gladstone took his position as leader by right of years and conspicuous service. Lord Randolph Churchill is almost the youngest member of the Ministry, and has not had a year's experience of office. Still lie is the leader who shows the way, without taking counsel, and apparently without caring whether he is followed. Though he said nothing new at Bradford, and albeit the speech regarded merely as an oratorical effort must take second rank among his elaborate efforts, it was of prime importance, .because it endorsed everything that had been said in the Dartford speech. "I am sorry I made that speech then," said Lord Randolph, and Mr. Chaplin, who was sitting near, pricked up his ears. Was Lord Randolph going to benefit by the lectures read to him publicly and privately, and was he going to disavow the Dargord speech? "I am sorry I made it then," Lord Randolph continued, "because if I had not I would have made it now. This is a hard blow for good:Tories. But they do no:; seem inclined to take independent action, and Ran- dolph is left master of the situation. Lord Rosebery has managed to achieve a feat in attempting which Lord Randolph Churchill and many other aspirants have failed. He has succeeded in paying an important political visit without a hint of the fact getting into the newspapers. At the end of last week he went from Mentmore to Hawarden to have a last word with Mr. Gladstone before leaving for India. It was a hurried visit, Lord Rosebery arriving at Hawarden at six o'clock in the evening, remaining for dinner, and leaving for London by the night train, which brought him here early in the morning. Lord Rosebery had, I believe, the fullest sanction of Mr. Gladstone both for his Newcastle speech and for the important letter he wrote to the people at Leith. Mr. Glad- stone is anxious above all things that the split in. the Liberal party shall be closed up as soon as pos- sible, and avows himself ready to do anything short of sacrificing principle to bring about that end. Unfortunately Mr. Chamberlain, in private conversation and correspondence, adopts an almost identical tone. Nothing distresses him more than the 'chasm from the o. her side of which a large majority of the Liberal party scowl at him. But Mr. Chamberlain, like Mr. Gladstone, believes that he is in the right, and will not abate one iota of his demands as a preliminary to bringing about that re-union which he so earnestly desires. This, of course, means nothing, and the unity of the Liberal party is as far off as ever. The fact is, though it is not a pleasant thing to write about, that the prolongation of the split in. the Liberal party is very clearly and precisely limi- ted. It will last, as far as Lord Hartington, Mr. Chamberlain, and their fliends are concerned, ex- actly as long as Mr. Gladstone's life. Lord Harting- ton, and above all, Mr. Chamberlain, are deter- mined that if they can help it, and until the next general election, they certainly can, Mr. Gladstone shall not again fill the office of Prime Minister. This is the rock upon which the fortunes of the Go- vernment of Lord Salisbury are anchored. But, as everyone can see, it may any day topple to a fall. If to-morrow Mr. Gladstone were to announce his retirement from political life there woula be an end of Tory supremacy. Lord llartington might per- haps stand by the Conservatives in that progressive Liberalism with which Lord Randolph Churchill has succeeded in inoculating it. But Mr. Chamber- lain would immediately begin to strike out for him- self. All the hopes and fears of the Conservatives are, in this new and striking departure, bound up with the life and health of Mr. Gladstone. Thc political existence of the two are coterminous. Your readers will doubtless remember that two or three days ago I gave a pretty full summary of the leading points in a statement drawn up on behalf of Sir Charles Dilke with reference to the case of Crawford versus Crawford. One of the London even- ing journals has now got hold of the document, and 1- as printed it verbatim. It is assumed in. some quarters that this has been done at the instance of Sir Charles Dilke. I happen to know that this is a mistake, and that no one was more surprised than the right honorable baronet to find the text of what was circulated as a confidential document in a pub- lic print. The statement is judicial in tone, is drawn up with great skill, and, as would appear from the digest supplied to you, it contains some points which, had they been submitted to the jury, might have led to a different issue. Sir Charles is, however, owing to a concatenation of circum- stances, in a position that though one rose from the dead to prove his innocence the public would not listen. Years may have the effect of toning down this feeling, but in the meantime silence is the best course for Sir Charles Dunce to adopt, a cruel sen- tence if it be applied to the case of an innocent man. There is, I believe, some foundation for the report that Sir Charles Dilke intends to embark in journalism. He is already the proprietor of the ".-ktlienum" and two other weekly papers, which are admirable properties. But he wants something nearer to politics than that, and has been making inquiries as to the prospects of a new evening paper. As yet no determination has been come to on the subject. div.head: DROWNING FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: DROWNING FATALITY AT WAR- RINGTON.

At abou eight o'clock on Tuesday evening, the body of a man named William Harrop, 25 years of age, was found in the river Mersey at Howley Quay wharf. Deceased, who was a labourer, had been mis- sing since Sunday, and was supposed to have fallen into the water as he was returning from visiting some friends.

Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an in- quiry into the circumstances attending the death of deceased at the General Wolfe Inn, Church-street, on Thursday afternoon, when the following witnesses were called :—John Lawrenson, labourer, Brick-street, said he and others were grappling in the Mersey at eight o'clock on Tuesday night for the body of the deceased, which was found near Howley Quay. There were no marks of violence on it. There would be from 19 to 20 feet of water in the river at the spot where the body was found. A person could walk into the river, as it was close to the roadway, and a person going that way on a foggy night might fall into the water; there was nothing to prevent him doing so.— Ellen Dutton, wife of William Dutton, labourer, employed at Mersey Mills, identified the body of the deceased as that of her son, who was 26 years of age, and had worked at the Bewsey Wire Ropery. She last saw him alive on Saturday. On Saturday he went to see Joseph Simcock, of Welling- ton-street, and as he did not come home on Saturday night she made inquiries about him on Sunday morn- and ascertained that he had left Simcock's about two o'clock on Sunday morning. Deceased and Sim. cock had been friends for some time.—Joseph Sim- cock. joiner, 72, Wellington-street, said deceased and William Dutton, his step-father, went to his house about eleven o'clock on Saturday night. Deceased was then the worse for liquor, and brought two pints of beer with him. Dutton left witness's house some time before deceased, who remained until two o'clock. Deceased was net sober when he started for home. I was not until Tuesday morning that witness was informed that the deceased had not gone home.— Constable Griffiths stated that he saw the body of the deceased on Tuesday night in a boat. On searching it he found a small knife and 3s 4d in money. There was a small scratch on deceased's forehead, but there was no discolouration.—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that deceased was found drowned, but that there was no evidence to show how he got into the water.

RESIGNATION OF JUDGES.—We learn that Lord Black- burn, Justices Grove, Denman, Field, and Huddleston are about to resign their seats on the judicial bench. Sir James Hannen will, it is said, be raised to the House of Lords. EXTRAORDINARY SCENE IN A DOCIL—At the Middlesex Sessions, on Tuesday afternoon, on a man named Strachan being found guilty of robbery he turned upon a fellow- prisoner named Heath, who had tendered evidence, and seized him by the throat and tried to strangle him. Heath, who is a small man, was unable to offer effective assistance, but he was rescued by the warders and detectives, who leaped into the dock. Strachan was then sentenced to twelve months' imprisonment, and Heath to two days. FO3NDERING OF A STEAMER: THIRTY LIVES LOST.—A Special Lloyd's telegram received on Thursday morning from Nantes states that five circular lifebuovs marked Flaw- steed, have been picked up at Roscoff, on the French coast, having apparently been only a short time in the water. Underwriters are of opinion that they belonged to the large iron steamer Flamsteed, of North Shields, 1,934 tons regis- ter, homeward bound from Odessa with a full cargo of grain, which vessel left Malta on the 3rd met, and was due in the Channel on the 15th inst. bat has not yet been reported. There is no doubt she went down in the recent heavy gale, and that her crew of 30 men have perished.

amendment to the closure rule which met with the boisterous approval of Lord Randolph Churchill and enjoyed the united support of the Conservative party. Lord Randolph has now gone clean round, and the party, in spite of Mr. Chaplin's lament, are preparing to follow him. But what will Mr. Mar- riott do? It will be a painful thing to resign his office. But if he does not he must be prepared to lose the last shred of political character. Definite action is being taken to bring about a practical issue to the late cOntroversy about the royal Academy. During the last few weeks meet- ings of artists have been held in a friend's studio, where a project has been elaborated for starting a new thing in exhibitions in opposition to the Royal Academy. It is to be called the National Exhibi- tion of the Arts, and will include painting, sculp- ture, architecture, engraving, and decorative de- signs. Mr. Clausen, Mr. Crane, and Mr. Holman dunt, the early leaders of the revolt, are among the better known names of the Executive Committee. About forty artists have already joined the Pro- visional Committee. They are not all known to fame, but they form a fair representation of the working class of British artists who kick against the alleged favouritism of the Royal Academy. The fundamental principle of the new undertaking is that the juries for selecting and piaci', sr works of art in the exhibition must be elected from and by the artists of the Kingdom. The artists have come forward in considerable numbers to support the guarantee fund, and we may soon hear an an- nouncement of the first "National Art Exhibition.". It is a very modest undertaking to start with; but the men promoting it are much in earnest, and are strong in the assurance of public sympathy. That it is no amater- affair is shown by names cited, and is established by the rule that only artists who in the last two years have exhibited a work of art in any of the principal exhibitions may contribute to the new show.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM 01:711 OWN CORRESPONDE:siT j. 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The fortnightly settlement on the Stock Exchange which has engroersed the attention of operators to the exclusion of geueral business, unless mining sbares, can be called general business, ha, been both heavy and exciting. Various dis- quieting rumours were rife at the commencement of the week, which resulted in a scare. Several heavy failures were said to 1)e imminent, and the bold speculator who has recently acquired fame as the " Parioian plunger,"was re- ported to have devised some new schema for upsetting the markets. What truth there may be in these stories remains to be seen. The gold fever is rasing har4r than ever. New mining companies are coxling, out almost daily with the announcement that the share jist will close within twenty-four hours. Of course it is impossible for the public on such notice to subscribe, but the professional dealer takes them up feeling sure that the tiblic will come in after, when the excitement gets sufficiently worked up, and the dealer is able to work off all the rubbish at a good premium. There are already a number of gold mining companies whose shares a short time since cotild have been bought for as many shillings as they now fetch pounds, and this rise in many instances is not due to any dividends that should have been paid, nor was the previous fall' dine to any cause save market operations. Therefore it is of undoubted testimony that more often than not this class of shares is not judged on its merits, and there can be little doubt that discriminate investors have had the opportunity of making good returns.

The sensation of the week, however, has been the issue of shares in the great brewery home of Arthur Guineas and Co. The six millions asked for was applied for ten times over in the twenty-four hours, and the shares are at an un- precedented premium. Small fortunes have been made by those lucky enough to be first in, the market. It is signifi- cant enoegh that while an almost national concern like that of the Manchester Ship Canal vainly endeavoured to raise six millions, supported by the powerful name of Rothschild, a brewery could obtain ten times- the amount of capital simply by a bare announcement of its requirements. Me amount applied for also shows there is plenty of money waiting for in7estment.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
The Glasgow Exhibition guarantee fund has reached the sum of £65.000.

The Ayrshire coal masters have refused their workmen any advance in wages. Dr. Bewick, Catholic Bishop of Hexbam and Newcastle, died on Friday afternoon at Tynemouth. It is said that the Marquis of Lorne has been approached with a view to becoming the Liberal candidate for Tor- quay. The " Gazette " publishes a Privy CouncWorder prohi- biting the landing in Great Britain of animals brought from Norway. Lord Iddesleigh receival the Russian and German Am- bassadors and Austrian Charge de Affairs at the Foreign Office on Friday.

A New York correspondent writes : It is agreed by all competent authorities that Mr. Henry George has no chance of election as Mayor. The Shop Hours Regulation Act, by which employers of persons under eighteen years of age in shops, public-houses, Stc.„ is limited, comes into operation on Monday next. THE CLYDE SHIPBUILDING TBADE.--it is stated that there is at length a prospect of a- revival in the Clyde ship- building trade. Of four recent contracts for vessels for the China coasting trade three have been secured by Clyde firms, and one by a Belfast firmi and the engines of all will be made at Glasgow.

GBRAT FIRE IN GLASGOW.—EarIy on Friday morning a fire occurred in the premises of William Adam and Sons, bleachers, dyers, and finishers, Millbank, Townmill-road, Grlasgow, causing damage estimated at £4400% which is covered by insurance. The chain drying stove, the calender- ing house, and the starch stuffing house were almost wholly destroyed. _ _

DEATH or TER EARL OF STRAFFORD.-The Earl of Strafford died at half-past one o'clock on Friday morning, at Wroth= Park, near Barnet, where he has been lying ill for some time past. The deceased, George Stephens Byng. second Earl of Strafford, was born in 1806. He is succeeded by his eldest son. Viscount Enfield, who was born in 1830. and who already sits in the House of Lords as Baron Strafford.

WIFE MURDER HT BIRMINGRAII.—•-011 Friday morning. a woman Darned Sarah Norbury died at the Queen's Hos- pital, Birmingham, from the effects of terrible injuries in- flicted upon her by her husband. The husband went home drunk, seized a billhook, slashed her across the head, and and then when the woman put up her arms to save a second blow he chopped one of them off at the wrist. The husband is in custody. AIICYITIBR RAILWAY TRAGEDY. —A mysterious discovery was made on the London and North-Western Railway, near Birmingham on Friday morning. A respectably-dressed man was found lying across the lines near Erdiogton Bridge, with both his legs cut off, his head smashed, and his body terribly mangled. His watch chain was banging, but no watch or money was found upon him. The police are in- vestigating the affair.

div.head: RUSSIA AND BULGARIA.
div.p: RUSSIA AND BULGARIA.

A telegram fro-si Sofia states that the Bulgarian Govern- ment have refused the Russian demand to raise the state of siege, despite the fact that General Kaulbars bas issued another threatening note. TERR,BLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—FIFTEEN , PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH.

PH/LADELP-11—IA7i'll—II—RS—D—AY.--AL —express train on the Chicago, Milwaukee. and St. Pawl Railroad about midnight ran off the rails near Portage, Wisconsin. The coaches were demolished and the wreck was burnt. Of eighteen persons in a passenger coach fifteen were burnt to death, their corpses being entirely consumed. One man and two children in the same coach escaped, but are badly in- jured. PRESIDENT CLEVELAND AND THE STATUE OF LIBERTY.

NEW YORK, FRlDAY.—President Cleveland, in signify- ing big acceptance yesterday of the Statue of Liberty, as a gift from France to the American nation, said this token of the affection and consideration of the French people de- monstrated the kinship of Republics, and conveys to us the assurance that in our efforts to commend to mankind the excellence of a Government resting on the popular will we shall have beyond the American continent a steadfast ally. Immediately after the ceremonyion Bedloes Island the Pre- &dent left for Washington, where he arrived at eleven o'clock last night.

LODGE DINNER.—On Saturday evening, the " Shepherds by Night" Lodge held their annual dinner at the Nag's Head Hotel. There were about 23 members present, and the catering of Mr. Thomas Winstanley, the host, gave mach satisfaction. After dinner Bro. F. J Leigh, W.M., who pre- sided, proposed the usual loyal toasts, which were duly honoured. P.M. Bro. George Astall proposed the" Shep- herds by night Lodge," which was responded to by the Secretary (Bro. G. H. Leigh), who said that the funds of the lodge had doubled during the last five years, and now amounted to £l2O. The number of members was 40, and the deaths were six in the 16 years during which the lodge had been established. Altogether the lodge was in a pros- perous condition, both financially and, numerically. During the past year they had only paid one week's sick pay out of the funds. He begged to thank them heartily for the man- ner in which they had received the, toast. The remaining toasts proposed were the " Warrington District of Shep- herds," "The Treasurer (P.M. Bro. Robert Ditchfielo7 and" The Chairman." During the course of the evening a number of songs, duets, and readings, were rendered toy Bros. Rance, E. Cliffe, Rowles, Davies, Ratcliffe, C. Barrow, R. Ditchfeld, and the Chairman. Mr. W. Rouse accom- panied on the piano.

Tomas Marshall, of Newton. There were good congregations, and a fair sum was realised.

ANTI-VAcCINATION.—During the present week sum- monses have been served on the following persons for breaches of the VaccinA ;on Act :—Arthur Doff:Loden, War- grave-road; Charles Kelly, queen-street Joseph Blake- more, Earlestown •, and Edward Dickens, Earlestown. The cases will be heard at the petty sessions, to be held at the Newton Town Hall to-day (Saturday). 1 REFUSING TO Qurr.—&t the Walrington Oecasionat Court House on Thursday, Daniel Garnett, late of Wood- street, Earlestown, was c-,:ged under a warrant with being 'disorderly upon the premises of Mr. William Melling, the New Market Inn, Earlestown, and refusing to leave when requested, on the 16th of July lat. The prisoner was sum- moned to appear at the Newton Petty Sessions on the 28th August last, but failed to do so, and a warrant for his ap- prehension was granted. He was apprehended at Leigh.— The prisoner was remanded until the Newton Petty See- sion.s,

Wye Lin-7 CoNcautG.A.TioNAL CHunc-H—On Sun- , day evening at short popular seryice was held in this church, the address being delivered by the Rev. J. Yonge from the words, "The wages of sin—or the gift of God: Which shall it be?" There was a very large congregation, the chapel being tilled. The hymns sung were those of Sankey and Moody, and after the address Mrs. R. H. Pearson. sang the solo, "Choose ye the day." FUNERAL OF THE LATE Mn. MATHER.—The re- mains of the late " Captain " Mather, who died last week under circumstan eel previously reported, were on Saturday interred in the cemetery. The funeral , ceremony was conducted by the Rev. E. C. E. Carle- ton, and a large number of relatives and friends I walked in the funeral procession. The thorough- :fare between the residence of the deceased in But- termarket-street, and tile cemetery was lined with spectators, and blinds were drusvn at many of the shops and houses. RETIREMENT OF THE REV. M. SCHONBERG.—OW ing to ill-health the Rev. M. Sch6nberg has decided to resign the living of St. Peters Mission, which has been held by him for years. Mr. Schonberg's services in the populous district in which his mission is placed have-been of an important though unostentatious character, and his retirement will be deeply regret- ted. It has already been suggested by Councillor John Platt thap Mr. Schonberg's devoted work amongst the poor should have a fitting recognition, and he has offered .ClO as a first subscription, and promises to increase the amount if necessary. ACADEMY-STREET MISSION ROOM.—On Sundayl Mr. J. J. Bradshaw, of Crewe, conducted three ser- vices in connection with the school and church of this Mission. There were good congregations morning: and afternoon, and in the evening the' building was filled_ At each service, in addition to the congregational hymns, anthems and hymns were sung by the children and choir, assisted by friends from other churches. Mr. Joseph Cotterill con- ducted, and Mr.. W.. B. Thornton accompanied on the harmonium.. The collections, which were for the school and the new chapel building fund, amounted tos.C7 4s. 104.

"THE HOME OF THE: ORANGR3rAN."—At the first ordinary meeting of Holy Trinity Literary and De- bating Society, held in the school-room in Museum- street, on Monday evening, Mr. Arthur Bennett read a paper under the title, "The Home of the Orange- man, giving an account of a summer holiday in the North of Ireland. A discussion followed the read- ing of the paper. On the motion of the Secretary, seconded by 3fr. H. J. Longton,, and supported by succeeding speakers, a vote of thanks was heartily accorded Mr. Bennett, who briefly replied. Several new members were elected..

LIBERAL CLUB DEBATING SOCTXTY.—A well at- tended meeting of the members of Liberal club was held on Thursday evening, with the view of form- ing a debating society in connection with the club. It was resolved. that one-be established, and a provisional committee was appointed to draw up rules and regulations.. This- com-mitte is expected to report to a meeting of. the members on Thursday next, when arrangements will be made for holding the first debate. It is intended that members shall have an opportunity of bringing their friends-to the debates, and,, as there will be a wide range of subjects,. it is expected that there will be some highly interesting meetings. It is to be hoped that there will be a good attendance next Thursday evening, and that the-members will enter into the undertaking with spirit and enterprise. lIENNY READINGS AT LATcHFortn,—The second of a series of Penny Readings was held in Wash-lane school-room, on Monday evening.. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and, in opening the proceedings, said that their good vicar, being always ready to promote any. movement for the good of the people, had reorganised the Penny Readings with great success. He (the Mayor) was. glad they had been re-introduced, as there were. no amusements, such as theatres, &c., in, the village, and the vicar ought to be congratulated ow trying to do what he could to amuse the inhabitants. The programme consisted of piano duets by. Miss Reynolds and Miss P. Reynolds, Mrs. J: Reynolds and Mr. Crossley; songs by Messrs. J. H. Warburton, Grounds, and Master l‘r. Knight; readings-by the May-N.; recita- tions by Mr. Brierley, and a- cornet solo by Mr. Grounds. The singing of the National Anthem brought the programme to, a close: Mr.. 11. Woods proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, and the ladies and gentlemen who had. contributed to the evening's enjoyment. The proposition was heartily carried, and the Mayor briefly responded. THE WARRINGTON HARRIERS:—The members of this club had their usual run on Saturday, 17 taking part in it. The hares, T. Gleave, J. Monks, and li. Maddock, were despatched with the paper at three o'clock, the pack folio wing at 3-30,, with J. Dum- bell acting as pace. R. Sherlock, T. Locker, D. Walsh, G. Ratcliffe, A. Ratcliffe, G.. Stokes, J. Burke, J. Bowen, J. Wadden, J.. Lowe, A.. McGowan, J. Bellian, and J. Massey also ran, the captain acting as whip. The-trail lay ;through Arpley-fields and over Walton Arches along the canal for about a mile. Here the pack ran about three miles out of their way, not being able to find- the. trail. They then came across it again- along the road to Moore. Then it lay towards Daresbury through Rose Wood, and came on the road again at Hatton. Here a turn was made for home by Hill Cliffe and Lower Wal- ton, and along Wilderspool Causeway.. The hares arrived home at 4-36, and the pack at 5-10, D. Walsh being first, R. Sherlock second,. J. Massey third, T. Locker fourth, G. Ratcliffe fifth, .I. Burke sixth, and the rest close up. The distance run was about twelve miles. Sale at HAYNRS'S of Boots and Shoes, to make room for winter goods-42 and 44, Horsemarket-street.--,A dd. THEFT FROM A FOOTBALL GROUND.—At the

Borough Court, on Thursday, two lads named-JOII-n- McCone (12), and Edward Rooney (.10), were brought up in custody on,a,charge of stealing two blue worsted football jerSeys, value 9s, the pro- perty of Thomas Pym Williamson, son of the Rev, -T: P. Williamson, Thelwall, and of

-ohn Johnson, another youth. There was a second charge against Rooney of. stealing 4s lid in money from the house of Mrs Holmes, 3, Jolley's Court, Brick-street. The particulars, as stated by Chief Constable Hunt, were to the effect that the prose- cutors are pupils at the Grammar School. in con- nection with the school is a ground at Arpley used as a football field, where there is a pavilion in which football dress is kept. The police discovered two jerseys at the houses of the prisoners, which it was afterwards found had been stolen from the pavilion mentiOned. As prisoner Rooney was found to have purchased a football and a pair of foot- ball slippers, inquiries were instituted as to how he became possessed of the money, which led oto the discovery that he had stolen 4s lid from the house of Mrs Holmes. The Bench directed that McCone be confined for three days and receive six strokes with the birch rod, and that Rooney be confined for the same Pericd, and receive eight strokes. _

' CoNslawATivE BANQUET.—On Thursday evening a complimentary banquet to Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., took place in the Assembly Room at the Lion Hotel, Warrington. Colonel J. Ireland-Black- , burne, of Hale, presided; and amongst the gentle- men present were Lord Gerard, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., and Mr. T. W. Legh, M.P. for the New- ton Division; Mr. Gilbert Greenall; the Mayor of ' Warrington (Alderman Harrison); Col. Greenall, ,Major Litton, Captain Reynolds, Captain Nicholson, the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. W. Quekett), the Revs. S: Wilkinson and E. C. E. Carleton, and Messrs. Robert Davies, Peter Stubs, Edward Green- all, Robert Pierpoint, W. Sharp, Dr. Mackie, Joseph Davies, -Warrington WOod, John White, W. C. Jones, S, M. Webster, J. Tinsley, Henry Appleton, J. 11, Buckton, Major Pickmere, and others. After the loyal and patriotic toasts had been proposed from the chair, Alderman Joseph Davies gave "-The Bishops and Clergy of all denomi- nations," to which the Rector responded. Dr. -Mackie proposed "The Army, Nay; and Reserve Forces," and Colonel Greenall responded —The-toast of the evening, "Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, M.P.," was proposed by the Chairman, and in responding, Sir Gilbert Greenall said he had been intimately mixed up with political occurrences in Warrington since the year 1847, and he could say without fear of contradiction, that during the whole of that time be had not given one vote which was not given conscientiously. (Cheers.) If he knew himself, he was not a man merely to give a popular vote. He had a country to serve, and he had principles to maintain. What he had ' been he would still strive to be, and with God's blessing he would never depart from his principles and his political sentiments, which were well known to his fellow-townsmen and constituents. (Cheers.)—Captain Reynolds. proposed "The In- vited Guests," to which Lord Gerard and Mr. W. Legh responded.—A number of other toasts were drunk in the course of the evening. BOROUGH OF ST. HELENS.—TO THE BURGESSES OIP WINDLE WARD. LAMM AND GENTLEMEN,—At the request of a large and in- fluential Deputation of Electors of your Ward, I have con_ sented to become a Candidate for the vacancy in the Council created by the necessary retirement of Mr. J. 0. Gamble, on his election as Alderman. Residing and carrying on business in your Ward, as well as being an owuer of property in it, my interests are, of course, identical with yours, and are completely bound up in the pros- perity of the Borough. If elected a member of the Council, I shell endeavour, by clase attention to the work of the committees, under whose supervision the town's money is laid out, to see that no ex- travagance takes place, and that every possible economy is practised. The business of the Corporation ought, in my opinion, to be man aged on strictly commercial principles. Nothing should be spent but what is necessary for good government; and for every penny expended we ought to get full value. These, at all ev:-.nts, are th, ideas upon which I shall act if successful in my candidature; and, trusting to be favoured with the support of the Ward, I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, HENRY MARTIN. London House,lChurch-st red, St. Helens, 20th 0ct.,1888.

IMPORTANT LETTER FROM MR. GLADSTONE.—The COE— tral News says Mr. Gladstone has written a letTer to Mr. Andrew Reid, author of " Why am I a Radical ?"in an- swer to a request from Mr. Reid that he would contribute to a new book edited by that gentleman, which will very shortly be published by Messrs. Swan, Sonnenschein and Co., under the title of "The New Liberal Programme." The letter is as follows:—"Hawarden Castle, October 15th, 1886. My Dear Sir,—l am obliged to make an answer to your kind letter which I fear will disappoint you. My friends forget my years. I bold on to politics in the hope of possibly helping to settle the Irish question, but the general operations both of part) and of particular subjects I am obliged and intended to leave in the hands of others. With all good wishes to the Liberal cause, I remain, yours very faithfully, W. E. GLADSTONE." The "New Liberal programme" contains articles by Mr. Labouchere, Lord Thurlow, Lord Kilcoursie, Mr. Jacob:Bright, Sir E. J. Reed, Sir W. Lawson, and other prominent members of the party.
